Game Theory × Health Insurance

The New Equilibrium

How the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson exposed a catastrophic failure in the game theory of American health insurance, and why the industry's old equilibrium was always unsustainable.

Last updated August 21, 2026

~413 min read · 550 sources

Key Findings
  • ■UnitedHealthcare's ACA marketplace denial rate was 33%, nearly twice the 19% industry average. Per-contract CMS-0057-F data shows its volume-weighted MA denial rate is 13.5% (contradicting its "95.4% approved" headline), with a 36× spread across contracts. Its nH Predict algorithm had an alleged 90% error rate, but only 0.2% of policyholders ever appealed. CMS plan year 2024 data shows UNH's ACA denial rate dropped from 34.2% to 19.1%, converging to exactly the national average. Of 8.8 million denied claims industry-wide, 77% were administrative, not medical necessity. The first standardized cross-market KFF analysis (Aug 13, 2026) confirmed UNH's 17% MA denial rate is the highest among major insurers (3.4x Elevance), appeal overturn rates of 67% in MA expose systematic wrongful denial, and the AELP now proposes a federal PA ban with 71% voter support.
  • ■The shooting destroyed $190 billion in UNH market capitalization, forced its CEO to resign, and triggered nearly 60 insurers to sign reform pledges eliminating 6.5 million prior authorizations. His replacement, Stephen Hemsley, received $60.95 million in total compensation (748:1 CEO-to-worker pay ratio, vs. Witty's 348:1), including a one-time $60 million stock option grant that cliff-vests in three years, creating a compensating differential for endogenous assassination risk that simultaneously selects for operational continuity and aligns CEO wealth with MCR reduction. The defense's 24-hour reversal of its psychiatric defense (EED withdrawal June 17-18, 2026) and subsequent pivot to a federal guilty plea with no deal reveals a Bayesian signaling game analyzed through Harsanyi's (1967-68) framework of games with incomplete information.
  • ■Fourteen states enacted binding restrictions on AI-driven claim denials across 2025 and 2026, with the 2026 wave alone producing seven new laws. Seven federal bills are moving through Congress, ranging from transparency mandates to an outright Medicare Advantage PA ban, with a seventh (H.R. 9734, the Protecting Patients from Automated Denials Act) requiring physician review of every AI-assisted denial and earning AMA endorsement. But the legislative pipeline faces a temporal trap: the CMS Marketplace Integrity Rule taking effect August 25, 2026, will remove millions from coverage through administrative action faster than Congress can pass protections, creating a shrinking denominator that reduces the reach of every reform still in the pipeline.
  • ■A Fermi estimate based on MSK, Cleveland Clinic, and AMA data suggests 2,000 to 5,000 statistical lives saved per year from post-shooting reforms, valued at $28 to $71 billion.
  • ■Seven formal game theory concepts explain why the old equilibrium collapsed: from asymmetric risk tolerance to the moral hazard of martyrdom. New evidence shows PA burdens fall disproportionately on Black, Hispanic, and lower-income patients, while CMS fines of $1.54M across 14 insurers reveal enforcement penalties below the indifference threshold. Hospitals have entered the game as a coordinated third player, filing $100M+ lawsuits against insurers, with a federal court rejecting Aetna's attempt to compel arbitration and exclude AHA's amicus brief in the Jefferson Health "level of severity" challenge (Aug 5, 2026). CMS's own WISeR pilot, deploying AI-driven PA in Traditional Medicare with a 62% initial approval rate, embodies the Regulator's Paradox: the referee has entered the game on the same side as the player it polices. The industry's voluntary June 2025 pledge is fracturing: eight signatories backed out of technology commitments, no federal dashboards exist, and a bipartisan Senate investigation with subpoena authority has demanded internal records from the three largest MA insurers. Meanwhile, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act cuts $990B from Medicaid over a decade and projects 5-10M coverage losses, and the expiration of enhanced ACA premium tax credits has triggered a parallel collapse: effectuated Marketplace enrollment dropped from 22.1M to 19.2M (-13%), with KFF projecting 8.2M additional uninsured from ACA changes alone, disproportionately hitting Southern red states (Florida 2.2M, Texas 1.7M, Georgia 690K), shrinking the insured population from two directions even as PA rules improve for those who remain. Marketplace insurers are now proposing a median 14% premium increase for 2027, the second consecutive year of double-digit hikes; if approved, premiums will have risen more than one-third since 2025. A federal court in Maryland stayed 8 provisions of the 2027 ACA benefit rule on July 16 (Columbus II), but the underlying premium spiral continues. A coalition of 21 attorneys general filed suit on August 3, 2026, challenging the 2027 ACA benefit rule that projects 2M additional coverage losses by 2027 and 5M by 2030. UNH has spent $8.7B acquiring home health and hospice providers (LHC Group + Amedisys), hedging against PA reform by vertically integrating into care delivery, with the DOJ requiring the largest outpatient healthcare divestiture in merger history (164 facilities, $528M revenue), but the Warren-Hawley Break Up Big Medicine Act now threatens to make that entire vertical integration strategy illegal, creating a two-front regulatory war where both the denial model and the ownership fallback face simultaneous legislative assault. AI-powered appeal tools and social media amplification are collapsing the information asymmetry that sustained the 0.2% appeal rate: Milgrom's unraveling result predicts that as appeal costs approach zero, the denial rate must converge to the clinically defensible floor. The defense fund ($1.6M+ from 40,000+ donors, median $15, nearing $1.75M goal) reveals a solved collective action problem: the shooting served as a Schelling focal point that collapsed Olson's free-riding barrier. Remarkably, 177 donors contributed $5,300 in the weekend after Mangione's guilty plea, demonstrating that the focal point survives criminal resolution. Mangione's open plea itself, entered without a deal while prosecutors seek life, is rational only as a multi-forum optimization (Bernheim & Whinston, 1990): unilateral cooperation in the federal forum is the dominated strategy in isolation but triggers a double jeopardy motion that may eliminate the state case entirely, converting a two-front legal war into a single sentencing hearing with a 24-to-30-year guideline anchor. The defense's demand to broadcast the state trial live inverts the standard defendant-publicity dynamic: when 10-20% of the public believes the killing was justified, maximum visibility becomes a jury nullification mechanism, and the prosecution's anonymous jury order and warnings about "spectator misconduct" confirm the strategic assessment (Fearon's audience costs framework applied to trial information environments). The December 2026 sentencing calendar creates a backward induction game visible to all players: the DA's Oct 9 response, the defense's Oct 30 reply, and Carro's double jeopardy ruling (Dec 10) shape Garnett's sentencing calculus (Dec 18), while Mangione's sworn allocution functions as a dual-use commitment device that strengthens the double jeopardy claim precisely because it is irrevocable, but becomes prosecution evidence if the strategy fails. The defense's August 15 filing accusing federal and state prosecutors of forming a "cartel" to circumvent double jeopardy protections maps directly onto Stigler's (1964) theory of cartel instability: documented cross-jurisdictional information flows (DA Seidemann's letter to Judge Carro warning about the federal plea) constitute the coordination evidence, and Mangione's uncoordinated open plea was the competitive defection that collapsed the prosecutorial equilibrium. And the legal system itself functions as an attrition shield: a $2.1B Medicare overbilling case dismissed after 15 years, provider antitrust plaintiffs forced into individual arbitration, and three simultaneous DOJ probes (the criminal investigation now broadened from Medicare billing to Optum Rx PBM practices and physician payments) producing headlines without penalties. The PBRT settlement wave reveals the endgame of the denial calculus: Anthem settled with ~140 cancer patients for $3.625M ($26K/patient) for treatments costing $30K-$95K, proving denial remains the dominant strategy even when the insurer loses, because settlement costs are less than claim costs, and most denied patients never sue. CMS plan year 2024 data reveals the convergence trap: UNH's denial rate dropped 15 points to 19.1%, converging precisely to the national average rather than below it, and 77% of remaining denials are administrative rather than clinical. The market rewarded this with UNH stock rising 0.55% on the day of Mangione's guilty plea, then declining to $384.85 by Aug 20 before recovering to $390 on Aug 21 (down 2.9% from the $401.73 plea-day close), while 61% of Americans are simultaneously patients and UNH shareholders through index fund ownership. The shooting also created a cross-industry security contagion: S&P 500 companies providing executive security perks rose 47.6% (to 31.3%) from 2021 to 2024, with average spending doubling to $94,276, and the threat-model update propagated to semiconductors (Broadcom: $1.37M), defense (Lockheed Martin: $1.34M), and pharmaceuticals (J&J mandated armed drivers for all executive travel). The 2025 proxy season confirmed the spending is compounding, not reverting: over one-third of S&P 500 now provide security perks (up 12.8% YoY), median value $130,468 (up 20%), with Oscar Health's proxy explicitly citing "the current climate and security risk profile for executives in the health insurance industry" to justify $361K for its CEO, and BlackRock updating its voting guidelines to scrutinize security perquisites. The MGMA 2026 Regulatory Burden Report reveals the system's hidden tax: 40% of practices now employ 3+ full-time administrative staff per physician for PA alone, 95% report increasing burden, 77% cite it as a major driver of physician burnout, and a 2026 JAMA Neurology scoping review found half of MS patients waiting for PA approval experienced relapses during the delay. Provider exit, analyzed through Hirschman's (1970) framework, is converting invisible administrative overhead into visible provider deserts. And while medical/surgical PA reform accelerates, a GAO report reveals the shadow system: 8 of 9 major MA organizations require PA for behavioral health using internal criteria CMS has never audited, behavioral health denial rates run 2-3x the medical average, and the only federal enforcement mechanism (MHPAEA) has been formally suspended by the Trump administration, creating a strategic displacement channel where insurers can reduce visible denials while shifting pressure to a patient population with the least political voice, but states are inverting the predicted race to the bottom: Georgia alone issued $24.85M in parity fines to 11 insurers (Jan 2026), exceeding all CMS civil monetary penalties from 2021-2024 combined, with Washington, Pennsylvania, and Connecticut escalating in parallel, while Rep. Kean (R-NJ) introduced the Mental Health Parity Enforcement and Funding Act (H.R. 9551) after disclosing his own hospitalization for depression (Besley & Case 1995 yardstick competition: federal retreat eliminated the enforcement ceiling, not the floor). Gold card programs, pioneered by Texas in 2021 and adopted by 11 states, attempt to fix the mechanism through reputation-based exemption (90% approval threshold earns PA waiver), but cover only ~20% of the Texas market (state-regulated plans) and are described as "underwhelming" in practice. An Annals of Internal Medicine study (Stanford/Georgetown, May 2026) exposed the structural reason: across four major insurers, only 3% of billing codes requiring PA overlap, more than half are unique to a single insurer, and none share the same approval criteria, meaning 97% of any reform effort must be duplicated per-insurer (Hayek's distributed-knowledge thesis inverted as a defensive weapon). Only one in three physicians trusts the reform pledges will produce meaningful change (AMA May 2026). Eighteen states passed PA reform legislation in 2025 alone (Health Affairs), yet 36 states have no binding AI restrictions, creating a regulatory patchwork that national insurers can arbitrage. The Consolidated Appropriations Act 2026 (signed Feb 3) enacted the most significant PBM reform in history: rebate pass-through, enhanced disclosures, and flat-fee mandates effective Jan 2028, closing the prescription drug gap that federal PA rules originally left open. PA consumes an estimated $35 billion annually in administrative spending, with nursing time alone equivalent to 100,000 full-time roles. Beyond claims denial, the surveillance dividend reveals a third extraction stage: BCBS embedded TikTok, Meta, Google, and LinkedIn tracking pixels on the website used by 5.5 million federal employees, monetizing the behavioral data patients generate while researching their coverage options and conditions (Aug 7, 2026 ruling; California privacy claim survives), while Allina Health operated patient-portal pixel tracking for eight years ($12.5M settlement). And the governance apparatus itself has collapsed: a 224-page shareholder derivative suit (Aug 2026) alleges UNH directors secured $237 million in insider stock sales while concealing systemic misconduct, including shutting down an internal audit that found $200 million in unsupported Medicare billing and weakening cybersecurity by switching from CrowdStrike to Microsoft Defender before the Change Healthcare breach, while a faith-based investor coalition (300+ Interfaith Center members) was blocked from even voting on patient-impact analysis at the 2026 proxy under the SEC's "ordinary business" exclusion, and Massachusetts AG Campbell is suing for $100M+ in Medicaid upcoding fraud (treble damages up to $300M), and the largest-ever ERISA fiduciary settlement ($69M) revealed the CFO personally overruling an investment committee to benefit a business partner, demonstrating that the mechanisms meant to catch self-dealing were controlled by the actors they were meant to constrain; shareholder voice is being fragmented across four incompatible channels (derivative suits, securities fraud, proxy proposals, public signaling), each defeated by a different institutional mechanism (Hirschman 1970 / Maug 1998 shareholder monitoring paradox). And a parallel denial front is expanding at the pharmacy counter: a Johns Hopkins/AEI study in JAMA (July 2026) found brand-name drug rejections surged 67% from 2018 to 2024 (24.3% to 40.7%), with 48.4% of denied patients never filling any medication in the same therapeutic class within 90 days, GLP-1 drugs hitting 85% rejection rates, and the pharmacy counter functioning as a strategic attrition mechanism where the patient stands alone without an institutional advocate (Klemperer switching-cost framework). And behind the denial system sits a second mortality filter: high-deductible health plans produce 46% worse survival among cancer survivors (Barnes et al. 2026, JAMA Network Open), Medicaid loss kills 2,900+ through administrative churn alone (Roberts et al. 2025, NEJM), and insurance disenrollment increases overdose mortality 56% among opioid patients (JAMA Psychiatry 2026), inverting Arrow's (1963) risk-transfer theorem so that patients pay premiums for the privilege of bearing the very uncertainty insurance was designed to absorb. Across four treatment categories in 2026, the reprocess ratchet reveals litigation as the sole effective coverage expansion mechanism: UNH reversed "experimental" classifications for prosthetics (1,000-patient Trujillo class, 9 years of denial), lumbar artificial disc replacement (coverage position changed mid-litigation), lipedema (Judge Alsup rejected initial settlement and demanded unlimited coverage), and residential behavioral health ($1.4M ERISA class), with Samuelson's (1938) revealed preference theory exposing the original classifications as strategic rather than clinical. And leaked internal Optum documents (ProPublica, May 2026) reveal the mechanism in its most concentrated form: while UnitedHealthcare publicly announces 66% pediatric PA reductions and behavioral health coaching expansion, internal playbooks simultaneously pursue "market-specific action plans" to limit autistic children's access to ABA therapy through provider network terminations, duration-based denial criteria that contradict the company's own clinical references, and "rigorous utilization management" targeting ~10,000 Medicaid children across two dozen states, with the public reform providing strategic cover for private cost-cutting on the most vulnerable population in the system (Spence/Crawford-Sobel signal decoupling). And the extraction operates bidirectionally: Kaiser Permanente's $556M False Claims Act settlement (Jan 2026, largest MA fraud case in history) reveals that insurers simultaneously inflate revenue by adding unsupported diagnoses (~500,000 codes, ~$1B in improper Medicare payments, physician bonuses tied to coding targets) and minimize payouts through claim denials. Tullock's (1967) rent-seeking framework applied to this dual mechanism predicts that enforcement against one vector (denial-rate reporting) will accelerate exploitation of the other (risk-score inflation), unless both sides of the extraction are subject to simultaneous regulatory constraint. The supply chain extends beyond insurers: $950 million in combined FCA settlements across seven entities (Kaiser $556M, Aetna $117.7M, DxID $100M, Seoul Medical $62.85M, Oak Street $60M, Matrix/HealthFair $56.5M, Complete Health $14.1M) documents an intermediary ecosystem where MSOs, coding vendors, home health assessment companies, and patient acquisition platforms each had independent contractual incentives to inflate risk scores; Akerlof's (1970) adverse selection model predicts the market selects for the most aggressive coders because conservative vendors generate lower revenue and lose business (the market for lemons applied to the MA coding vendor supply chain). The diagnostic device market inverts this further: UNH's nationwide deployment from 2017 of Semler Scientific's QuantaFlo PAD test, which had a 66% false positive rate and used technology Medicare has explicitly barred since 1980, demonstrates adverse diagnostic selection: when the insurer profits from false positives through inflated risk scores, the market selects for inaccuracy ($36.95M in FCA settlements, with the Part C whistleblower case against UNH proceeding into litigation). And the turnaround celebrated by Wall Street reveals the deepest paradox: UNH's Q2 2026 MCR of 86.7% (down from 89.4%) means roughly $2.3 billion less spent on patient care per quarter, while Hemsley replaced half the top 100 executives, exited 109 counties (2.9 million MA enrollees forced to find new plans nationally per JAMA), and raised guidance to $19.50-$20.00 EPS. The capital market rewards care reduction as "margin recovery" at the same time the political market demands care expansion through PA reform. The company satisfies both through signal separation: PA eliminations are visible and countable; MCR improvement is aggregate and quarterly. A company can eliminate millions of PAs and still reduce total care spending by exiting the markets and populations that generate the highest claims. And the $16 billion annual Star Ratings quality bonus system itself has collapsed as a mechanism: the Clover Health v. HHS ruling (May 2026) invalidated 20 measures and moved one plan from 3.5 to 4.5 Stars (~$120M in bonuses) without any change in care delivered, triggering $400M+ in cascading suits from Elevance ($115M), SCAN ($125M), Alignment ($50M), and CareFirst ($32M), with CMS simultaneously appealing to the Eleventh Circuit while applying a one-way ratchet that only raised ratings (never lowered them) for other contracts, and the ACHP demanding that this hold-harmless methodology be locked in for 2027 (strategic complementarity in cascading litigation: Bulow, Geanakoplos & Klemperer 1985). The industry is suing to inflate quality scores while resisting quality measurement of its denials. And the Lokken discovery order (Mar 9, 2026) has opened the algorithmic black box: a federal court compelled UNH to produce documents across six categories covering nH Predict's development, financial benefits, and employee incentives, creating a disclosure cascade where information forced into the open on one litigation front becomes available to the Senate subcommittee, CMS regulators, and state legislators simultaneously (Dye 1985 / Shin 2003). And precision medicine reveals the PA system's deepest structural failure: a JAMA Network Open study (Kang et al., 2025) found that cancer-related NGS claim denial rates rose from 16.8% to 27.4% after Medicare expanded coverage, with 50+ gene panels denied at 3x the rate of narrow tests, Anthem hereditary cancer panels denied at 40-80%, and children's exome sequencing denied at 25.7% by private insurers, while the Staffingly 2026 PA Burden Report quantifies the appeal gap that sustains the system: 80.7% of challenged MA denials are overturned, but only 11.5% are ever challenged, and a JAMA Internal Medicine study (Bruch et al., UChicago, Apr 2026) of 51,394 New York external appeals found 46.7% overturned overall and 78.4% for home health services, confirming through the largest independent dataset that the denial system functions as a war of attrition (Maynard Smith 1974) sustained by cost asymmetry rather than clinical accuracy (Arrow's 1962 information paradox applied to diagnostic innovation). And the academic convergence is now complete: the Columbia Law Review (Ziegler 2026), Nature's npj Digital Medicine (Raza et al. 2026, Harvard/Duke/UIUC), and the NAIC's own survey of 93 companies across 16 states have independently reached structurally identical conclusions about AI-driven denial practices. The NAIC data reveals that 84% of health insurers use AI, 68% for PA processing, but only 12% admit using it to deny, while 14% use AI to infer sensitive data including race. The 12%-vs.-68% gap is the survey's most important finding: Aumann's (1976) Agreement Theorem applied to the multi-disciplinary convergence means any rational decision-maker exposed to the full evidence base must arrive at the same posterior, and continued regulatory inaction can no longer be attributed to epistemic uncertainty. And the largest missing player in the reform coalition is the employer: 155 million Americans get coverage through employer-sponsored plans, but only 7% of companies track how often employees delay care due to insurer actions (Stanford 2025), while 40% of those employees are already delaying treatment they cannot afford (Paytient 2026) and 21% experienced a coverage denial in the past year (Commonwealth Fund), creating a bilateral monitoring failure where the entity with the contractual leverage to discipline insurers does not measure the harm its employees absorb. And the international comparison frames the entire system as a global outlier: US administrative costs consume $2,497 per capita (Papanicolas et al. 2018, JAMA), more than four times Canada's $551, funding an $812 billion annual Billing and Insurance-Related overhead (Woolhandler et al. 2020, Annals of Internal Medicine) that no other developed nation maintains. The Commonwealth Fund (2024) ranks the US last among 10 high-income countries on access, equity, and outcomes despite highest spending. Twenty-eight of 38 OECD nations achieve universal coverage without PA-scale gatekeeping, not because their policymakers were wiser but because their institutional paths never passed through the employer-sponsored insurance accident and managed care revolution that locked the US into its current equilibrium (Arthur 1989 / North 1990). And the arbitration paradox reveals that even legislation designed to protect patients from insurer pricing power can be co-opted: the Fifth Circuit's en banc ruling (Aug 11, 2026) struck down the No Surprises Act's QPA calculation methodology for including "ghost rates" (placeholder rates for unprovided services) and excluding provider bonuses, finding the agencies had "upended" the dispute resolution process; arbitrators had been choosing rates above the deflated QPA in 85% of resolved disputes, and it took four years and six successive lawsuits by TMA to partially correct a benchmark that systematically subsidized insurer payment positions (Kahneman-Tversky anchoring bias applied to mechanism design). And the first per-insurer cross-market KFF data reveals the calibration paradox: UNH's appeal overturn rates vary from 81% in Medicaid to 60% in MA to 38% in ACA, meaning denial quality (measured by defensibility on appeal) tracks population vulnerability rather than clinical appropriateness; KFF's own analysis warns that the percentage-only reporting mandate obscures absolute denial volumes, that PA determinations per enrollee are inversely related to denial rates (making per-enrollee denial counts similar across insurers with divergent percentages), and that gold card programs mechanically inflate reported denial rates for reform-oriented insurers (Ramsey 1927 inverse elasticity pricing applied to administrative barriers). And a broader MA exit cascade is underway: Humana is dropping plans covering 600,000 members, Presbyterian Healthcare Services is exiting after a $568M operating loss, Clear Spring Health is shutting down MA entirely, Molina is cutting prescription drug plans, and Providence Health Plan is winding down after failing to find a national carrier to absorb its MA business (10% of all MA enrollees had to disenroll heading into 2026 per JAMA), revealing through Hirschman's (1970) exit-voice-loyalty framework that when denial reform makes the old model unprofitable, insurers choose market abandonment over operational reform, concentrating survivors in geographies where the equilibrium denial rate is already profitable. Meanwhile, Indiana has begun carving nursing home patients out of Medicaid managed care entirely after 100 days, choosing to remove the intermediary from the game rather than regulate it (Tirole 1988 vertical separation), with Michigan and Nebraska pursuing similar reforms. But as incumbents flee, a non-traditional entrant is arriving: Costco announced an "enhanced strategic partnership" with SCAN Health Plan on August 18, 2026, to offer Costco-branded Medicare Advantage plans, the warehouse retailer's first entry into the $600+ billion MA market, leveraging consumer trust that incumbent insurers have spent decades eroding (Tirole 1988 entry theory applied to a market destabilized by the exit cascade). And a peer-reviewed JAMA Health Forum microsimulation (Basu et al., Waymark/UNC, Jul 16, 2026) projects the mortality cost of the coverage contraction: for every 100,000 people losing Medicaid, 13-14 excess deaths and 810-924 preventable hospitalizations annually, scaling to up to 2,284 excess deaths and 145,000+ preventable hospitalizations by 2034 under CBO projections of 7.6M-14.4M newly uninsured; a separate Annals of Internal Medicine study (Gaffney et al., Harvard/CUNY, Jun 2025) projects 16,642 medically preventable deaths annually from the House bill's Medicaid provisions alone, with 7.6M newly uninsured, 1.9M losing a physician, and 380,270 women missing mammograms, making it the most comprehensive single mortality estimate to date. And the regulatory apparatus itself is being deliberately dismantled: the Trump administration suspended the CY 2025 MA final rule requirements for health equity expertise on UM Committees and plan-level PA reporting by population, eliminating the first mechanism CMS had built to detect whether denials disproportionately affect disabled, low-income, and dually eligible enrollees (who face up to 2x denial rates). At the same moment, the HHS OIG's first-ever behavioral health PA audit found 0 of 100 sampled Medicaid denials met all federal requirements, a 100% non-compliance rate at the highest-volume denier in a major state. The information infrastructure that would have made disparate denial patterns visible was removed precisely when the first evidence of systemic failure was emerging (Myerson's 1981 mechanism design applied to regulatory information suppression). And the reforms themselves are becoming structurally irreversible: dismantled PA infrastructure, enacted state laws, published transparency data, compelled litigation discovery, and a 71% voter mandate create a hysteresis band where the sunk costs of reversal exceed the benefits of reimposition for any individual firm, and collective reversal faces the same Olson free-rider barrier that prevented collective reform before the shooting (Dixit 1989 / Arthur 1989 path dependence applied to the post-Thompson equilibrium). And formulary exclusion is emerging as the next displacement mechanism: GoodRx data shows 109 million Americans lost Zepbound coverage and 41 million lost Wegovy coverage through formulary decisions that fall entirely outside PA reform's regulatory reach, while Aetna's $2.56M L-ADR settlement (final approval Jun 5, 2026) confirms that "experimental" classifications blocking FDA-approved procedures for 7+ years are reversed only through litigation, not clinical evidence (Laffont & Tirole 1993 constrained regulatory instruments). And the corruption extends upstream to the enrollment channel itself: the DOJ alleges that CVS/Aetna, Elevance, and Humana paid eHealth, GoHealth, and SelectQuote "hundreds of millions" in illegal kickbacks from 2016 to 2021 to steer Medicare beneficiaries into their plans regardless of suitability, while simultaneously pressuring brokers to enroll fewer disabled seniors, with a federal judge denying all motions to dismiss in March 2026 (Diamond 1971 / Dulleck & Kerschbamer 2006 corrupted search intermediaries). And the market is beginning to route around the intermediary entirely: Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Wellness platform, launched January 2026, connects self-insured employers directly with providers through publicly posted contracts with no PA, no hidden fees, and insurers explicitly barred from participating, while PBGH data shows employer RFP activity tripling from 12% to 37% in two years, signaling that the bilateral monitoring failure documented in the Employer's Blind Spot section is triggering disintermediation rather than reform (Hurwicz 1972 mechanism design applied to structural monitoring failure). And the FTC's August 14 probe of Epic Systems reveals the meta-game beneath every game documented here: the company whose software holds 280 million Americans' medical records and controls 42% of the EHR market is now under antitrust investigation for using its dominant position to block rivals from patient data access, with the Texas AG suing and a federal court allowing Particle Health's antitrust claim to proceed; Epic's Payer Platform mediates the PA data exchange between insurers and providers, making the company a Grossman-Hart (1986) residual-control-rights holder that does not participate in denial decisions directly but structures the information environment in which every payer-provider game is played, while CMS's January 2027 electronic PA mandate was designed to break this infrastructure lock-in through open FHIR APIs, but the largest health systems are the ones most deeply embedded in Epic's ecosystem, and switching costs estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars create Williamson (1975) asset specificity that makes exit practically impossible on any reform-relevant timeline.
Section I

The Facts

On December 4, 2024, UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was shot and killed outside the Hilton Midtown in Manhattan. The words "delay," "deny," and "depose" were carved into the shell casings. Five days later, 26-year-old Luigi Mangione was arrested at a McDonald's in Altoona, Pennsylvania.

What followed was not mourning. An Emerson College poll found 41% of voters aged 18-29 considered the killing "acceptable." NORC found 70% of Americans blamed insurance denials and profits for creating the conditions that led to it. The shooting forced a question the industry had spent decades avoiding: whether its denial practices had engineered the conditions for their own destabilization.

The Pre-Shooting Baseline

Before December 2024, the health insurance industry operated under implicit assumptions about the costs and benefits of aggressive denial. The data made the strategy transparent:

ACA Marketplace In-Network Claim Denial Rates by Insurer (2023)

Among high-volume insurers on the federal marketplace, UnitedHealth Group and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama led with denial rates above 33%, while Kaiser Permanente denied just 6% of in-network claims. The industry average sat at 19%. These figures come from CMS public use files analyzed by KFF, and they capture only marketplace plans, not employer-sponsored or Medicare Advantage coverage.

Read those numbers together. UnitedHealthcare's AI algorithm, nH Predict (acquired via naviHealth in 2020), had what plaintiffs in a 2023 class action described as a 90% error rate, measured by overturn rates on review. But only 0.2% of policyholders ever appealed. The math is brutal: deny aggressively, bet on exhaustion, collect the spread.

When appeals happened, the lawsuit alleges they succeeded overwhelmingly. The system was not making accurate medical decisions. It was making a bet that sick people wouldn't fight back.

UnitedHealth disputes these characterizations. A company spokesperson stated that nH Predict "is not used to make coverage determinations" but rather as "a guide to help us inform providers, families and other caregivers." UNH says its overall claims approval rate is 98% for eligible members with timely, complete, non-duplicate submissions. The company called the KFF marketplace denial data "grossly misleading," noting it represents only about 2% of total claims volume. UnitedHealthcare Newsroom, "Get the facts: How many claims are denied?" / InsuranceNewsNet, Feb 2025

The Financial Reckoning

The shooting's financial impact on UnitedHealth Group was severe and sustained. The stock became a real-time barometer of how markets priced the new reality:

UNH Stock Price: The Cascading Collapse
Dec 4, 2024
Brian Thompson shot and killed outside Hilton Midtown, Manhattan. Stock initially rises, then falls sharply over two sessions as social media backlash explodes.
Dec 9, 2024
Luigi Mangione arrested at McDonald's in Altoona, PA. "Wanted" posters of other healthcare CEOs appear in Manhattan. Companies begin removing executive photos from websites.
Dec 2024
Emerson College poll: 41% of voters age 18-29 find the killing "acceptable." NORC poll: 70% of Americans blame insurance denials and profits for creating conditions that led to the shooting.
Apr 17, 2025
UNH reports Q1 earnings miss (first since 2008). EPS guidance slashed from $29.50-$30.00 to $26.00-$26.50. Stock drops 22.4% in a single day, wiping out $119 billion in market cap. CEO Witty calls results "unusual and unacceptable."
May 7, 2025
Shareholders file class action suit (Faller v. UnitedHealth Group, SDNY No. 25-03799), alleging UNH concealed that backlash-driven reform was eroding profitability.
May 13, 2025
CEO Andrew Witty resigns. All 2025 guidance withdrawn. Stock falls another 17%. Total market cap loss since shooting exceeds $190 billion. Former CEO Stephen Hemsley (age 72) returns.
May 2025
DOJ opens investigation into UnitedHealth Group billing and coding practices. Separately, Change Healthcare cyberattack (Feb 2024) continues generating legal fallout with over 100 lawsuits consolidated in MDL.
Jun 23, 2025
Nearly 60 insurers sign voluntary prior authorization reform pledge with CMS/HHS. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz explains why reform is happening now: "There's violence in the streets over these issues."
Aug 15, 2025
Berkshire Hathaway discloses a $1.6 billion stake in UNH (5 million shares acquired at ~$271 during Q2 2025). Stock surges 14% in a single day. Warren Buffett's purchase, made while UNH was near a 15-year low after losing 50%+ since early 2025, is read as a signal that the crisis is overdone. Other hedge fund managers follow. The stock rallies 37% through year-end.
May 15, 2026
Berkshire Hathaway's Q1 2026 13F filing reveals a complete exit from UNH, all 5 million shares sold at approximately $394 (45% profit in ~9 months). Under new CEO Greg Abel, the rapid flip is read as profit-taking rather than loss of conviction. UNH declines only 2% on the news. The Buffett trade's full arc: in at crisis, out at recovery.
