The equilibrium prediction is a clustering around the mean, not a race to zero, because the scorecard rewards strategic compliance, not clinical excellence. And the 67% appeal overturn rate confirms the scorecard is measuring the wrong thing: it reports denial rates, not wrongful denial rates. A system that denies 12% of requests and reverses 67% of appeals is wrongfully denying approximately 8% of all requests, but the scorecard treats the initial denial and the appeal reversal as separate metrics rather than a single quality indicator.

The Autism Playbook: When Internal Documents Reveal the Mechanism

ProPublica obtained what it described as the strategic playbook for Optum's management of applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy for autistic children covered through Medicaid. The leaked internal documents acknowledge that ABA is the "evidence-based gold standard treatment for those with medically necessary needs." Then they outline how to limit access to it.

The playbook's "key opportunities" include preventing new ABA providers from joining the network, terminating existing ones (including "cost outliers"), and deploying "rigorous utilization management" that produces an "approach to authorizing less units than requested." In some states, the network reduction could impact more than two-fifths of ABA provider groups and up to 19% of patients in therapy. The company calculated this. It is not a side effect of cost management. It is the strategy's intended output.

The population targeted is structurally defenseless. These are children with severe autism covered through Medicaid, the insurance program for the nation's poorest and most vulnerable patients. Under Medicaid managed care, states pay UnitedHealthcare a fixed capitation rate per patient regardless of services used. When the company spends less than the allotment, it keeps the remainder. The incentive to deny is structural, not aberrational. The denominator of autism diagnoses has quadrupled in two decades (from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36), increasing the financial burden the playbook is designed to manage. Optum anticipates spending approximately $290 million on ABA therapy within its Medicaid plans in 2026, with expenses rising $75 million year-over-year. The playbook is the institutional response to a growing financial obligation the company would prefer not to meet.

Benji Menard's case, documented by ProPublica, illustrates the mechanism at the individual level. His clinicians determined he needed 33 hours of weekly ABA therapy to maintain progress. After six years of treatment that had brought him from non-verbal to producing small words and reducing self-injurious behavior, Optum denied the increase. "Your child has been in ABA for six years," the insurer wrote. "After six years, more progress would be expected." Autism experts interviewed by ProPublica called this reasoning fundamentally at odds with professional guidelines for the therapy, which Optum's own clinical criteria reference: "there is no specific limit on the duration of a course of treatment."

What makes this case significant for the game theory analysis is the timing. On May 29, 2026, UnitedHealthcare publicly announced it would eliminate nearly two-thirds of prior authorization requirements for members under age 18 by year-end. On August 18, 2026, UnitedHealthcare announced an expansion of child and family behavioral coaching access to 13 million commercial members. These public signals are Spence-type costly signals: they generate press coverage, policy goodwill, and stock-price stability. The leaked playbook reveals the simultaneous private strategy: while eliminating PA for well-established pediatric procedures with high approval rates (diagnostic imaging, routine surgeries, standard testing), the company is intensifying utilization management on the most expensive behavioral therapy for the most vulnerable children through a separate operational channel. The public reform and the private cost-cutting are not contradictory. They are complementary components of the same optimization: reduce visible friction on low-cost, high-approval services while tightening invisible friction on high-cost, politically invisible services.

Game Theory Concept
Signal Decoupling: Cheap Talk on the Observable Channel, Costly Action on the Hidden One (Spence 1973 / Crawford & Sobel 1982)

In Spence's signaling framework, a costly signal is credible because the signaler incurs real expense. Crawford and Sobel's (1982) cheap talk model demonstrates that when sender and receiver interests diverge, information transmission degrades. The Optum autism playbook reveals a third configuration: the insurer sends a costly signal on the observable channel (eliminating 66% of pediatric PA, generating press, political goodwill, and stock stability) while simultaneously executing the opposite strategy on a hidden channel (intensifying ABA denials, shrinking provider networks, applying duration-based termination criteria for Medicaid children with autism). The game-theoretic innovation is that the visible reform makes the hidden restriction more sustainable, not less. The pediatric PA reduction creates political cover ("we already reformed children's care") that makes legislative scrutiny of ABA-specific denials less likely. The signal is not merely cheap talk. It is strategic concealment dressed as reform. The leaked documents are significant precisely because they collapse the information asymmetry that sustains this dual-channel strategy, converting private institutional knowledge into public domain evidence that shifts the game's information structure.

The advocacy response confirms the legal exposure. Karen Fessel, whose Mental Health and Autism Insurance Project helps families access care, called the tactics "unconscionable and immoral." Attorney Dan Unumb, president of the Autism Legal Resource Center, noted: "Yes, this therapy can be expensive. But solving the problem by denying kids access to medically necessary care is a terrible solution." The federal government affirmed in 2025 that ABA therapy is a protected benefit, and all 50 states require insurance coverage for it. If Optum restricts ABA more stringently than comparable physical care, it may violate the federal mental health parity law under which UnitedHealth already agreed to a multimillion-dollar settlement for similar conduct. This is the same parity enforcement gap documented in the Parity Paradox subsection, now concentrated on the youngest, most dependent patients in the system.

UnitedHealth Group earned $22 billion in net profits last year. The $290 million it anticipates spending on ABA therapy in its Medicaid plans represents 1.3% of that figure. The playbook's strategic rationale is not survival. It is margin optimization at the expense of children whose condition makes them unable to advocate for themselves, funded by a government program designed to protect them.

The Revenue Multiplier: Risk Adjustment Fraud as Bidirectional Extraction

The game theory analysis to this point examines one extraction vector: denying claims to reduce payouts. But Medicare Advantage creates a second, complementary vector that operates in the opposite direction. On January 14, 2026, Kaiser Permanente affiliates agreed to pay $556 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations that they submitted invalid diagnosis codes to inflate Medicare Advantage risk scores, the largest MA fraud settlement in history. The government alleged Kaiser added approximately 500,000 unsupported diagnoses between 2009 and 2018, generating roughly $1 billion in improper Medicare reimbursements.

The mechanism was structurally embedded. Federal prosecutors alleged Kaiser pressured physicians to retroactively add diagnoses through medical record addenda, sometimes months or more than a year after encounters, for conditions that were not evaluated or treated during the original visit. Internal tools mined patients' historical records for diagnoses that had not been submitted to CMS. The company set aggressive coding targets, flagged underperforming physicians, and tied compensation incentives to diagnosis submission rates. Dr. James Taylor, a longtime Kaiser physician and former medical director responsible for coding governance, filed the whistleblower complaint after identifying what he described as systemic practices that added or retained diagnosis codes not supported by patients' medical records. The relators' share of the settlement was $95 million.

Kaiser described the case as reflecting "industrywide challenges" in applying Medicare Advantage risk adjustment standards. The defense is itself an admission of systemic scope. CMS pays Medicare Advantage organizations a fixed monthly amount per enrollee, adjusted for risk. Higher-risk patients generate higher payments. Every unsupported diagnosis added to a patient's record shifts the risk score upward, increasing the capitation payment regardless of whether the patient receives any additional care. The incentive structure is the inverse of the denial mechanism: where denials extract value by reducing payouts on the right side of the ledger, risk adjustment fraud extracts value by inflating revenue on the left side. An insurer executing both strategies simultaneously extracts value bidirectionally from the same patient population.

UnitedHealth Group faces its own version of this exposure. As documented in the Governance Reckoning subsection, UNH has confirmed it is cooperating with criminal and civil DOJ Medicare probes alongside a separate antitrust investigation. A shareholder derivative suit filed August 13, 2026, alleges $200 million in unsupported Medicare billings and the elimination of internal audit functions that would have caught them. The Mass AG investigation alleges more than $100 million in Medicaid upcoding fraud between 2015 and 2025, with treble damages potentially reaching $300 million. The pattern is not unique to Kaiser or UNH. It is structural to the Medicare Advantage payment model itself, which converts diagnosis documentation from a clinical record into a revenue instrument.

Game Theory Concept
Bidirectional Rent Extraction: Revenue Maximization + Payout Minimization as Complementary Strategies (Tullock 1967)

Tullock's (1967) rent-seeking framework analyzed how actors expend resources to capture transfers rather than create value. The Medicare Advantage payment model enables a uniquely efficient form of rent-seeking: the insurer can simultaneously inflate the revenue it receives (by upcoding risk scores) and minimize the care it provides (by denying claims). These strategies are complementary, not substitutes. Upcoding increases the per-patient capitation payment; denial reduces the per-patient cost of care delivered. The margin between them is pure extraction. The Kaiser settlement reveals the revenue-side mechanism at scale: 500,000 added diagnoses, $1 billion in improper payments, physician incentive structures that converted clinical documentation into a revenue optimization function. Combined with the denial-side mechanisms documented throughout this analysis, the total value extracted from Medicare Advantage exceeds what either mechanism could achieve alone. The game-theoretic prediction is that enforcement against one vector (e.g., mandatory denial-rate reporting under CMS-0057-F) will accelerate exploitation of the other (risk-score inflation through more sophisticated coding practices), unless both sides of the ledger are subject to simultaneous regulatory constraint.

The $556 million Kaiser settlement amounts to roughly half the estimated improper payments, a recovery rate consistent with the Settlement Calculus documented earlier. More significant is the enforcement signal: whisteblower-driven False Claims Act litigation can now target both vectors of the MA extraction model. The DOJ's Whistleblower Rewards Program, expanded in 2026 to cover private-payer fraud beyond the False Claims Act's traditional scope, creates financial incentives for employees who observe either upcoding or systematic denial to report both. The 30% whistleblower share on recoveries exceeding $1 million means a single physician inside an MA organization who documents both risk-score inflation and inappropriate claim denial can trigger liability on two fronts simultaneously. The game-theoretic equilibrium shifts: the bidirectional extraction that makes MA plans uniquely profitable also makes them uniquely exposed when internal information reaches enforcement.

The Turnaround Paradox: When Recovery Requires the Disease

The most revealing data point in the entire post-shooting reform story is not a denial rate, a legislative vote, or a settlement figure. It is UnitedHealth Group's medical cost ratio for Q2 2026: 86.7%. The MCR measures the percentage of premium revenue an insurer spends on actual medical care. The lower the number, the less money goes to patients and the more goes to shareholders. In Q2 2025, UNH's MCR was 89.4%. One year later, under new CEO Stephen Hemsley, it fell to 86.7%, beating Wall Street's already optimistic estimate of 88.47% by nearly two full percentage points. In Q1 2026, the MCR was even lower: 83.9%, against an expected 85.5%. The stock surged 8% on the Q2 earnings release. Analysts applauded the "turnaround."

Translate that into dollars. UnitedHealthcare's insurance unit reported $86 billion in Q2 2026 revenue. A 270-basis-point MCR improvement on that base means approximately $2.3 billion less spent on medical care in a single quarter compared to the prior year's rate. On an annualized basis, the turnaround narrative Wall Street is celebrating represents roughly $9 billion per year redirected from patient care to operating earnings. This is the same company that pledged to eliminate 30% of remaining prior authorizations by year-end 2026. The pledges and the MCR improvement are not contradictory in UNH's framing. They can both be true if the eliminated PAs were low-value administrative friction that cost more to process than they saved in denied claims. But the MCR is an aggregate metric. It captures everything: denied claims, exited markets, sicker patients dropped from enrollment, and favorable pricing on remaining products. The market does not distinguish between margin improvement from genuine efficiency and margin improvement from abandoning unprofitable patients.

Hemsley's playbook makes the mechanism transparent. After returning as CEO in May 2025 (Andrew Witty resigned amid a triple crisis of soaring Medicare costs, a rare earnings miss, and Thompson's murder), Hemsley replaced approximately half of UNH's top 100 executives, exited unprofitable insurance products, committed $1.5 billion to AI investment, and raised the company's 2026 earnings guidance from "at least $17.75" per share to $19.50-$20.00. On an adjusted basis, UNH earned $6.38 per share in Q2 2026, beating the $4.90 consensus by 30%. The stock climbed 25% in the first half of 2026, the best performance of any mega-cap healthcare stock in the S&P 500. CFO Wayne DeVeydt framed the improvement bluntly: "These results are not a reflection of a trend bending or coming under control, but rather our efforts to start pushing down what is already an elevated number." The "elevated number" is the cost of providing medical care to patients.

The parallel data makes the paradox complete. A peer-reviewed JAMA study (Meiselbach et al., Johns Hopkins/Georgetown, February 2026) found that 10% of all Medicare Advantage enrollees, approximately 2.9 million people, were forced to find new plans in 2026 as insurers exited markets and discontinued coverage. Between 2018 and 2024, the mean annual forced disenrollment rate was 1%. It jumped to 6.9% in 2025 and 10% in 2026. In 12 states, more than 20% of MA enrollees lost their plans. In Vermont, 92.2% were disenrolled. Rural beneficiaries experienced disruption at twice the rate of urban populations. UnitedHealthcare accounted for 14% of all forced disenrollments nationally, the highest share of any individual insurer, followed by Aetna at 8.65% and Elevance at approximately 8%. UNH itself disclosed that Medicare Advantage membership declined from 8.4 million to 7.6 million year-over-year, reflecting 109 county exits and over 100 plan closures. These are not random market adjustments. They are the operational mechanism behind the MCR improvement. Drop the sickest, most expensive populations from enrollment; keep the younger, healthier ones; reprice the remaining products at higher premiums. The MCR falls. Wall Street applauds. The 2.9 million disenrolled patients become someone else's problem.

Game Theory Concept
The MCR Paradox: Market Pricing of Care as Cost (Leibenstein 1966 / Arrow 1963)

Leibenstein's (1966) X-efficiency theory distinguished between allocative efficiency (producing the right things) and X-efficiency (producing things at minimum cost). In most industries, reducing the cost ratio is unambiguously good: it means delivering the same output with fewer resources. Health insurance inverts this logic. The MCR is not a cost-efficiency metric. It is a care-delivery metric. A lower MCR means, by definition, that less of each premium dollar reaches patients. Arrow's (1963) foundational insight was that the demand for medical care is irregular, unpredictable, and associated with states of the world the consumer cannot control. Insurance exists to pool this risk. But when the insurer's stock price is explicitly a function of how little care it delivers per premium dollar, the market creates a structural incentive to minimize the very output the product was designed to provide. The "turnaround" celebrated by investors is Leibenstein's concept applied in reverse: not X-efficiency (same output, lower cost) but X-inefficiency-by-design (lower output, same revenue). The game-theoretic consequence is a contradictory equilibrium: the capital market rewards care reduction while the political market punishes it. The company must satisfy both markets simultaneously, which it does through signal separation. PA reform satisfies the political market (visible, countable, headline-friendly). MCR improvement satisfies the capital market (aggregate, quarterly, expressed in basis points). The two signals are not measuring the same thing. PA eliminations remove specific administrative requirements. MCR improvement captures the net effect of all care-reduction strategies, including market exits, product repricing, and population selection. A company can eliminate 6.5 million PAs and still reduce total care spending if it simultaneously exits the markets and populations that generate the highest claims. This is not a contradiction. It is the strategy.

The JAMA data reveals the selection mechanism at work. The plans most frequently terminated were PPO plans, which offer broader provider networks and greater patient choice. Plans with lower star ratings, operated by smaller carriers, and serving rural markets were disproportionately discontinued. This is not random attrition. PPO plans are more expensive to operate because they give patients access to more providers, which generates more claims. Rural markets have higher per-capita costs due to limited provider competition and sicker populations. By exiting these segments, insurers improve their aggregate denial statistics (fewer complex claims to deny), reduce their MCR (fewer expensive patients in the risk pool), and concentrate their remaining membership in urban, younger, healthier populations where the margin between premiums and claims is widest. Mark Meiselbach, lead author of the JAMA study, described the trend as "a substantial and sudden reversal" of two decades of stable growth, noting that in some states, "there may no longer be any MA plans available."

The market's assessment of UNH's turnaround makes the paradox explicit. UNH's stock recovered from its mid-2025 trough near $256 (52-week low) to approximately $390 by August 21, 2026, a 52% recovery that still leaves it 38% below its pre-shooting high of $630. The recovery tracks Hemsley's MCR improvements almost perfectly. Each quarterly earnings beat that demonstrated lower care spending produced a stock surge. The $1.5 billion AI commitment was positioned as administrative efficiency, but the operational effect is the same: AI replaces human reviewers who might exercise clinical judgment in borderline cases with algorithmic systems optimized for the same MCR reduction that drives stock appreciation. DeVeydt said Optum's AI tools have "reduced the administrative burden and increased the amount of time Optum Health clinicians can spend treating patients," but Optum Health's operating income simultaneously jumped 29% year-over-year to $4 billion in Q2 2026, a margin expansion that requires revenue growth to outpace cost growth, meaning the "time clinicians spend treating patients" must generate more billable revenue per hour. The AI is not a neutral efficiency tool. It is the mechanism through which the MCR paradox is operationalized at scale.

The Temporal Trap: When Demolition Outpaces Reform

The reform pipeline documented in this analysis is real. Six federal bills, fourteen state AI bans, mandatory disclosure rules, gold card programs, an enforcement ratchet driven by OIG audits, AMA pressure, and class action settlements. But the pipeline has a structural vulnerability that the policy debate has largely ignored: the speed at which coverage can be demolished through administrative action far exceeds the speed at which it can be protected through legislation.

Consider the calendar. The Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act was first introduced in 2019. It passed two House committees unanimously (42-0, 45-0), accumulated 298 cosponsors, and by August 2026 it still has not received a floor vote. Seven years from introduction to pending. The Stop Deadly Denials Act was introduced in April 2026 and has not had a committee hearing. The DeSaulnier ERISA package was introduced in June 2026. Same.

Now consider the administrative timeline. The CMS Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Rule was proposed, finalized, and takes effect August 25, 2026. It eliminates the low-income special enrollment period that gave roughly 3 million Americans year-round access to marketplace coverage. It imposes a $5/month surcharge on automatically re-enrolled members. It adds income verification and documentation requirements that CMS's own estimates project will affect 3.3 million applicants. It ends DACA recipient eligibility, removing approximately 100,000 enrollees. Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms described the rule's cumulative effect as "death by a thousand paper cuts." Combined with the enhanced premium tax credit expiration already documented in the Coverage Vacuum subsection, KFF projects 8.2 million additional uninsured from ACA marketplace changes alone.

The Columbus II ruling on July 16 stayed seven of the rule's most aggressive provisions. But the core enrollment barriers survived the injunction: documentation verification requirements, the automatic re-enrollment surcharge, and key eligibility changes take effect on schedule. A second legal front opened August 3, 2026, when 21 attorneys general filed suit in Massachusetts federal court challenging the 2027 benefit parameter rule that projects 2 million additional coverage losses by 2027 and 5 million by 2030. The litigation will take months or years. The rule takes effect in days.

This is the temporal trap. The PA reform pipeline moves at legislative speed: introduce, refer, mark up, report, schedule, vote, conference, sign. Each step requires coalition-building, committee calendars, floor time, and political negotiation. The coverage demolition pipeline moves at administrative speed: propose, comment, finalize, effective date. The executive branch can remove millions from the insured population in a single rulemaking cycle that takes months. Congress has not passed a single binding PA reform bill in the 20 months since the shooting, despite the most intense public pressure on the insurance industry in living memory.

The game-theoretic consequence is a shrinking denominator problem. Every PA reform bill, every gold card program, every AI ban, every mandatory disclosure requirement applies only to people who have coverage. The reforms documented in Section III of this analysis benefit the insured population. But that population is contracting from three directions simultaneously: Medicaid work requirements (CBO: 5.2 million by 2034), Medicare Advantage market exits (2.9 million forced disenrollments in 2026 alone), and ACA marketplace collapse (3 million effectuated drop already, 8.2 million more projected). By the time Congress passes the Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act, the population it protects will be materially smaller than the population it would have protected had it passed in 2019 when it was first introduced.

The newest legislative entry underscores the paradox. On July 16, 2026, Representatives Conaway (D-NJ) and Murphy (R-NC) introduced H.R. 9734, the Protecting Patients from Automated Denials Act. The bill requires that every AI-assisted prior authorization denial in Medicare Advantage be reviewed by a licensed physician who attests to independent medical judgment. It grants HHS audit authority over AI algorithms used in coverage decisions and mandates disclosure of denial data broken down by AI involvement. The American Medical Association formally endorsed it in a July 29 letter. The bill is bipartisan. It targets the specific mechanism the data shows is most problematic: the 67% MA appeal overturn rate documented in the KFF cross-market analysis (August 13, 2026) demonstrates that a majority of AI-assisted denials are reversed when a human physician reviews them. It addresses what the public wants: 71% of voters support prohibiting PA entirely.

H.R. 9734 has not had a committee hearing. It joins a legislative queue behind five other PA reform bills, a DeSaulnier ERISA package, and a bipartisan WISeR resolution, all competing for the same limited floor time, committee attention, and political capital. Meanwhile, CMS is running WISeR (AI-driven PA in traditional Medicare, 62% initial approval rate), the ACA marketplace is shedding millions of enrollees through administrative rule, and Medicaid work requirements begin national enforcement January 1, 2027. The reform side of the ledger adds bills. The demolition side adds effective dates.

Game Theory Concept
Stackelberg Leadership in Regulatory Destruction (von Stackelberg 1934 / Downs 1957)

Heinrich von Stackelberg's (1934) leadership model demonstrates that in sequential games, the player who moves first captures a structural advantage because the second mover must optimize against an already-established position. Applied to the reform-demolition asymmetry: the executive branch functions as the Stackelberg leader, moving first through administrative rules that reshape the coverage landscape before Congress can respond. The CMS Marketplace Integrity Rule (effective Aug 25, 2026), the Medicaid work requirement enforcement (beginning Jan 1, 2027), and the WISeR PA expansion (launched Jan 15, 2026) all established facts on the ground that the legislative pipeline must now work around rather than prevent. Downs's (1957) median voter theorem predicts that democratic outcomes converge on the preferences of the median voter, and 71% of voters support prohibiting PA entirely. But Downs's model assumes the legislature moves at the speed of voter preference. When the administrative branch moves faster, the legislative equilibrium becomes aspirational rather than binding: by the time Congress enacts the PA reform that supermajority public opinion demands, the covered population that reform would protect has already been reduced by millions through administrative action that never required a vote. The temporal asymmetry is not an accident. Concentrated interests (insurers, administrators) can act through the fast channel (rulemaking), while diffuse interests (patients, voters) must act through the slow channel (legislation). The result is a structural advantage for coverage demolition over coverage protection, regardless of public opinion.

The Screening Cascade: When Coverage Loss Produces Countable Deaths

The mortality estimates in the Statistical Lives Saved section of this analysis are, by design, conservative Fermi approximations. A JAMA Oncology research letter published January 8, 2026, by Adrian Diaz and Sarah Shubeck of the University of Chicago provides the first peer-reviewed projection of a specific mortality channel: cancer screening losses from Medicaid coverage contraction under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Diaz and Shubeck drew on Arkansas's experience with Medicaid work requirements between 2018 and 2019, when approximately 18,000 enrollees lost coverage, to model the national impact of the OBBBA's mandatory work and recertification requirements. Their central estimate: 7.5 million screening-eligible adults (range: 5.0 to 10.8 million) will lose Medicaid coverage within two years of full enforcement. That coverage loss translates directly into missed preventive care: an estimated 405,706 missed mammograms, 679,745 missed colorectal cancer screenings, and 67,213 missed lung cancer screenings. The result: 1,055 breast cancers, 748 colorectal cancers, and 538 lung cancers that would have been detected at early, treatable stages will instead go undiagnosed. The authors project 155 excess cancer deaths within two years: 70 breast, 50 colorectal, 35 lung.

These are not speculative projections from an advocacy group. They are modeled from real coverage-loss data in a state that actually implemented work requirements, combined with CDC self-reported screening prevalence rates and NCI two-year incidence risk data. The Arkansas precedent is particularly instructive because it revealed the mechanism that CMS's own model now confirms nationally: of the roughly 200 Nebraskans who lost coverage on August 1, 2026, CMS projects that 40% of all disenrollments will result from paperwork failures rather than actual noncompliance with work requirements. The coverage losses are not filtering out people who do not need Medicaid. They are filtering out people who cannot navigate the documentation system, a population that overlaps heavily with those least likely to navigate the healthcare system independently after losing coverage.

The screening cascade introduces a temporal dimension the denial-rate analysis misses. Prior authorization denial is immediate and visible: a physician requests approval, the insurer says no, the patient either appeals or does not. Coverage loss is gradual and invisible: a person loses Medicaid, does not schedule a mammogram, does not detect a tumor at Stage I, and presents at Stage III two years later. The excess mortality from denial reform (the statistical lives saved calculation) and the excess mortality from coverage contraction (the Diaz-Shubeck projection) operate on different timescales and through different causal mechanisms, but they affect the same population. The working-age adults losing Medicaid coverage through OBBBA work requirements are disproportionately the same demographic facing high prior authorization burdens: lower-income, less likely to appeal denials, more likely to abandon treatment when administrative barriers arise.

Senator Durbin cited the study on February 19, 2026, noting that Illinois alone faces a projected $48 billion federal Medicaid funding cut (19% of its federal Medicaid spending), with an estimated 500,000 Illinoisans losing coverage. Nationally, the screening cascade represents a quantifiable, peer-reviewed mortality floor beneath the broader coverage contraction: even if every prior authorization reform in the legislative pipeline passes tomorrow, the cancer deaths from coverage loss will proceed on their own timeline, because screening requires insurance and insurance requires enrollment and enrollment now requires documented compliance with work requirements that the administrative system is designed to make difficult.

Game Theory Concept
The Delayed Payoff Problem: Why Screening Deaths Never Enter the Political Calculus (Samuelson 1937 / Frederick et al. 2002)

Samuelson's (1937) discounted utility model predicts that decision-makers systematically underweight future costs relative to present benefits. Frederick, Loewenstein, and O'Donoghue's (2002) comprehensive review of time discounting documented the empirical reality: individuals and institutions discount future health outcomes hyperbolically, valuing immediate savings far more than deferred mortality. The screening cascade is the clearest application of this principle to health policy. The budget savings from Medicaid work requirements ($325 billion over ten years per CBO) are immediate and scoreable. The cancer deaths from missed screenings are delayed by two to five years, attributable only through epidemiological modeling, and distributed across millions of individual medical records that no single agency aggregates. A policymaker evaluating the OBBBA sees the $325 billion in savings in the CBO score. The 155 excess cancer deaths per year do not appear in the CBO score because CBO does not model downstream health outcomes from coverage changes. The mortality is real but actuarially invisible: it occurs outside the budget window, outside the coverage reporting system, and outside the political accountability horizon. The game-theoretic consequence is that the legislative coalition for coverage contraction (which captures scoreable budget savings) will always move faster than the coalition against it (which must prove deferred, diffuse mortality), regardless of the net welfare calculation. This is the temporal trap applied to the human body: the policy moves at budget speed, and the deaths arrive at biological speed.

The Risk Pool Siphon: Short-Term Plans as the Third Contraction Vector

The coverage contraction documented in this analysis operates through two channels: Medicaid work requirements (removing enrollees from the bottom of the income distribution) and ACA marketplace collapse (removing enrollees through premium increases and administrative barriers). A third channel is opening. On August 20, 2026, CMS published the regulatory timetable for a proposed rule (CMS-9881, RIN 0938-AV92) that would expand short-term, limited-duration insurance (STLDI) plans from the current maximum of four months to 364 days, with renewal options that effectively make them permanent coverage.

Short-term plans are exempt from the ACA's consumer protections. They can deny coverage for pre-existing conditions. They can exclude essential health benefits, including prescription drugs, maternity care, and mental health treatment. They are not subject to the medical loss ratio requirement (which mandates ACA plans spend at least 80% of premiums on care). They face no risk adjustment obligation. They can charge premiums based on health status. They are, in every structural respect, the pre-ACA individual market reborn under a regulatory exemption.

The game-theoretic mechanism is straightforward adverse selection. STLDI plans attract healthy enrollees with low premiums (because they can medically underwrite and exclude costly conditions). Those healthy enrollees leave the ACA risk pool. The remaining ACA pool becomes sicker on average. Premiums rise. More healthy people leave. The Wakely Consulting Group estimated that a prior iteration of the STLDI expansion would increase ACA premiums by up to 12.8%. The Urban Institute estimated 18.3%. CBO projected 2 million people would enroll in STLDI plans under the expanded rule, with less than 500,000 purchasing coverage that CBO itself considers "health insurance" by any meaningful definition. The remainder would hold policies that nominally constitute "coverage" but exclude the conditions most likely to generate claims.

The STLDI expansion interacts with the other two contraction vectors in a specific way. The enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025. Premiums for unsubsidized ACA enrollees have already doubled or tripled in some markets (Georgetown CHIR, July 2026). Marketplace insurers are proposing a median 14% premium increase for 2027, the second consecutive year of double-digit hikes. For a healthy 35-year-old earning $63,000, an unsubsidized ACA Silver plan now costs several hundred dollars per month. A medically underwritten STLDI plan might cost $100. The rational choice for a healthy individual is clear. The systemic consequence for the ACA risk pool is equally clear: every healthy enrollee who exits accelerates the premium spiral for those who remain.

PwC's Health Research Institute forecasts that the cost of caring for people with employer-sponsored coverage will rise 9% in 2027. That figure captures a parallel feedback loop: hospitals and physician practices are deploying AI-driven billing optimization tools that identify higher-reimbursement diagnostic codes, a practice that increases charges to employer plans independently of any change in patient acuity. The same AI technology that insurers use to deny claims, providers are using to maximize billing. The employer, paying $18,500 per employee and rising, absorbs the cost increase from both sides without measuring the quality of what it purchases. The STLDI expansion adds a third pressure: as healthy employees discover they can purchase cheaper coverage outside their employer plan (STLDI is available to individuals, not groups, but employees who waive employer coverage become STLDI candidates), the employer risk pool undergoes the same adverse selection that the ACA pool is already experiencing.

Game Theory Concept
Rothschild-Stiglitz Separating Equilibrium Applied to Coverage Fragmentation (Rothschild & Stiglitz 1976)

Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) proved that in insurance markets with asymmetric information, no pooling equilibrium exists. Insurers will always offer separating contracts: a high-coverage, high-premium plan that attracts high-risk enrollees, and a low-coverage, low-premium plan that attracts low-risk enrollees. The ACA attempted to prevent this separation through community rating (prohibiting price discrimination by health status), essential health benefit mandates (preventing coverage exclusions), and risk adjustment (redistributing premiums from low-risk to high-risk pools). The STLDI expansion reinstates the separating equilibrium by creating a parallel market where all three mechanisms are absent. Short-term plans can price by health status (separating the risk types the ACA pooled together), exclude benefits (reducing coverage for conditions that generate claims), and avoid risk adjustment (keeping the low-risk premiums for themselves). Rothschild and Stiglitz showed that the low-risk contract in a separating equilibrium is always suboptimal: it provides less coverage than the socially efficient level because it must be unattractive to high-risk types. The STLDI market validates this prediction: CBO itself classifies most STLDI enrollees as holding coverage that does not meet its definition of health insurance. The Rothschild-Stiglitz framework predicts that the separating equilibrium, once established, is self-reinforcing: each healthy enrollee who exits the ACA pool raises premiums for those who remain, pushing the next-healthiest enrollee toward exit, until the pool contains only those too sick to qualify for STLDI. The ACA's architects understood this dynamic and designed community rating and risk adjustment to prevent it. The STLDI expansion removes the prevention while leaving the ACA's coverage mandates in place for the shrinking pool of enrollees who cannot exit.

The $27 Gambit: When Prior Authorization Costs More Than It Saves

The political debate over prior authorization assumes a trade-off: administrative burden in exchange for cost savings. Two peer-reviewed studies published in 2026 suggest the trade-off is fictional. The burden is real. The savings, for everyone except insurers, are not.

Leung et al. analyzed 33,178 prior authorization requests for anti-VEGF eye injections (treatments for macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy) across Medicare Advantage, commercial, and Medicaid plans using the SamaCare electronic PA database. The results: 97.7% of all prior authorization requests were ultimately approved. 97.9% experienced delays. The direct savings to the insurer from the 2.3% of requests that were denied averaged $27.11 per injection. But the total societal cost increase per prior authorization request was $637.78: $588.17 in annual workplace productivity loss, $362.92 in patient and family burden, and $11.61 in provider administrative costs. The insurer's annual savings? $4.92 per patient. In Monte Carlo simulations, PA was not cost-saving in more than 99.9% of modeled scenarios. Insurance companies were the only sector of society that could potentially save money. Everyone else paid more, not less, so that 2.3% of requests could be denied.

A separate study in the Spine Journal examined 740 patients referred for spine surgery at a single academic medical center. The researchers tested whether clinical indicators (myelopathy, cord compression, neurological deficit, cord signal change on imaging) predicted which patients required prior authorization or which were denied. None did. The only significant predictor of both PA requirement and denial was payor type: which insurance company covered the patient. The prior authorization process added a 14-day delay to the final insurance decision and an 11-day delay to surgery. Clinical severity was irrelevant to the process. The mechanism was not filtering for medical appropriateness. It was filtering by business relationship.

Game Theory Concept
Cost Externalization as Negative-Sum Equilibrium (Pigou 1920 / Coase 1960)

Pigou's framework of social vs. private cost identifies situations where a firm's privately rational decision imposes costs on third parties that exceed the firm's benefit. When the insurer's PA savings ($4.92/patient/year) are smaller than the costs imposed on patients ($362.92), providers ($11.61), and employers ($588.17), the system is a textbook negative externality. In a two-player Coasean framework, the parties could theoretically bargain to eliminate the deadweight loss. But PA operates across millions of atomized encounters where no individual patient has bargaining power, transaction costs are prohibitive, and the property right to deny is legally allocated to the insurer. The result is a stable but socially destructive equilibrium: the process persists because the costs are diffuse and the benefits are concentrated. The 97.7% approval rate makes this legible. A process that approves nearly everything is not screening. It is a toll booth.

These findings reframe the entire PA debate. The industry's defense relies on the premise that prior authorization prevents unnecessary care. If that were true, the denial rate should correlate with clinical indicators, and the cost savings should exceed the administrative burden. Neither condition holds. The Leung data shows the net transfer is $632.86 per PA request from society to the insurer (the $637.78 societal cost minus the $4.92 insurer savings). Across 6.5 million PA requirements eliminated in the post-shooting reforms, that arithmetic suggests the reforms eliminated something on the order of $4.1 billion in annual deadweight loss, even before accounting for the health consequences of the delays. The 97.7% approval rate means the system's primary function was never to prevent inappropriate care. It was to impose a processing tax on care delivery, one whose costs fell on everyone except the entity that imposed it.

The Open Plea: Unilateral Cooperation as Multi-Forum Optimization

On August 14, 2026, Mangione entered a guilty plea to two federal stalking charges without a plea agreement. Federal prosecutors confirmed at the post-hearing press conference that no deal had been reached. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said his office intended to seek the maximum sentence: life in prison. Judge Margaret Garnett informed Mangione that federal sentencing guidelines placed the recommended range at 24 to 30 years, though she was not bound by it. Sentencing was set for December 18.

In standard criminal defense, an open plea (guilty plea with no negotiated terms) is the weakest possible move. The defendant surrenders the right to trial without extracting any binding concession on sentencing. It is the legal equivalent of unilateral cooperation in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma: you cooperate, your opponent defects, and you receive the worst payoff. Prosecutors are free to seek the maximum sentence, and the judge has unconstrained discretion. Defense attorneys almost universally prefer either a negotiated plea (cooperation-cooperation) or trial (defection-defection).

Mangione's open plea is rational only when modeled as a multi-forum game, not a single proceeding. The plea operates simultaneously across three strategic theaters, and the expected value calculation requires integrating payoffs across all of them.

Forum 1: Federal sentencing. Without a deal, Garnett has full discretion within the statutory range (zero to life). The guidelines range of 24 to 30 years functions as an anchoring mechanism. Decades of sentencing research show that guidelines exert gravitational force on judicial decisions even when judges are not bound by them. Acceptance of responsibility typically earns a two- to three-level reduction under USSG §3E1.1, though prosecutors stated they would not recommend the reduction, an unusual move that signals the open plea was not a cooperative gesture toward the government. The plea nevertheless converts a jury trial (outcome uncertain, sentence uncertain) into a sentencing hearing (outcome certain, sentence partially bounded by guidelines). The allocution itself became a platform: "Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour." Each word was chosen. The criminal proceeding became the venue for the insurance industry argument that generated public sympathy.

Forum 2: State case. Within hours of the federal plea, Mangione's defense team filed a motion to dismiss the state murder charges under New York's double jeopardy statute (CPL §40.20(2)), which is broader than the federal constitutional standard. The state trial, previously scheduled for September 8, was postponed. Justice Carro gave the DA until October 9 to respond, set the defense reply for October 30, and moved the next hearing to December 10, eight days before the federal sentencing. Former Manhattan prosecutor Anthony Capozzolo told CNN it was "more likely than not that the state case goes away." If the motion succeeds, the open plea eliminates not one trial but two, converting a two-front legal war into a single sentencing hearing with a 24-to-30-year guideline anchor.

Forum 3: Public narrative. A negotiated plea would have required Mangione to adopt the prosecution's factual narrative, typically including language emphasizing the wrongfulness of the conduct and cooperation with the government. The open plea let him control his own allocution. His statement drew a direct line from his back pain, to insurer indifference to patient communications, to the immediate response he received when posing as an investor managing $50 million. The allocution was simultaneously a legal instrument (establishing the factual basis for the plea) and a rhetorical document (reinforcing the insurance industry critique). In the weekend following the plea, 177 donors contributed $5,300 to his defense fund, and post-plea media coverage reproduced his allocution language extensively. The prosecution's counter-narrative ("No grievance, political belief or ideological cause can ever justify murder") competed in the same information environment but against a defendant who had just spoken in his own voice in a federal courtroom.

Game Theory Concept
Multi-Forum Sequential Optimization / Linked Games (Bernheim & Whinston, 1990)

In a single-forum prisoner's dilemma, unilateral cooperation is the dominated strategy. But when the same action simultaneously determines payoffs in multiple independent games, the optimal strategy in any single game can be suboptimal in isolation. Bernheim and Whinston (1990) showed that multimarket contact between firms creates strategic linkages that change equilibrium behavior in each individual market. Applied to sequential legal proceedings: Mangione's unilateral cooperation in the federal forum (guilty plea, no deal) is the dominated strategy within that forum alone. But it triggers a double jeopardy motion in the state forum that may eliminate the state case entirely. The combined expected payoff (24-30 year federal guidelines with one trial eliminated) can exceed the expected payoff of fighting both trials independently (risk of life sentence federally plus 25-to-life state sentence consecutively). The open plea is not cooperation. It is a portfolio hedge across forums, where accepting a bounded loss in one game eliminates unbounded exposure in another. The prosecution's response, seeking life despite cooperation, confirms they understood the strategic logic: the open plea was not a concession but a move in a larger game.

The multi-forum structure also explains the timing. The federal plea came during a conference hastily scheduled hours after Mangione appeared in state court to discuss the upcoming September trial. CNN reported that defense attorneys had been in plea negotiations with federal prosecutors, but no agreement was reached. The plea was entered the same day. This suggests the defense team calculated that the cross-jurisdictional hedge was more valuable than whatever terms federal prosecutors were offering: a negotiated plea might have included a cooperation agreement or sentencing stipulation that would have weakened the double jeopardy argument or constrained the allocution narrative. The open plea preserved maximum flexibility across all three forums simultaneously. It is a move that looks irrational in one game and reveals itself as optimal only when the game board is expanded to include the forums the prosecution cannot reach.

The Cartel Accusation: When Independent Sovereigns Coordinate

On August 15, 2026, Mangione's defense team filed a motion that reframed the double jeopardy question in explicitly economic terms. The filing accused federal and state prosecutors of coordinating "to maximize the punitive effectiveness of the two cases at the expense of Mr. Mangione." The specific allegation: "This coordinated deal between them had a specific purpose: The scheme was designed solely to ensure dual successive prosecutions, in order to attempt to avoid double jeopardy protections." Defense attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo put it simply: "It was a single tragic event, yet he's being prosecuted twice for the same conduct."

The dual sovereignty doctrine in American constitutional law assumes that federal and state prosecutors operate independently, like firms in a competitive market. Each jurisdiction pursues its own "product" (federal stalking versus state murder), and the constitutional permission to prosecute the same conduct twice rests on the fiction that independent sovereigns are bringing genuinely separate cases. The defense's filing is, in game-theoretic terms, an antitrust claim: the prosecutors formed a cartel to circumvent the market constraint that double jeopardy was designed to enforce.

The industrial organization literature provides the analytical framework. George Stigler's 1964 "A Theory of Oligopoly" identified the three conditions that make cartels possible: (1) information exchange among participants, (2) a mechanism to detect and punish defection, and (3) a coordination equilibrium that all members prefer to competition. Richard Posner extended this in 1970, arguing that coordinated behavior is distinguishable from independent behavior by examining information flows and payoff structures. The defense's filing satisfies all three prongs of the Stigler-Posner framework with documented evidence.

First, information exchange. Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg's office sent a letter to state Judge Carro explicitly warning about the federal plea before it was entered. This is not the behavior of an independent actor pursuing a separate case. It is a participant in a coordination game sharing intelligence about a counterparty's expected move. In Stigler's cartel framework, this communication serves the same function as a price-fixing agreement: it allows both parties to adjust their strategies to maintain the coordinated outcome (dual prosecution) rather than the competitive outcome (whichever jurisdiction files first preempts the other through double jeopardy).

Second, the coordination equilibrium. The two jurisdictions' agreement to let the state case proceed first was not an accident of scheduling. It was a strategic sequencing that maximized aggregate punishment: a state murder conviction (25-to-life) followed by a federal stalking enhancement (additional consecutive time). This is the cartel's "agreed price," the coordinated output that both parties prefer to the competitive alternative where one jurisdiction's conviction triggers double jeopardy protection against the other. CNN legal analyst Joey Jackson assessed the defense argument directly: "I do believe that based upon the law that the state trial goes away. I do think that this double jeopardy argument is real," because both cases involve "the same sort of transaction and occurrence, the same set of facts." New York criminal defense attorney Stacy Schneider called the motion a "calculated, good shot" but "not a slam dunk," noting that prosecutors will argue "the act of stalking was a prelude to the murder" and that the acts "are not the same as actually pulling the trigger."

Third, the cartel's vulnerability. Stigler proved that cartels are inherently unstable because every member has a private incentive to defect from the coordinated price. Applied here: Mangione's open plea was the defection that shattered the prosecutorial cartel. By entering a guilty plea in federal court unilaterally, without coordination with state prosecutors and without any deal, the defense exploited the structural gap between the prosecutors' coordinated strategy and the legal system's assumption of sovereign independence. The "agreement" to let the state case go first was the cartel equilibrium. The surprise federal plea was the competitive entry that collapsed it. The prosecutors had designed a sequential game; the defense made it simultaneous.

Game Theory Concept
Prosecutorial Cartel Instability (Stigler, 1964 / Posner, 1970)

In industrial organization, Stigler (1964) showed that cartels are inherently unstable because each member has a private incentive to deviate from the agreed pricing. Posner (1970) extended this to antitrust, arguing that coordinated behavior is distinguishable from independent behavior by examining information flows and payoff structures. Applied to inter-jurisdictional prosecution: the dual sovereignty doctrine assumes prosecutors are independent "firms" pursuing different "products" (state murder vs. federal stalking). When they coordinate scheduling, share information about plea strategies, and time their proceedings to prevent defense exploitation of double jeopardy, they transform independent prosecution into coordinated prosecution, collapsing the independence assumption that justifies dual jurisdiction. The defense's filing is, in game-theoretic terms, an antitrust claim: the prosecution cartel has engaged in conduct that only makes sense as coordination, not as independent action. The open plea was the competitive response: entering a market (federal court) at a price (life sentence exposure) that the cartel did not anticipate, breaking the coordinated equilibrium. DA Seidemann's letter to Judge Carro warning about the federal plea is the smoking gun of information exchange. The 24-to-30-year federal guideline range is the "competitive price" that the defense is willing to accept, which is lower than the "cartel price" of consecutive state and federal sentences that prosecutors had coordinated to achieve.

The cartel analogy illuminates why the defense's motion is stronger than it might appear on a simple double jeopardy reading. Federal courts have traditionally granted extreme deference to dual sovereignty, reasoning that each government has a distinct interest in prosecution. But Stigler's framework exposes the hidden assumption: that deference is warranted only when the sovereigns are actually behaving independently. When DA Seidemann writes to a state judge to coordinate timing around a federal proceeding, and when federal prosecutors delay their case to allow the state case to go first, the observed behavior is indistinguishable from cartel conduct. The defense does not need to prove a formal agreement. It needs to show, in Posner's framework, that the pattern of behavior makes sense only as coordination. The documented information flows may be sufficient.

The outcome of this motion will establish precedent for every multi-jurisdictional prosecution in the country. If Judge Carro finds that the prosecutors' coordination vitiated the independence assumption underlying dual sovereignty, the state case collapses, and Mangione faces only the federal sentencing hearing with its 24-to-30-year guideline range. If the motion fails, the cartel holds, and the defense's Stiglerian gambit becomes a data point for future defendants challenging coordinated prosecution. Either way, the filing has introduced antitrust logic into constitutional criminal procedure. The question is no longer whether two sovereigns can prosecute the same conduct. It is whether two sovereigns that coordinated their prosecutions can still claim to be independent.

The Ratings Revolt: When Quality Metrics Become Legal Weapons

While insurers publicly resist quality oversight of their denial practices, they have simultaneously weaponized the courts to inflate the quality ratings that determine their federal bonus payments. The result is a two-front regulatory arbitrage that exposes the deepest structural contradiction in Medicare Advantage governance: the same companies that fight transparency on denial rates are suing to inflate the scores that are supposed to measure whether they deserve more taxpayer money.

On May 27, 2026, Judge Lisa Godbey Wood of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia handed Clover Health a ruling that sent shockwaves through the Medicare Advantage industry. The court held that CMS had improperly calculated Clover's 2026 Star Rating by including twenty quality measures that lacked statutory authorization: ten relied on data sources Congress never approved, and ten were adopted without the notice-and-comment rulemaking required under the Medicare Act. CMS was ordered to recalculate. Clover's primary PPO contract jumped from 3.5 Stars to 4.5 Stars. The financial difference: approximately $120 million in quality bonus payments that Clover alleged it had been denied.

What makes the decision seismic is not its outcome for one insurer but its legal reasoning. Applying the Supreme Court's 2024 Loper Bright decision, which ended decades of Chevron deference to federal agencies, Judge Wood held that CMS possesses only those powers expressly granted by Congress. The court rejected CMS's longstanding position that it had broad discretion to define quality measures through subregulatory guidance. Star Rating specifications are not merely technical tools, the court found, but "substantive legal standards" that directly determine payment outcomes. This transforms every annual Technical Note CMS has ever issued into a potential legal vulnerability.

The ruling's financial blast radius is vast. CMS's quality bonus pool has ballooned to $16 billion annually, nearly the entire CDC budget and double the 2020 level. An estimated 175 MA prescription-drug-plan contracts received 3.5-Star ratings for 2026 and narrowly missed the 4-Star threshold that unlocks enhanced benchmarks, increased rebate percentages, and quality bonus payments. Even modest methodological changes from the ruling could shift billions in aggregate reimbursement. Recognizing this, CMS voluntarily recalculated certain 2027 quality bonus payment ratings on June 17, removing all disputed Part D measures and several Part C measures implicated by the Clover litigation.

But CMS's voluntary recalculation created a new problem: it only applied to some contracts. Elevance Health filed suit on July 1 in the Southern District of Georgia, alleging CMS gave Clover favorable treatment while refusing the same recalculation for five Elevance MA contracts. Elevance claims $115 million in lost 2027 bonus payments. CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield had already sued in January, alleging a single corrected data point released after the plan preview period closed cost it $32 million when its rating missed the 4-Star threshold by a "statistically insignificant margin." Multiple other insurers, including UnitedHealth itself, have filed challenges over the past two years. The industry is no longer debating quality. It is litigating the measurement system into submission.

The game theory is transparent. In a standard principal-agent model, the regulator (CMS) designs quality measures to incentivize the agent (insurers) to deliver better care. The star rating system was supposed to function as a mechanism design solution: publicly reported scores that channel $16 billion in bonuses toward high-performing plans. But mechanism design theory (Hurwicz, Maskin, Myerson, 2007 Nobel) assumes the principal can commit to the rules of the game. When agents can challenge the rules in court and the judiciary strips the principal of deference, the mechanism collapses. The quality metrics become not a constraint on insurer behavior but a surface for strategic litigation. Insurers that score below the bonus threshold do not improve care. They sue to change the methodology until their score crosses the threshold. The quality measure becomes Goodhart's Law in its most literal form: the moment it becomes a target for payment, it ceases to be a measure of quality.

Game Theory Concept
Regulatory Mechanism Collapse via Judicial Forum-Shifting (Hurwicz 1960 / Goodhart 1975)

Hurwicz's (1960) mechanism design framework assumes the mechanism designer can commit to the rules of the game. Quality incentive programs like CMS Star Ratings function as mechanisms that allocate $16 billion annually based on performance metrics. But when agents (insurers) can challenge the mechanism's rules in a separate forum (federal courts), and when that forum has removed deference to the mechanism designer (Loper Bright, 2024), the mechanism loses its credibility. Agents rationally invest in litigation to reshape the mechanism rather than in care quality to satisfy it. Goodhart (1975) identified the parallel dynamic in monetary policy: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." Applied to MA Star Ratings, the measure specifications that determine $16 billion in quality bonuses have become targets for strategic manipulation through litigation. Clover's successful challenge moved its rating from 3.5 to 4.5 Stars, representing approximately $120 million in bonus payments, without any change in the quality of care delivered. The measure did not improve. The methodology was litigated away. When the mechanism designer (CMS) then voluntarily recalculated other plans' ratings in response, it signaled that the mechanism is negotiable, further weakening its incentive properties. The result is a race to the courthouse rather than a race to the quality floor, transforming a mechanism designed to reward care delivery into a mechanism that rewards litigation capacity.

The contradiction with the article's broader thesis is damning. The same UnitedHealth that claims its "overall claims approval rate is 98% for eligible members" and fights transparency on per-contract denial data is simultaneously suing CMS over the quality metrics that were designed to hold it accountable. The same Elevance whose 5% MA denial rate (the lowest among major insurers per the August 13 KFF report) should place it at the top of quality rankings is suing to inflate those rankings further through methodological changes rather than care improvements. The industry wants to resist scrutiny of its denials while demanding more favorable measurement of its quality. These positions are not merely inconsistent. They reveal that "quality" in Medicare Advantage has been decoupled from clinical outcomes and attached instead to litigation strategy, lobbying capacity, and methodological arbitrage. AARP's analysis underscores the structural flaw: Star Ratings include too few measures of clinical outcomes and do not reflect documented issues like inappropriate prior authorization denials and difficulty accessing post-acute care. The bonus program does not penalize low performers at all, unlike traditional Medicare's quality incentive programs. Sixty-four percent of MA enrollees are in plans rated 4 Stars or higher, yet the denial, provider, and patient-harm data documented throughout this analysis describes a system in crisis. The quality scores and the quality reality are measuring different things.

The cascade deepened in July 2026. On July 8, SCAN Health Plan sued CMS in the D.C. District Court, alleging that CMS's refusal to extend the full Clover recalculation methodology to its H5425 and H0976 contracts cost it approximately $125 million in 2027 rebates. SCAN had asked CMS on June 29 to remove the same ten disputed measures from its calculation and allow a revised bid at 4.5 Stars; CMS rejected the request that same day. Three days later, Alignment Healthcare filed its own complaint, alleging $50 million in lost payments across three contracts (H3815, H4961, H3443), each stuck at 4 Stars when 4.5 was attainable under the Clover methodology. Alignment had submitted its recalculation request on July 7; CMS denied it within hours. Combined with Elevance's $115 million claim, the three post-Clover suits alone seek $290 million in additional federal payments for 2027, and the total across all pending star rating challenges now exceeds $400 million.

CMS's response revealed a regulator trapped between conflicting strategic imperatives. On July 21, the agency filed its appeal of the original Clover ruling to the Eleventh Circuit, signaling that it intends to contest the legal framework that spawned the cascade. But on the same day, CMS released the results of its voluntary recalculation for all other contracts: ratings remained the same for 61%, increased for 9%, and decreased for 30% of contracts. The critical detail is the asymmetry: CMS applied a one-way ratchet, updating overall ratings only when the recalculation produced a higher score. Plans that would have received lower ratings under the new methodology were held harmless. This is not a neutral recalculation. It is a regulatory concession structured as a floor with no ceiling, guaranteeing that every affected insurer either wins or stays even. Four additional contracts reached 5-Star status, unlocking the most generous rebate percentages and special enrollment period privileges.

The Alliance of Community Health Plans recognized the strategic instability immediately. In a July 27 letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, ACHP President and CEO Ceci Connolly urged CMS to apply the same "better-of" hold-harmless methodology to the 2027 Star Ratings, calculating each contract's overall rating under both the pre-Clover methodology and the post-Clover methodology and assigning whichever is higher. The letter's logic is explicitly about expectation management: "Adopting a different methodology while the same legal questions remain unresolved would create inconsistency, increase uncertainty and produce inequitable results across contracts." If CMS reverses course in 2027 by reintroducing the disputed measures after the Eleventh Circuit hears its appeal, every plan that invested in care delivery based on the June 2026 methodology faces retroactive financial punishment. ACHP's ask is, in game-theoretic terms, a demand for credible commitment: lock in the rules before the measurement year begins, so that agents can invest in quality with confidence that the scoring system will not shift beneath them.

Game Theory Concept
Strategic Complementarity in Cascading Litigation (Bulow, Geanakoplos & Klemperer 1985 / Schelling 1960)

Bulow, Geanakoplos, and Klemperer (1985) identified strategic complementarity as the condition under which one firm's aggressive action increases the returns to the same action by other firms. Clover's star rating victory creates precisely this condition in the MA litigation market. Before the ruling, any individual insurer challenging CMS's methodology faced uncertain judicial reception, high legal costs, and the risk of regulatory retaliation. Clover's win resolved the uncertainty: the legal theory works, the precedent exists, and the court's statutory roadmap is available to any plaintiff's attorney who can read. Each subsequent suit (Elevance, SCAN, Alignment) reduces the remaining uncertainty for the next plaintiff, while CMS's voluntary recalculation for non-litigating plans creates an additional complementarity: plans that do not sue receive only the one-way ratchet, while plans that sue can demand the full Clover methodology, making litigation strictly dominant over waiting. Schelling (1960) showed that coordination problems are solved by focal points that make one equilibrium salient. Clover's ruling is the focal point that coordinates the industry's strategic shift from regulatory compliance to regulatory litigation. The result is a litigation cascade where the costs of not suing exceed the costs of suing for any insurer near a ratings threshold. CMS's appeal to the Eleventh Circuit is the regulator's attempt to destroy the focal point, but the one-way ratchet it has already applied means the concession cannot be recalled: even if the appellate court reverses, the 2027 bonus payments based on recalculated ratings have already been committed. ACHP's hold-harmless request completes the trap by asking CMS to extend the asymmetric ratchet to 2027 ratings, transforming a one-time concession into a permanent methodological floor. The cascade has converted the star rating system from a principal-designed incentive mechanism into an agent-driven litigation tournament where the $16 billion bonus pool is allocated by judicial outcome rather than clinical performance.

The Disclosure Cascade: Forced Revelation and Algorithmic Transparency

On March 9, 2026, a federal magistrate judge in Minnesota ordered UnitedHealth Group to produce documents across six of seven categories in Estate of Gene B. Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (No. 23-CV-3514, D. Minn.), the class action alleging that UNH's nH Predict algorithm systematically denied post-acute care to Medicare Advantage members without meaningful human review. The court granted or partially granted discovery requests covering: (A) policies and procedures for post-acute care, (B) the development and use of nH Predict, (C) business acquisition data and the financial benefits of nH Predict to UNH, (D) internal and government investigations into UNH's use of AI, (E) naviHealth employee incentives for using nH Predict, and (F) oversight of AI use by UNH. The court denied only category G, which sought nH Predict's source code and underlying medical guidelines. The order's scope is remarkable. Category C compels UNH to reveal how much money nH Predict saved by denying care. Category E compels disclosure of whether employees were financially rewarded for overriding physician recommendations with algorithmic outputs. These are not peripheral discovery requests. They are demands for the internal accounting of the denial machine.

UNH's defensive posture illuminates the information game. An Optum spokesperson told Becker's that "claims that naviHealth is used to make adverse benefit or coverage decisions are false. Medical necessity determinations are made by qualified physicians following CMS guidance, not AI." The company characterized nH Predict as a "care-support tool" that factors in cognition, mobility, and daily activities to "help guide recovery planning." Optum emphasized that nH Predict "is not generative AI." In 2024, the company rebranded naviHealth to "Home & Community Care," changing the corporate identity of the entity most associated with algorithmic denial precisely as litigation scrutiny intensified. The original complaint alleged a 90% error rate, calculated from the percentage of nH Predict-informed denials reversed on internal appeal or by administrative law judges. The plaintiffs' framing and UNH's framing describe the same system from opposite ends of the disclosure spectrum: the plaintiffs see an algorithm that overrides physicians and produces 90% wrong answers; UNH sees a care-support tool that informs but does not dictate.

The game theory of forced disclosure is distinct from the voluntary unraveling analyzed earlier in this article. Milgrom's (1981) unraveling result applies when firms can choose whether to disclose favorable information, creating market pressure for universal disclosure. The Lokken discovery order operates through a different mechanism: Dye's (1985) model of mandatory disclosure under litigation risk. Dye showed that when the probability of forced disclosure is sufficiently high, the optimal corporate strategy shifts from silence (which is informative in Grossman's framework because rational observers infer that withheld information is unfavorable) to preemptive controlled disclosure designed to frame the narrative before courts compel unframed revelation. UNH's behavior maps onto this prediction with precision. The "care-support tool" characterization is not merely a legal defense. It is preemptive framing: establishing a narrative about nH Predict's role before discovery materials reveal the operational reality. The naviHealth-to-Home & Community Care rebrand is the corporate equivalent of evidence sanitization through naming: changing the entity's identity so that future disclosures about "Home & Community Care" do not carry the accumulated negative associations that "naviHealth" had acquired through years of press coverage and litigation.

Game Theory Concept
Multi-Vector Forced Disclosure and the Disclosure Cascade (Dye 1985 / Shin 2003)

Dye's (1985) voluntary disclosure model demonstrated that firms withhold information when they can plausibly claim ignorance, because the market cannot distinguish between a firm that has unfavorable information and one that has no information. Litigation discovery collapses this ambiguity: a court order compels production regardless of strategic preference, eliminating the "no information" pooling equilibrium. Shin (2003) extended the analysis to multi-audience settings where the same disclosure reaches different recipients with different priors. Applied to nH Predict: the Lokken discovery order forces UNH to produce documents that will be read simultaneously by the Lokken plaintiffs' attorneys, the Blumenthal-Hawley Senate subcommittee (which has independent subpoena authority over the same category of documents), plaintiff attorneys in parallel class actions across multiple jurisdictions, CMS regulators drafting the CMS-0057-F reporting framework, and state legislators in the 14 states that have enacted or proposed AI disclosure requirements for insurance. Each recipient extracts different strategic value from the same forced disclosure. The plaintiffs use it to establish liability. The Senate uses it to draft legislation. CMS uses it to calibrate reporting requirements. State legislators use it to justify new restrictions. This creates what Shin's model identifies as a "disclosure cascade": information forced into the open on one front becomes freely available on all fronts, and the cumulative regulatory and litigation exposure from multi-audience disclosure exceeds the sum of individual exposures, because each audience's use of the information generates new public signals that inform the others. The insurer's optimal strategy in a single-front game (concede narrow discovery, contest framing) becomes dominated in a multi-front game where information cannot be compartmentalized. The Lokken order does not merely compel UNH to show its hand to one plaintiff. It compels UNH to show its hand to every player at the table simultaneously.

The operational significance extends beyond one lawsuit. The court's decision to waive the Medicare Act's administrative exhaustion requirement, which normally requires patients to complete all levels of internal and external appeal before suing, was based on the plaintiffs' allegations of irreparable injury and the "futility of exhaustion." This waiver is itself a game-theoretic finding: the court determined that the appeals mechanism was so compromised by the same algorithmic system being challenged that requiring plaintiffs to exhaust it would be circular. You cannot appeal a denial to the entity whose algorithm generated the denial and expect the algorithm to overrule itself. The OIG's June 2026 finding that 95% of appealed skilled nursing facility denials were overturned, and naviHealth's 97% overturn rate, validates the court's reasoning retroactively: the appeals process works, but the initial denial process is so systematically miscalibrated that requiring exhaustion before litigation is functionally a delay mechanism rather than a remedial one.

The Anthem PBRT settlement, which reached its final approval hearing on August 19, 2026, provides a contemporaneous benchmark for what forced algorithmic disclosure produces in practice. Anthem denied proton beam radiation therapy to approximately 140 cancer patients by classifying it as "experimental or not medically necessary." The $3.625 million settlement ($26,000 per patient for treatments costing $30,000-$95,000) confirms the settlement calculus analyzed earlier: denial remains the dominant strategy even when the insurer loses in court. But what the PBRT case adds to the Lokken analysis is an endpoint. The PBRT litigation ran its full course from denial to discovery to settlement to final approval. The Lokken case is at the discovery stage, where the information about nH Predict's financial incentive structure, employee compensation ties, and operational accuracy is being compelled into the record. If the PBRT timeline is any guide, the full cycle from forced disclosure to settlement to structural change takes years, during which the algorithm continues operating. The disclosure cascade may accelerate that timeline by enabling parallel actions across multiple forums to proceed with shared evidentiary foundations rather than each reinventing the factual record from scratch.

The Complexity Trap: How Engineered Fragmentation Defeats Reform
