The prior authorization pledge promised simplification. The data shows something closer to an arms race against coherence. A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in May 2026, conducted by researchers at Stanford University, Georgetown University, and UnitedHealth Group itself, compared prior authorization policies across four major insurers: Aetna, Humana, UnitedHealthcare, and Anthem California. The findings quantify a structural barrier that no reform pledge can overcome through voluntary action alone.

Only 3% of Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System billing codes requiring prior authorization overlapped across all four insurers. More than half of the codes requiring authorization were unique to a single insurer. The number of HCPCS codes requiring PA varied from 1,162 at Aetna to 3,048 at Humana, a 2.6-fold range. And crucially, none of the four insurers used the same criteria to evaluate the same codes, even when they all required PA for the same procedure. A physical therapy code required authorization at Humana but not at Aetna or UnitedHealthcare. An enzyme replacement injection required it at Aetna but not at Humana or UnitedHealthcare. As the study's lead author, David Scheinker of Stanford, put it: "the same few rules and ideas applied in just enough different ways to make them difficult to work with." The fragmentation is not accidental. It is the product of independent corporate bureaucracies optimizing their own cost-containment algorithms without any coordination mechanism, and the lack of coordination itself functions as a defense against regulation.

The physician experience confirms the structural effect. An AMA survey published May 18, 2026, found that only one in three physicians trusts that insurers' voluntary PA reform pledges will produce meaningful change for patients. Only 24% of physicians agreed that health-plan denials based on medical necessity are actually being reviewed by a licensed and qualified physician, the very commitment that insurers made in their June 2025 pledge. Only 16% of physicians who participated in peer-to-peer reviews reported that the health plan's "peer" often or always had appropriate qualifications to evaluate the clinical decision at issue. The gap between pledge and practice is not a matter of implementation lag. It is a structural mismatch between what insurers promised (fewer PA requirements, real-time decisions, qualified clinical review) and what physicians encounter (incompatible rule systems, opaque criteria, unqualified reviewers).

Game Theory Concept
Inverted Hayek: Distributed Complexity as Strategic Defense (Hayek 1945 / Weitzman 1974)

Hayek's (1945) foundational insight was that distributed knowledge is efficient because no central planner can aggregate all local information. Each economic agent's private knowledge, when expressed through price signals, produces coordination outcomes superior to central planning. The PA fragmentation data inverts this framework. When four insurers create four incompatible PA rule systems, each with different code requirements, different approval criteria, and different documentation standards, the combinatorial complexity facing any individual physician practice explodes. A practice with patients across four insurers must navigate four independent rule sets for every procedure, and a gold card earned at one insurer is worthless at the other three. The 3% overlap rate means 97% of any reform effort must be duplicated per-insurer. Weitzman's (1974) analysis of prices vs. quantities under uncertainty predicts this outcome: when the costs of compliance are convex (each additional PA system imposes disproportionately higher marginal administrative costs), fragmented systems impose welfare losses that exceed those of any single system, even if each individual system is independently well-designed. The strategic implication is that insurers do not need to coordinate to resist reform. The absence of coordination is itself the defense. By independently optimizing their own PA criteria without standardization, insurers create a regulatory environment too complex for any single legislative action to simplify. The 6.5 million eliminated PAs, while real, are a reduction within approximately 59 million annual PA requests fragmented across incompatible systems. Eliminating a PA requirement at one insurer does nothing at the other three. Miranda Yaver of the University of Pittsburgh, drawing on physician interviews for her book Coverage Denied, captured the structural futility: "I don't need a timelier denial. I need an approval for the medically necessary care I'm prescribing." The industry pledged faster processing. The physicians need fewer denials. These are not the same problem, and the fragmentation data explains why: you cannot standardize the denial process when every insurer defines the denial differently.

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule, which takes effect January 1, 2027, mandates standardized electronic PA interfaces. But as the study's authors warned, the rule will merely "digitize" the complexity if insurers continue to use different approval criteria and documentation requirements. Standardizing the electronic interface without standardizing the underlying clinical criteria produces faster processing of incompatible rules, the digital equivalent of paving four different roads to four different destinations and calling it a highway system. The April 2026 CMS-0062-P drug PA proposed rule, which would extend electronic PA reporting to prescription drugs, compounds the issue: more transparency about more fragmented systems reveals the scope of the problem without solving it. The gold card programs enacted across 11 states address a symptom (high-approval physicians still face PA delays) without addressing the cause (each insurer defines "high-approval" using different criteria, different lookback periods, and different code pools). The Annals study suggests that the entire prior authorization reform architecture, from voluntary pledges to state gold card laws to federal interoperability mandates, is optimizing around the wrong variable. The problem is not that PA is too slow or too opaque. The problem is that four insurers built four separate denial infrastructures with 97% non-overlap, and no reform short of standardization will make four incompatible systems behave as one.

The Innovation Tax: When Prior Authorization Blocks Precision Medicine

The prior authorization system was built for a world of standardized treatments: one drug, one procedure code, one coverage determination. Precision medicine operates by a fundamentally different logic. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) can scan a tumor for dozens or hundreds of actionable mutations simultaneously, matching each patient to a targeted therapy based on their individual genomic profile rather than their disease category. This is the most important diagnostic advance in oncology in decades, and the prior authorization system is systematically blocking it.

A cohort study published in JAMA Network Open in April 2025 (Kang et al., Georgetown University, funded by the National Cancer Institute) examined nearly 30,000 cancer-related NGS claims filed by approximately 25,000 unique Medicare beneficiaries between 2016 and 2021. The central finding inverts the expected trajectory of a coverage expansion: after Medicare issued its first National Coverage Determination for NGS testing in 2018, and amended it in 2020 to include hereditary mutations in breast and ovarian cancers, the denial rate increased. Before the NCD (pre-2018), 16.8% of cancer-related NGS claims were denied. After the NCD took effect, 20.3% were denied. After the 2020 amendment that expanded coverage criteria, 27.4% were denied. Medicare created a national coverage standard specifically to reduce uncertainty around genomic testing reimbursement. The uncertainty grew.

The denial pattern reveals something deeper than administrative lag. Claims for NGS panels testing 50 or more genes were approximately three times more likely to be denied than smaller panels. Claims processed through independent laboratories were nearly twice as likely to be denied as those processed through hospitals, even though roughly half of all NGS testing occurs outside hospital settings. The median charge among denied claims was $3,800; if the test is covered, patients pay nothing. As lead author So-Yeon Kang observed: "We expected that there would be more certainty around how NGS services are covered with the NCD in 2018, but what we found is that there is a lot of uncertainty still, and potentially even growing uncertainty." The data describes a system that penalizes diagnostic comprehensiveness: the more genes you test, the more information you gather, the more likely the claim is denied. The PA mechanism is calibrated against the exact feature that makes precision medicine valuable.

The pediatric data is worse. A study of 801 patients in a pediatric genomic research cohort (PMC, 2023) found that 20.4% of children who had clinical genetic testing ordered experienced at least one insurance denial. Private insurance produced the highest denial rate: 25.7% of privately insured children had testing denied, compared with 14.6% on public insurance. Among the 147 children denied, 44.2% had all testing requests rejected, not a single test approved. The highest denial rates were for exome sequencing (16.6%) and chromosomal microarray (10.4%), the most comprehensive and diagnostically powerful tests available. Katherine Janeway, director of Clinical Genomics at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, told Managed Healthcare Executive at the ASCO 2026 annual meeting that reimbursement policies for molecular diagnostics "have failed to keep up with the evidence base," especially for pediatric bone cancers, where no NCCN guidelines exist for genomic testing and research protocols are "the only reliable pathway to get testing done." Insurance companies require guideline concordance to approve tests. The guidelines do not yet exist for the cancers that kill children.

Anthem's prior authorization program for hereditary cancer panels demonstrates the mechanism at the insurer level. According to genetic counselors and testing laboratories surveyed by GenomeWeb, between 40% and 80% of hereditary cancer panel tests were denied after Anthem introduced PA requirements, even though labs and providers believed the majority of denied claims met Anthem's own coverage criteria. The fundamental problem: the NCCN's clinical guidelines recommend multi-gene panel testing when "more than one gene can explain an inherited cancer syndrome," because testing genes individually is slower, more expensive, and exhausts patients who rarely complete the sequential process. Anthem's coverage policy does not incorporate this NCCN position. One genetic counselor described a patient with a family history of breast cancer whose multi-gene panel was denied even though the patient met NCCN criteria. An AIM Specialty Health representative advised ordering the genes one at a time, a process that costs more per-gene, requires multiple authorization requests, and extends the diagnostic timeline from weeks to months. The counselor proceeded with the panel and appealed. The stepwise alternative is not a clinical recommendation. It is a barrier designed to reduce the number of tests that reach completion.

Radiation oncology, the specialty with the highest rate of nondrug prior authorization in Medicare Advantage, provides the downstream evidence. An ASTRO survey of 754 radiation oncologists (September-October 2024) found that prior authorization drove 82% of responding physicians to administer less optimal treatments than initially prescribed, with 65% reporting this occurs in more than 10% of cases, up from 32% in 2019. Thirty percent of respondents reported prior authorization had caused adverse events including emergency room visits, hospitalization, or permanent disability. Seven percent reported it as a contributing factor to patient deaths. Average PA delays lasted 5 days or longer. These are cancer patients. Five days of delayed radiation while a tumor grows is not an administrative inconvenience.

The Staffingly 2026 Prior Authorization Burden Report, published August 7, 2026, quantifies the structural reason the denial system persists despite its documented failure rate: the appeal gap. According to the report's analysis of CMS data, 80.7% of appealed Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials were partially or fully overturned in 2024. But only 11.5% of denied requests were ever appealed. A separate HHS OIG finding cited in the report determined that 13% of denied requests actually met Medicare coverage requirements. The arithmetic is the mechanism. If an insurer denies 100 claims, 13 of which meet coverage requirements on their face, but only 11.5 are appealed, and 80.7% of those appeals succeed, the insurer successfully blocks approximately 4 claims that would have been overturned had they been challenged. Across millions of annual denials, this gap represents billions in care that was owed, denied, and never recovered. Dan Nandan, founder of Staffingly, captured the structural absurdity: "When practices challenge a Medicare Advantage denial, they usually win, and yet almost no one challenges." The system does not need to win on the merits. It needs to make challenging the denial more expensive than absorbing it.

Game Theory Concept
Arrow's Information Paradox Applied to Diagnostic Innovation (Arrow 1962 / Akerlof 1970)

Arrow's (1962) foundational analysis of the economics of invention identified a structural paradox: the value of information cannot be known until it is revealed, but once revealed, the buyer has acquired it without paying. This creates systematic underinvestment in information production. Applied to precision medicine, the paradox operates in reverse: the PA system suppresses information acquisition rather than information production. A 50-gene NGS panel's clinical value lies in what it might find, not in what the insurer expects it to find. But the PA system requires the provider to justify the test's expected value before running it, a logical impossibility for a diagnostic whose purpose is to discover the unexpected. The 3x denial rate for comprehensive panels versus narrow panels is not a coincidence. It is the mechanism design consequence of requiring prospective justification for a tool whose value is inherently retrospective. Akerlof's (1970) "market for lemons" framework extends the analysis: when the PA system disproportionately denies comprehensive tests, it creates adverse selection in the diagnostic market. Providers who persist in ordering multi-gene panels bear higher administrative costs (appeals, peer-to-peer reviews, resubmissions), while providers who default to narrow, less informative tests face lower friction. Over time, the testing mix shifts toward less comprehensive panels, not because they produce better clinical outcomes, but because they produce fewer denials. The information asymmetry is between the insurer's PA criteria (optimized for standardized single-gene lookups, calibrated to historical coding patterns) and the clinical reality of genomic medicine (where the value of testing increases nonlinearly with the number of genes interrogated, because actionable mutations in unexpected genes cannot be identified without testing for them). The appeal gap (11.5% appeal rate against an 80.7% overturn rate) reveals the equilibrium outcome: the system denies informative tests at a rate calibrated to the probability that the denial will go unchallenged, not to the probability that the test lacks clinical value. The denial rate and the overturn rate are not contradictory. They are complementary components of the same extraction mechanism: deny broadly, rely on low appeal rates, and harvest the gap between clinical merit and administrative friction as profit. Arrow's original insight was that markets underinvest in information because its benefits are nonexcludable. The PA system achieves the same underinvestment through a different channel: it makes the cost of acquiring information artificially high by interposing an administrative barrier between the physician's clinical judgment and the test that would confirm or refute it. The result is that the patients who most need precision medicine, those with rare mutations, unusual cancer subtypes, or multi-gene risk profiles, are the patients most likely to be denied access to it, because their clinical profiles are the least legible to a PA system designed for population-level cost containment.

The pediatric cancer data makes the innovation tax concrete. Children with bone sarcomas cannot access genomic testing through insurance because no NCCN guideline exists for their disease, and insurance companies require guideline concordance for approval. The guideline does not exist because the evidence base for rare pediatric tumors is still accumulating. The evidence base cannot accumulate efficiently without widespread genomic testing. And widespread testing cannot occur when insurers deny it for lack of guidelines. This is not a market failure in the traditional sense. It is a mechanism design trap: the PA system requires evidence of value before permitting the test that would generate the evidence of value. For adult cancers with established NCCN guidelines, the trap operates through a different channel: Anthem denies multi-gene panels that the NCCN explicitly recommends, substituting its own coverage policy for the clinical standard. The result is the same. Whether the barrier is "no guideline exists" (pediatric bone cancers) or "we don't incorporate the existing guideline" (Anthem hereditary cancer panels), the PA system functions as a tax on diagnostic innovation, collecting its revenue in delayed diagnoses, missed mutations, and patients who never learn which targeted therapy could have worked because no one tested them for the gene that would have shown it.

The Academic Indictment: When Every Discipline Reaches the Same Verdict

Between late 2024 and mid-2026, something unusual happened in the academic literature. Five independent research teams, working across four disciplines at institutions with no coordinating body, published analyses of AI-driven insurance denial practices. Each team used its own methodology. Each drew on its own data. Each reached structurally identical conclusions. This is worth examining not because academic consensus is inherently interesting, but because it has concrete legal and regulatory consequences that change the game.

The Columbia Law Review published the first peer-reviewed legal scholarship specifically addressing AI-generated denials in Medicare Advantage. Emma Ziegler's Note, "AI-Generated Denials: Medical Necessity in Medicare Advantage Today" (126 Colum. L. Rev. 129, January 2026), argued that MA insurers "hold vast power over access to care" through medical necessity determinations, and that the turn to artificial intelligence has "exacerbated both inaccuracy and opacity in the coverage determination process." The Note's prescription was structural, not incremental: government must demand greater information sharing from MA insurers and enhance beneficiaries' access to the appeals process. Ziegler's analysis did not treat AI-driven denials as a technology problem requiring technical fixes. It treated them as an information asymmetry problem requiring forced disclosure, the same structural diagnosis this analysis reaches through game theory.

Two months later, a team spanning Harvard Law School, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign College of Law, and Duke's Margolis Institute for Health Policy published "Medicare Advantage Becoming a Disadvantage with Use of Artificial Intelligence in Prior Authorization Review" in Nature's npj Digital Medicine (Raza, Gerke, Silcox, Hendricks-Sturrup & Shachar, 2026). Where Ziegler's Columbia analysis mapped the legal architecture, Raza et al. documented the mechanical implementation. Their findings included the PxDx system's average review time of 1.2 seconds per claim, a speed that "clearly does not allow for meaningful human confirmation." They documented EviCore's practice of "turning the dial," in which the third-party utilization management company makes small adjustments to the threshold score for algorithmic review, placing more requests below the approval threshold and sending them for clinical review by in-house staff, generating fee-for-service revenue while increasing the volume of denials. The result, as the authors stated: "more patients facing denials at a faster AI-driven rate." The paper also documented that UnitedHealthcare's post-acute care denial rate jumped from 10.0% in 2020 to 22.7% in 2022, the period during which it was automating the PA process, and that MA PA denial rates rose from 5.6-5.8% in 2019-2021 to 7.4% in 2022.

The regulatory data confirmed what the academics had diagnosed. The NAIC's Health Insurance AI/ML Survey, conducted across 16 states with responses from 93 insurance companies, found that 84% of health insurers use AI/ML across their product lines. The adoption breakdown was revealing: 68% use AI for prior authorization processes, 71% for utilization management, 61% for disease management. But only 12% of companies reported using AI specifically for denying prior authorizations. The gap between 68% (using AI for PA) and 12% (admitting AI denials) is the survey's most important finding, though the NAIC did not frame it that way. If 68% of insurers run AI systems in their PA workflow, and only 12% classify those systems as performing denials, then either the remaining 56% have built AI systems that process PA requests without ever denying them, or the classification reflects a strategic distinction between "AI-assisted PA processing" and "AI-driven denial" that does not survive functional scrutiny. The survey also found that 14% of companies use AI to infer sensitive data such as race, and that 55% rely on third-party AI components, with 15% using entirely third-party solutions. EviCore, the dominant third-party UM vendor whose "turning the dial" practice Raza et al. documented, operates in this ecosystem.

A concurrent analysis in the Columbia Business Law Review (2026) examined "The Legal Implications of Using AI and Algorithms to Combat Health Insurance Administrative Costs," documenting the same 1.2-second PxDx review time and the same structural tension: insurers claim AI reduces administrative burden while the evidence shows it reduces claim approval rates. The piece mapped the emerging patchwork of state regulation, from California's SB 1120 (prohibiting AI-based denial of medical necessity without physician review) to New York's proposed algorithm certification requirements, concluding that "insurers are proceeding at their own risk" in the majority of states with no express AI regulation.

What makes this convergence analytically significant is not that multiple academics agree, which happens in every field, but that each analysis independently identified the same structural mechanism: the information asymmetry between what the AI system does (process claims at 1.2-second speed, apply adjustable threshold scores, generate denials at rates correlated with automation timing) and what the insurer discloses (aggregate approval rates, voluntary reform pledges, compliance with coverage criteria). Ziegler identified the asymmetry through legal doctrine. Raza et al. identified it through clinical and regulatory evidence. The NAIC survey revealed it through the insurers' own admissions. The Columbia Business Law Review mapped its legal exposure. None cited each other. None shared data. They converged because the underlying structure left no room for divergence.

Game Theory Concept
Aumann's Agreement Theorem and the Common Knowledge Transformation (Aumann 1976)

Aumann's (1976) Agreement Theorem proves that rational agents with common priors who communicate their posterior beliefs cannot "agree to disagree": once each agent's conclusion is common knowledge, all posteriors must converge. The theorem has a precise application to the academic convergence on AI-driven denial practices. When the Columbia Law Review (legal analysis), Nature's npj Digital Medicine (clinical/regulatory evidence), the NAIC survey (industry self-report), and the Columbia Business Law Review (liability mapping) independently reach structurally identical conclusions, Aumann's theorem predicts that any rational decision-maker exposed to the full evidence base must arrive at the same posterior. This transforms the regulatory calculus. Before the convergence, a regulator or judge could treat AI-driven denials as a contested empirical question with legitimate disagreement. After five independent analyses from four disciplines reach the same conclusion, continued inaction cannot be attributed to epistemic uncertainty. It must instead reflect either incomplete information exposure (the decision-maker has not read the evidence) or a prior weighted by considerations other than the evidence (regulatory capture, political pressure, industry lobbying). The legal consequence is direct: tort law's "knew or should have known" standard maps precisely onto Aumann's epistemic framework. A regulator who has access to the NAIC's own survey data showing 84% AI adoption, the npj Digital Medicine documentation of 1.2-second review times, and the Columbia Law Review's doctrinal analysis of disclosure failures can no longer claim reasonable uncertainty about whether AI-driven PA systems produce inappropriate denials. The academic consensus has collapsed the information asymmetry between critics and defenders, converting what was a debatable practice into a documented mechanism. Aumann's theorem does not guarantee that regulators will act. It guarantees that if they do not act, their inaction reveals information about their utility function that is no longer consistent with the claim of protecting beneficiary welfare. The common knowledge transformation has a second-order effect: it changes the game for litigators. Every class action plaintiff can now cite peer-reviewed analyses across four disciplines documenting the same mechanism. The defense that "our AI system is proprietary and its effects are contested" becomes untenable when the effects have been characterized independently by Harvard, Columbia, Duke, and the NAIC itself. The 12% vs. 68% gap in the NAIC data (12% admit AI denials vs. 68% use AI for PA) functions as a revealed preference signal in Aumann's framework: the gap between disclosed use and disclosed denial is either an admission that 56% of AI-PA systems genuinely never deny anything (implausible), or evidence that the disclosure itself is strategically constructed to minimize regulatory exposure (Milgrom 1981, "Good News and Bad News: Representation Theorems and Applications"). In either case, the gap provides the evidentiary foundation for mandatory disclosure requirements, because voluntary disclosure has been demonstrated to produce systematically incomplete information.

The NAIC survey's 14% figure for AI systems that infer sensitive data including race adds a dimension that none of the individual analyses fully explored. If 14% of health insurers use AI to infer racial identity, and AI-driven PA denials are known to fall disproportionately on minority populations (as documented in separate Health Affairs and JAMA analyses), then the combination of race inference and denial automation creates a disparate impact pathway that maps directly onto Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act and the HHS Office for Civil Rights' 2024 clarification that nondiscrimination principles apply to AI in clinical decision support. The npj Digital Medicine team flagged this connection: CMS "clarified that Medicare services must be provided equitably, without discrimination, including MA services using AI." But the enforcement mechanism remains unclear, especially after the current administration's rollback of AI-specific executive orders.

The practical consequence of the academic convergence is already visible in litigation. Every major pending case against health insurers, from Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group to the Jefferson Health challenge to the Anthem PBRT settlement (final approval hearing held August 19, 2026, covering approximately 140 prostate cancer patients denied coverage for treatments costing $30,000 to $95,000 and settling for $3.625 million, or roughly $26,000 per patient), can now cite a peer-reviewed evidentiary base across four independent disciplines. The Aetna PBRT settlement, separately finalized in federal court, established a parallel precedent: 71 prostate cancer patients whose claims were denied between 2015 and 2024 received $12,000 to $48,000 each, without being required to demonstrate medical necessity. The settlements themselves function as revealed preference evidence: insurers are paying to resolve claims they originally classified as not medically necessary, implicitly conceding that the classification was strategic rather than clinical. But the settlement amounts ($26,000 per patient for treatments costing $30,000-$95,000) confirm that the denial-and-settle strategy remains cheaper than full coverage, meaning the academic consensus has not yet changed the payoff structure enough to make denial the dominated strategy. It has only changed the evidentiary landscape in which the next round of enforcement actions will be evaluated.

The Employer's Blind Spot: When Plan Sponsors Pay for Harm They Don't Measure

There is a player in this game who could discipline insurers but has chosen not to. Approximately 155 million Americans get their health insurance through an employer. The employer selects the plan, negotiates the contract, and pays most of the premium, spending on average $18,500 per employee in 2026, the highest amount on record and rising at 6.5% annually, the fastest pace in fifteen years (Mercer 2025 National Survey). The employer is the insurer's customer. The employee is the insurer's subject. And the employer, with remarkable consistency, measures the cost of the relationship but not its quality.

A Stanford study published in January 2025 (Singer, Pfeffer, and colleagues) surveyed large employers about what health plan metrics they track. The results were stark: 74% of companies tracked trends in health benefits costs. Only 8% tracked how long employees spent getting questions answered by their insurer. Only 7% tracked how often employees delayed getting care because of insurer actions, whether a denied prior authorization, a rejected claim, or an unresolved appeal. Seven percent. Three out of four employers meticulously monitor what they pay. Fewer than one in ten monitor whether their employees actually receive care.

The consequences of this measurement gap are now documented at population scale. The Commonwealth Fund's 2025 Affordability Survey (6,353 adults, published June 2026) found that 21% of privately insured working-age adults, most of them on employer-sponsored plans, had coverage denied for themselves or a family member in the past year. Among those who experienced a prior authorization denial, 41% said it delayed their care and 28% said a health problem worsened as a result. Sixty-three percent reported significant worry or anxiety. Forty-three percent of those with a claim denial said it led to medical debt they were still paying off. But only about half ever appealed, and of those who did not, 56% said they were not sure they had the right to challenge the decision, 34% did not know who to contact, and only 55% believed an appeal would make a difference.

A separate Paytient study ("The Hidden Lives of Workplace Insured Americans," 2026) found that 40% of employees with employer-sponsored coverage have delayed or forgone medical treatment because they could not afford it. Thirty-nine percent delayed primary care. Forty-eight percent postponed specialist referrals. Fifty-six percent went without dental treatment. Non-adherence driven by these cost barriers accounts for up to 69% of medication-related hospitalizations, costing the healthcare system roughly $100 billion annually. And a Prudential survey of 3,096 full-time workers (January 2026) found that 71% saw medical costs rise at least 5%, with 22% experiencing increases of 15% or more. Thirty-two percent reported financial stress from rising medical costs. Twenty-two percent reported impacts on their mental health. Yet only 13% of employees turned to their employer's resources for help.

The game-theoretic structure is a bilateral monitoring failure. The employer is the principal in two simultaneous relationships: with the insurer (contracting for coverage) and with the employee (offering benefits as compensation). In the first relationship, the employer monitors cost because cost is observable, contractual, and directly affects the corporate budget. In the second relationship, the employee's experience with denials, delays, and abandonment of care is invisible to the employer because the employer does not measure it. The insurer, as the agent, optimizes for the metrics the employer tracks. Cost containment is rewarded. Denial rates, appeal barriers, and employee health outcomes are not penalized because they are not observed.

This creates a perverse feedback loop. When Mercer reports that 51% of large employers plan to shift even more cost to employees in 2026, through higher deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, the employers are responding to the only signal they measure (rising plan costs) without knowing that their employees are already delaying care at crisis levels (40% per Paytient), accumulating medical debt from denied claims (43% per Commonwealth Fund), and experiencing health deterioration that will manifest as higher future claims, absenteeism, and productivity loss. The employer is paying $18,500 per employee for a product whose performance it does not evaluate. The insurer's incentive, under these conditions, is clear: reduce visible costs (the metric the employer watches) by increasing invisible harm (the metric nobody watches). Prior authorization is the mechanism that converts one into the other.

Game Theory Concept
Bilateral Monitoring Failure in Multi-Tier Agency (Holmström 1979)

Holmström's (1979) moral hazard framework established that an agent's effort on unmonitored dimensions of performance will deteriorate to the minimum tolerable level, because the principal cannot reward or punish what it does not observe. In the employer-insurer-employee triad, the employer monitors cost (premium, claims, MCR) with 74% adoption but monitors care access (denial rates, delay frequency, employee health impact) at 7-8%. The prediction is precise: insurer performance on cost containment will be satisfactory (this is what the contract enforces), while performance on care delivery will deteriorate (this is what no one measures). The 21% denial rate among privately insured adults (Commonwealth Fund) is not a bug in the system. It is the equilibrium output of a monitoring structure that penalizes cost but not harm. The employer's measurement gap does not merely fail to detect the problem. It creates the problem, by signaling to the insurer that care quality is not a contractual performance metric. Stiglitz's (2002) extension of moral hazard to information asymmetry in insurance markets anticipated precisely this dynamic: when the party with bargaining power (the employer) does not acquire information about the agent's (insurer's) impact on the third party (employee), the third party's welfare becomes an externality that the contract does not internalize. The employer pays for insurance. The employee pays for denial. The gap between them is the monitoring failure.

The measurement gap also explains why ERISA reform has been so difficult to achieve politically. Employers who sponsor ERISA plans are the natural constituency for PA reform, because their employees bear the harm and their benefit budgets bear the downstream cost of delayed care. But because employers do not measure denial rates, they do not perceive themselves as harmed. The 74%-vs.-7% measurement ratio means employers experience PA as a cost control tool (which they track and appreciate) rather than a care barrier (which they do not track and cannot evaluate). The DeSaulnier ERISA package (four bills targeting transparency, appeal rights, and clinic assistance, introduced July 2026) and the House Ed & Workforce Committee's "Denied" report (April 2026) have not generated significant employer lobbying support, despite the fact that employer-sponsored plans cover the largest segment of the insured population. The employers are absent from the reform coalition because the measurement structure makes denial invisible to the only party with the contractual leverage to stop it. As the Stanford researchers concluded: "Our findings suggest that companies focus on what their health plans cost the company rather than how they benefit their employees' health and well-being." That focus is not neutral. It is the mechanism by which 155 million Americans' insurance quality goes unmonitored.

The Global Outlier: When Other Nations Solved the Same Game

Every developed nation faces the same fundamental coordination problem in healthcare: how to allocate finite medical resources among patients with effectively infinite demand while compensating providers fairly and keeping costs sustainable. The game theory is universal. The equilibrium the United States reached is not.

The scale of the divergence is quantified. Papanicolas, Woskie, and Jha (JAMA, 2018) compared US healthcare spending to ten other high-income countries and found that Americans spent $2,497 per capita on administrative costs, more than four times Canada's $551 and more than twelve times Japan's $199. Administrative costs consumed 8% of US GDP devoted to healthcare, compared to 1-3% in peer nations. The US spent 17.8% of GDP on healthcare overall, five points above the next-highest spender and nearly double the OECD average. The result: among the 11 countries studied, the US had the highest infant mortality rate, the lowest life expectancy, and the highest rate of avoidable deaths. Americans paid the most and received the least.

Woolhandler, Campbell, and Himmelstein (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2020) quantified the structural mechanism: Billing and Insurance-Related (BIR) costs in the US totaled $812 billion annually, accounting for 34.2% of total healthcare expenditure. In Canada's single-payer system, BIR costs consumed 16.7%. The difference, roughly $600 billion annually in excess administrative spending, is larger than the entire defense budget. It funds the bureaucratic infrastructure this article has spent 200+ pages analyzing: the PA processing, the denial algorithms, the appeal reviews, the provider credentialing, the benefits verification, the claim adjudication, the utilization management, and the 100,000 full-time nursing equivalents spent filing paperwork instead of treating patients.

The Commonwealth Fund's Mirror Mirror report (2024, 10 countries, 71 performance metrics) ranked the United States last overall, last on access to care, last on equity, and last on health outcomes. Australia, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom occupied the top three positions. The US ranked first in only one category: healthcare spending per capita. The countries that solved the coordination problem most effectively share a structural feature absent from the US system: the entity that pays for care also has the institutional authority and incentive to monitor its quality. In the UK, the NHS is both payer and system administrator. In Germany, sickness funds negotiate directly with provider associations under a federal legal framework. In Japan, the government sets fee schedules that apply universally. In Australia, Medicare (the national program, not the US program of the same name) provides universal coverage with centralized quality monitoring. None of these systems use prior authorization at the scale the United States does, because none of them needed to: when the payer is also the steward, the adversarial relationship between insurer and patient that PA was designed to mediate does not exist in the same form.

The game theory explains the divergence precisely. In the US system, the insurer's profit function is directly proportional to the gap between premiums collected and claims paid. Every denied claim improves the medical cost ratio. Every delayed treatment reduces the present value of the obligation. The PA system is the institutional mechanism by which this profit motive is operationalized. In systems with universal coverage, the payer's incentive structure is different: the government pays for care and also bears the downstream cost of delayed or denied treatment (disability, lost productivity, emergency department visits, social services). The externalities that the US system exports to patients and employers are internalized by a single payer, which means the payer has no incentive to create administrative friction, because that friction's costs flow back to the same entity. The prior authorization system is not just an American regulatory choice. It is the equilibrium output of a specific incentive structure that exists only in market-based, multi-payer systems where the insurer can externalize the costs of denial onto parties (patients, providers, employers, the public health system) who lack the contractual leverage to object.

Path Dependence and Institutional Lock-In (Arthur 1989 / North 1990)

W. Brian Arthur's (1989) model of competing technologies showed that early advantages, historical accidents, and increasing returns can lock an economy into an inferior equilibrium even when all participants recognize that a superior alternative exists. Douglass North's (1990) extension to institutional economics demonstrated the same dynamic in regulatory and governance structures: once a nation's institutions crystallize around a particular organizational logic, the coordination costs of switching to an alternative exceed the efficiency gains, even when the alternative is Pareto-superior. The US healthcare system exhibits textbook lock-in. The employer-sponsored insurance model emerged from a historical accident (WWII wage controls that made employer-provided health benefits tax-exempt), evolved through a managed care revolution in the 1980s-90s that introduced PA as a cost-containment mechanism, and now sustains an $812 billion administrative infrastructure that employs millions of workers whose livelihoods depend on the system's continuation. Every insurer, hospital billing department, PA processing vendor, utilization management company, and healthcare IT firm represents a constituency with a concentrated interest in preserving the current equilibrium. The patients who bear the cost of the system are diffuse; the entities that profit from it are concentrated. This is Olson's (1965) logic of collective action applied to institutional persistence: the beneficiaries of the current system can organize to defend it more effectively than the victims can organize to change it. Other nations avoided this lock-in not because their policymakers were wiser but because their institutional histories did not pass through the same sequence of path-dependent choices. The UK established the NHS in 1948 before an employer-sponsored insurance industry could form. Canada adopted single-payer province by province between 1947 and 1966, preempting the multi-payer complexity that makes US reform so difficult. Germany's sickness fund system predates modern insurance markets entirely, originating in Bismarck's 1883 legislation. Each nation's equilibrium reflects its institutional starting point, not a deliberate choice among alternatives. The US did not choose PA-heavy gatekeeping. It arrived at it through a sequence of locally rational decisions that, cumulatively, produced a globally suboptimal outcome.

The lock-in has a measurable cost beyond administrative spending. The Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker (2024) found that Americans use healthcare services at roughly average rates compared to peer nations, visit doctors less frequently than citizens of Germany or France, and have shorter average hospital stays than patients in Japan or Germany. The spending difference is almost entirely driven by higher prices and higher administrative overhead, not by higher utilization. The US spends more per capita on healthcare than any other country and achieves worse population health outcomes, not because Americans consume too much care but because too large a fraction of each healthcare dollar is absorbed by the administrative apparatus that decides whether care will be provided.

The international comparison reveals that the game the US healthcare system is playing is not the only game available. Twenty-eight of the 38 OECD member nations achieve universal or near-universal coverage through systems that do not require patients to obtain insurer approval before receiving physician-ordered care. The PA system that this article has analyzed across 60+ subsections and 360+ sources is not a universal feature of modern healthcare. It is a structural artifact of the American institutional path, maintained by the concentrated interests that profit from it and imposed on the diffuse population that cannot organize effectively against it. Every year that the system continues, the lock-in deepens: more workers are employed in healthcare administration, more IT systems are built around PA workflows, more insurers develop proprietary denial algorithms, and more institutional capital accumulates on the side of the status quo. Arthur's model predicts that switching becomes harder over time, not easier, even as the evidence of the alternative's superiority becomes more overwhelming. The 6.5 million PA eliminations celebrated as reform in 2025-2026 must be understood against this baseline: they represent marginal adjustments within a locked-in equilibrium, not a phase transition to a different game. The fundamental structure, an adversarial relationship between payer and patient mediated by administrative gatekeeping, remains intact. Other nations never built it. The US may never be able to dismantle it.

The Retiree Revolt: When Forced Migration Exposes the Hidden Game

There is a population uniquely positioned to recognize the game being played: retirees who have spent decades inside the healthcare system and understand, through accumulated personal experience, the difference between coverage on paper and care in practice. When employers try to migrate this population from traditional Medicare plus a supplemental plan into Medicare Advantage to cut costs, the retirees resist. Not because they are irrational. Because they are the most informed players in the game.

New York City has been trying to force approximately 250,000 retired municipal workers from traditional Medicare with GHI Senior Care supplemental coverage into a Medicare Advantage plan since 2021. Former Mayor Bill de Blasio initiated the switch, projecting $600 million in annual savings for the city. Mayor Eric Adams continued the push. The Municipal Labor Committee, dominated by the UFT and DC37 (the city's two largest unions), voted to approve the migration over objections from the FDNY union, the Police Benevolent Association, and thousands of individual retirees. The PBA formally opposed "forcing Medicare-eligible members into the Medicare Advantage Plan." The FDNY union president, Oren Barzilay, reported that Aetna, the proposed MA provider, had told retired members its plan "doesn't cover certain medicines to the same degree traditional Medicare does." The retirees heard the admission. They organized.

The NYC Organization of Public Service Retirees (NYCOPSR), led by Marianne Pizzitola, filed suit in Manhattan Supreme Court in 2022, challenging both the forced MA migration and $15 copays that the city had imposed on medical visits under the GHI Senior Care plan between January 2022 and January 2023. Judge Lyle Frank sided with the retirees, blocking the MA switch and granting a temporary injunction that halted the copays for two years, saving retirees an estimated $110 million. The city appealed. In June 2025, the state's highest court, the Court of Appeals, ruled that the city's oral and written assurances to retirees did not constitute a "clear and unambiguous promise" of supplemental coverage for life, clearing the legal path for a future MA migration. But the retirees had already won the copay fight. On July 30, 2026, the city and EmblemHealth agreed to a $53 million settlement, representing 100% of the disputed copays, one of the largest class action settlements in New York City history. The settlement also froze the $15 copay through at least December 31, 2027.

The game theory is a multi-round negotiation between asymmetrically informed parties within an incomplete contract. The original employment agreements between the city and its workers specified "health benefits" but did not freeze the plan structure or prohibit copays that did not exist at the time of hiring. When the city exploited this contractual incompleteness by imposing $15 copays and proposing MA migration, it was engaging in ex post renegotiation of terms the workers had relied upon for decades. A 100-year-old retired firefighter, Dan Stromer, lives on a $26,000 annual pension. The $15 copay per medical visit, which Pizzitola described as "one of the worst, most regressive burdens making healthcare unaffordable," falls disproportionately on retirees who need care most frequently and can afford it least. Retirees are now skipping oncology appointments, occupational therapy, and other treatments. The city saved money. The retirees lost care. The same transaction, seen from two sides.

New York is not alone. Delaware retirees sued their state over a similar forced MA migration in 2022, arguing the State Employee Benefits Committee failed to follow Administrative Procedures Act requirements for notice, comment, and public hearings. The complaint alleged that the state's communications to retirees "have been, at best, confusing and misleading. At worst, the realities of Medicare Advantage have been hidden." State Rep. John Kowalko called the plan "an atrocity to retirees." The state cited a $10 billion unfunded liability for retiree healthcare, projected to reach $31 billion by 2050, as justification. The pattern is structural: public employers facing fiscal pressure discover that migrating retirees from traditional Medicare to MA transfers the cost of care from the employer's budget to the retiree's body. The employer sees lower premiums. The retiree encounters the denial rates, prior authorization barriers, and network restrictions that this article has documented across 60+ subsections.

The retirees' resistance is rational precisely because they possess information that the employer's cost models do not capture. They know, from lived experience, that MA plans deny 12% of standard prior authorization requests (KFF, CMS-0057-F data), that 67% of those denials are overturned on appeal but only 11.5% are ever appealed (Staffingly 2026), and that the "savings" the employer projects are achieved by denying care that traditional Medicare would have covered automatically. The $600 million NYC projected in annual savings from the MA switch is the employer's version of the insurer's medical cost ratio improvement: money saved by not paying for care. The retirees are the only players in this game who understand that the savings are extracted from their health.

Game Theory Concept
Incomplete Contracts and Ex Post Renegotiation (Grossman & Hart 1986 / Hart & Moore 1990)

Hart and Moore's (1990) theory of incomplete contracts established that when a contract cannot specify all future contingencies, the party with residual control rights can exploit the incompleteness to extract surplus ex post. Employment contracts that promise "health benefits" are paradigmatically incomplete: they specify a benefit category without fixing the plan structure, network, formulary, or prior authorization requirements that determine whether the benefit delivers actual care. The employer retains the right to change plans (residual control) while the retiree depends on the benefit for survival (relationship-specific investment). This creates what Williamson (1975) called a "fundamental transformation": after retirement, the employee cannot renegotiate compensation, switch employers, or acquire alternative coverage without paying a substantial premium. The retiree's investment in the employment relationship is sunk. The employer's ability to restructure benefits is intact. The resulting hold-up problem predicts exactly the dynamics observed in NYC: the city extracts surplus from retirees by degrading the quality of their healthcare benefit (adding copays, proposing MA migration) after the retirees have lost all bargaining alternatives. The NYCOPSR litigation, which recovered $53 million in copays plus $110 million in avoided charges, represents the courts' intervention as a third-party enforcement mechanism for the implicit terms of an incomplete contract. But enforcement is reactive and expensive. The 250,000 retirees needed collective organization, legal representation, and four years of litigation to recover money the city should never have charged. The asymmetry persists: the employer can impose costs unilaterally, while the retirees must litigate collectively to reverse them. Every year the litigation continues is a year retirees skip oncology appointments because they cannot afford the copay.

The Arbitration Paradox: When Patient Protection Becomes Insurer Subsidy

The No Surprises Act of 2020 was supposed to fix one of the system's cruelest games: patients receiving emergency care at out-of-network facilities, then being bankrupted by "surprise" bills they had no ability to avoid or negotiate. The law channeled payment disputes into an independent dispute resolution (IDR) process anchored by a Qualifying Payment Amount (QPA), the median contracted in-network rate for a given service in a given region. The QPA was designed to be a neutral benchmark. It was not.

On August 11, 2026, the full 17-judge 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled en banc that the government's QPA calculation methodology was unlawful on two of three challenged points. The ruling was the Texas Medical Association's sixth consecutive legal victory against the NSA's implementation since November 2022. The court found that federal agencies had directed insurers to include "ghost rates" in QPA calculations: placeholder rates for services a provider lists in their contract but never actually performs. An OB-GYN who does not deliver babies might have a contract listing obstetric services at $1. Including that $1 in the median calculation deflated the QPA, because providers had no incentive to negotiate rates for services they would never bill. The district court had found that the rules allowed insurers to include rates "for services that are not provided, never have been provided, and never will be provided." The Fifth Circuit agreed, holding that the agencies had "upended" the IDR process. The court also ruled that the QPA must include bonus and incentive payments, which represent a material component of many provider compensation structures. The agencies' exclusion of these payments further suppressed the benchmark.

The numbers confirm how thoroughly the methodology was gamed. CMS told the New York Times that arbitration awards to doctors through the NSA process tripled from $4.1 billion in 2024 to $14.9 billion in 2025, calling the system "gamed." But the data tells the opposite story: providers prevailed in more than 80% of resolved disputes, and arbitrators chose a payment rate above the QPA in 85% of decisions. The arbitrators, presented with evidence from both sides, consistently concluded that the QPA was too low. The 85% figure is not evidence that providers are gaming the system. It is evidence that the QPA was designed to produce a number that does not reflect the actual cost of care.

This is the same mechanism design failure documented throughout this analysis, expressed in a different institutional setting. The insurer's private information, which rates are genuinely negotiated versus which are contractual ghosts, was used to construct a purportedly neutral benchmark that systematically favored the insurer. The regulator validated this construction, and for four years the artificially low anchor shaped every arbitration outcome. The 5th Circuit's six successive rulings have progressively stripped away the layers of methodological advantage, but the structural pattern recurs: every attempt to create a "neutral" mechanism within the US healthcare system is colonized by the party with information asymmetry and lobbying resources.

Anchor Manipulation in Arbitration Design (Kahneman & Tversky 1974 / Schelling 1960)

Kahneman and Tversky's (1974) anchoring bias demonstrates that initial reference points disproportionately influence final judgments even when the anchor is arbitrary. Schelling's (1960) focal point theory shows how parties coordinate around a salient number in bargaining. The QPA was designed to serve as both: the official anchor and the coordination focal point for IDR proceedings. By controlling the methodology behind the anchor's calculation, the insurer effectively predetermined the arbitration outcome before the hearing began. Including ghost rates as low as $1 for unprovided services is not a neutral statistical choice; it is strategic focal-point manipulation. The Fifth Circuit identified this when it found that ghost rates had "upended" the dispute resolution process. The ruling restores the anchor to reflect actually negotiated, actually performed, actually compensated services, but it also illustrates a broader principle: in any arbitration mechanism where one party controls the reference-point construction, the mechanism will produce outcomes that reflect the constructor's interests, not the parties' true costs. The NSA's fundamental design error was delegating anchor construction to agencies captured by the industry they regulate, reproducing the same information asymmetry the law was meant to correct.

The ruling's implications extend beyond surprise billing. The QPA methodology was built on the same logic that underlies prior authorization: the insurer uses its superior information position to set the terms of engagement. In PA, the insurer decides which treatments require approval and which criteria to apply. In NSA arbitration, the insurer supplies the contracted rates that compute the QPA. In both cases, the patient or provider faces a take-it-or-challenge-it proposition where the challenge is expensive, time-consuming, and structurally disadvantaged. The Fifth Circuit had to sit en banc, all 17 judges, to reverse its own prior three-judge panel decision. Six judges partially dissented. The legal system required four years and six separate lawsuits to identify and correct a calculation methodology that a healthcare economist could have flagged in an afternoon. The Sidley Austin lawyers representing TMA called it their sixth victory. Providers will not always have elite counsel willing to litigate for four years. The patients protected by the No Surprises Act, those rushed to the nearest emergency room regardless of network status, are the least equipped to notice or challenge how their payment disputes are resolved. The arbitration paradox is complete: legislation designed to protect patients from insurer pricing power was implemented using a methodology that subsidized insurer pricing power, and required half a decade of litigation to partially correct.

The Calibration Paradox: When Denial Quality Tracks Vulnerability, Not Medicine

The KFF analysis of August 13, 2026, did more than rank insurers by denial rate. It exposed a pattern that the aggregate numbers obscure: the same insurer applies materially different denial standards to different market segments. UnitedHealth Group denied 17% of standard Medicare Advantage requests, 11% of Medicaid managed care requests, and 21% of ACA Marketplace requests. These percentages suggest that UNH is most permissive with Medicaid patients and most restrictive with ACA enrollees. The appeal overturn data tells the opposite story. When Medicaid patients appealed UNH denials, 81% were overturned. When MA patients appealed, 60% were overturned. When ACA patients appealed, only 38% were overturned. The 81% Medicaid overturn rate means that more than four in five challenged denials could not withstand scrutiny. The 38% ACA overturn rate means that nearly two in three challenged denials were upheld. The insurer is not applying a uniform clinical standard across business lines. It is constructing more defensible denials where patients are more likely to fight and less defensible denials where patients are less likely to challenge.

The pattern holds across insurers. Centene overturned 93% of MA appeals, 47% of Medicaid appeals, and 54% of ACA appeals. CVS overturned 89% of MA appeals but only 22% of Medicaid appeals. Every major insurer exhibits different denial defensibility across market segments, and the variation does not track clinical complexity. A Medicaid patient and an ACA patient with the same condition, requesting the same procedure, adjudicated by the same insurer, face denials of systematically different quality. The difference is the patient's insurance type, which correlates with their resources, sophistication, and institutional support for navigating appeals. KFF noted that denials are rarely appealed in any market, citing the 11.5% MA appeal rate documented by the Staffingly report. Medicaid patients appeal at even lower rates, because the population faces higher barriers: fewer English-proficient family members to navigate the process, less access to legal aid, more precarious employment that cannot absorb the time cost of a multi-week administrative challenge. The insurer's rational response is to invest less in the clinical defensibility of Medicaid denials, because the probability that any individual denial will be tested is lower.

KFF identified a second structural distortion that compounds the first: CMS requires insurers to report only percentages, not absolute numbers of requests received or denied. A previous KFF analysis of MA found that the number of prior authorization determinations per enrollee was inversely related to the denial rate. Insurers that processed more requests denied a smaller share of them. As a result, the absolute number of denied requests per enrollee was similar across insurers with very different denial rates. The headline rankings, UNH at 17%, Elevance at 5%, are percentages. They may not reflect a proportional difference in the number of patients denied care. An insurer with a 5% denial rate processing 3.0 PA requests per enrollee denies 0.15 requests per enrollee. An insurer with a 17% denial rate processing 1.0 request per enrollee denies 0.17. The patient experience converges even as the reported statistics diverge. CMS chose to require the metric that allows divergent presentation and made the metric that would enable convergent analysis, the denominator, optional. KFF's InsuranceNewsNet analysis noted that most insurers did not provide the optional numeric counts. In July 2026, CMS published an updated template for the 2027 reporting period specifying that numerators and denominators are "expected," and a proposed rule would make them mandatory. The correction arrives years after the first report.

Gold card programs introduce a third distortion. Insurers that exempt high-compliance providers from PA requirements will mechanically report higher denial rates in their public filings, because the denominator no longer includes the routinely approved requests from gold-carded providers. The remaining request pool is enriched for edge cases, novel procedures, and providers who historically trigger more denials. The insurer most committed to PA reform looks worse on the CMS scorecard than the insurer that processes every request through the full bureaucratic pipeline. KFF acknowledged this: "Insurers that rely heavily on gold carding may, in turn, report lower approval rates: since providers that are most clinically compliant are exempt from prior authorization, reported statistics from these insurers include only providers that may inherently have lower approval rates." The scorecard penalizes the behavior it was designed to encourage.

Ramsey Pricing Applied to Administrative Barriers (Ramsey 1927 / Robinson 1933)

Ramsey's (1927) inverse elasticity rule, originally derived for optimal commodity taxation, demonstrated that the least-distortionary tax system charges higher rates on goods with less elastic demand. Robinson (1933) generalized this to monopoly pricing, showing that a price-discriminating firm optimally charges higher prices in market segments with lower demand elasticity. The KFF per-insurer, cross-market appeal overturn data reveals a structural analog applied to PA denial behavior. The insurer is not varying the price of a service. It is varying the quality of a denial, measured by defensibility on appeal, inversely to each population's "appeal elasticity," the probability that a given denial will be challenged. In Medicaid, where patients have the most inelastic appeal demand (fewest resources, least institutional support, highest opportunity cost of administrative challenge), UNH's overturn rate is 81%, meaning most denials lack clinical justification. In the ACA Marketplace, where patients have more elastic appeal demand (higher incomes, commercial insurance literacy, access to employer HR departments and legal aid), UNH's overturn rate is 38%, meaning most denials are clinically defensible. The insurer is not applying medicine differently across markets. It is applying Ramsey pricing to administrative obstruction: lower-quality denials where patients cannot fight, higher-quality denials where they can. The Medicaid patient absorbs the unjustified denial. The ACA patient receives a denial that was actually reviewed. The cross-market variance in overturn rates is invisible in the percentage-only reporting CMS mandated, because the scorecard reports the denial rate (the toll) and not the wrongful denial rate (the toll multiplied by the overturn probability). A transparency mechanism that measures the wrong variable does not produce accountability. It produces the appearance of accountability, which is worse, because it forecloses the political demand for a mechanism that would actually work.

The interaction between these three distortions, percentage-only reporting, cross-market denial calibration, and gold card selection bias, produces a scorecard that is worse than useless. It is actively misleading. An insurer can rank as the "most permissive" in a given market while denying care with less clinical justification than its competitors. An insurer that eliminates PA for compliant providers can see its reported denial rate rise. And the aggregate overturn rates (67% MA, 47% Medicaid, 43% ACA) mask per-insurer variations so large that the averages tell almost nothing about any individual company's behavior. Centene's 93% MA overturn rate and Kaiser's 40% MA overturn rate are both inside the 67% average. They describe fundamentally different institutional practices, but the reporting framework treats them as members of the same distribution. CMS's 2026 proposed rule would require numeric counts, standardize denominators, and expand the metrics. If finalized, it would correct the most elementary design failures. But the first year of mandatory reporting has already established a baseline that will shape public perception, legislative debate, and insurer strategy for years. The rankings published on August 13 became the reference point. The methodological caveats buried in KFF's technical analysis did not. This is not accidental. It is how information asymmetry reproduces itself in a transparency regime: the insurer shapes the metric, the metric shapes the headline, and the headline shapes the policy response.

The EMTALA Arbitrage: When Emergency Rooms Exit the Social Contract

For forty years, the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act of 1986 functioned as American healthcare's bedrock commitment device. Any hospital that accepted Medicare, which was virtually all of them, was legally required to screen and stabilize every patient who arrived at its emergency department regardless of ability to pay. The enforcement mechanism was the "Medicare Death Penalty": loss of CMS certification, which would eliminate access to the over-65 population (roughly a third of hospital revenue) and effectively force closure. For four decades, no rational hospital operator would voluntarily exit Medicare, because the revenue loss would be catastrophic. EMTALA compliance was universal not because operators were altruistic, but because the penalty made noncompliance financially suicidal. The mechanism worked.

Then the No Surprises Act of 2022 changed the payoff matrix.

The NSA, designed to protect patients from balance billing by out-of-network providers, created an Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process through which out-of-network providers could submit billing disputes to federal arbitrators. The arbitrators would select either the provider's or the insurer's proposed rate, with no compromise. For a certain class of provider, this created a revenue stream that exceeded Medicare reimbursement. A STAT investigation published June 29, 2026, documented the result: Houston-based Nutex Health, operating 27 microhospitals across 12 states, declined Medicare at most of its facilities. Without Medicare participation, those facilities are not legally bound by EMTALA. Nutex nearly quadrupled its revenue to $875 million in 2025 by staying out-of-network and routing most bills through the NSA arbitration process. Profit grew nearly twelve-fold.

The strategic logic is precise. Nutex opens in wealthy, well-insured suburban areas. It charges emergency-room prices for emergency care. It avoids the Medicare population (lower reimbursement rates, higher acuity, regulatory compliance costs). And it is freed from the legal obligation to treat anyone who cannot pay. Dr. Amber Sabbatini, an emergency medicine professor at the University of Washington, described the model as "exploiting the benefits" of emergency care without taking on its obligations. Over 60% of Nutex's revenue derives from the NSA arbitration process, intermediated by a Texas-based firm called HaloMD whose tactics are the subject of multiple lawsuits. Nutex investors are suing the company for concealing the HaloMD partnership, and state regulators in Idaho and New Mexico are investigating.

What happens to patients who arrive at an EMTALA-exempt facility without commercial insurance? Robert Behounek, 34, went to an Albuquerque Nutex ER with chest pain, difficulty breathing, and swelling. Staff told him the visit could cost more than $1,600 up front and that he could not be seen without paying. "It was literally just, 'No money, you don't get treatment,'" he told STAT. No one checked his blood pressure or listened to his chest. He drove himself to another hospital, where doctors diagnosed systolic heart failure and a minor heart attack. In a separate case, Julie Bliss rushed her 11-year-old daughter to a Nutex facility near Oklahoma City after the child fainted and appeared to have a seizure. A staffer stopped the exam over payment. Bliss handed over a credit card and was charged $100 to resume care. Nutex CEO Dr. Tom Vo responded: "If you're going to die, we treat you." The company said its records did not support the patients' accounts.

The EMTALA mechanism was designed against a world where Medicare participation was economically necessary. The CMS fine for violation ($50,000 per occurrence) plus the Medicare Death Penalty constituted sufficient deterrence because no hospital could survive without Medicare revenue. The NSA created a world where Medicare participation is optional for a certain operator class, neutralizing both the fine (irrelevant to a non-participant) and the death penalty (inapplicable to a non-participant). The safety net does not have a hole. It has an exit. And the exit is located precisely where the commercially insured population is densest and the uninsured population is thinnest, because that is where the NSA arbitrage generates the highest returns.

Regulatory Unraveling via Exogenous Payoff Shift (Roth 2002 / Lucas 1976)

Roth's (2002) theory of market design demonstrated that centralized mechanisms unravel when participants discover profitable strategies outside the mechanism. Medical residency matching, entry-level labor markets, and judicial clerkship markets all exhibited unraveling when early contracting offered higher expected payoffs than waiting for the centralized match. The EMTALA framework is a centralized mechanism: hospitals participate in Medicare and, in exchange, accept universal treatment obligations enforced by the Medicare Death Penalty. The mechanism's stability depended on a payoff structure in which no hospital could profitably operate outside Medicare. The No Surprises Act's IDR process created exactly the exogenous payoff shift that Roth's framework predicts will trigger unraveling: a revenue stream (arbitration payouts at or above in-network rates, without network participation costs) that makes non-participation viable for operators targeting commercially insured populations. Lucas's (1976) critique of econometric policy evaluation provides the macroeconomic parallel: changing one policy parameter (the NSA's creation of IDR) changes agent behavior (Medicare opt-out by for-profit ER operators) in ways that undermine other policy goals (EMTALA's universal-treatment mandate). Nutex's revenue quadrupling to $875 million is the behavioral response that the Lucas Critique predicts and that EMTALA's designers did not model. The mechanism has not failed. It has been exited. The distinction matters: reform efforts targeting denial rates, PA timelines, and AI-in-coverage-decisions all presuppose that the patient is inside the system. For patients who arrive at an EMTALA-exempt facility, the entire regulatory apparatus documented in this article, 60+ subsections of reform, litigation, and legislative action, does not apply. They are outside the game.

The Nutex model is not an anomaly. It is a proof of concept. Any operator that can assemble commercial insurance volume sufficient to fund operations through NSA arbitration can replicate the strategy. The facilities that result look like emergency rooms, are staffed like emergency rooms, and bill like emergency rooms. They are not emergency rooms in the regulatory sense, because they bear none of the obligations that define emergency care in American law. As of mid-2026, Nutex is the largest known operator of this model, but its revenue trajectory, from near-bankruptcy to $875 million in under three years, has attracted investor attention and regulatory scrutiny simultaneously. Idaho and New Mexico investigations may constrain the model in those states. But the structural arbitrage, the gap between EMTALA's assumption of universal Medicare participation and the NSA's creation of an alternative revenue pathway, exists in every state where for-profit operators can open facilities in commercially dense markets. Every subsection of this analysis, from the Enforcement Gap's $48,000 UNH fine to the Calibration Paradox's cross-market denial manipulation, describes pathologies within the regulated system. The EMTALA arbitrage describes the emergence of a parallel system that is not subject to any of them. The game theory of healthcare denial is predicated on the existence of a relationship between insurer and patient that triggers legal obligations. When the provider exits the framework that creates those obligations, the patient arrives at a facility whose only commitment is the one Dr. Vo articulated: "If you're going to die, we treat you." Everything short of death is negotiable, and the negotiation begins with a credit card.

The Revenue Leakage Spiral: When the Denial System Consumes Its Own Infrastructure

The Provider Exodus subsection documented how PA-driven burnout is pushing physicians out of the profession. A companion dynamic is now pushing entire practices and hospitals into financial collapse. Kodiak Solutions' inaugural "State of the Healthcare Revenue Cycle" report, published in April 2026 with data from 2,300 hospitals and 350,000 physicians on its platform, quantified the damage: hospitals and physician practices lost over $48 billion in 2025 from final claim denials and uncollected patient bills combined, a 25% increase in net revenue leakage from the prior year. The median final denial rate rose from 2.5% to 2.7%, with clinical denials, the category that includes prior authorization and medical necessity, accounting for nearly all of the increase. Initial denial rates climbed to 11.6% from 11.4%. And providers became less successful at fighting back: the average overturn rate on denied claims dropped to 42.1% from 42.7%, meaning insurers are not only denying more but winning more of the disputes that follow.

The financial consequences are now visible in bankruptcy filings. Gibbins Advisors' midyear healthcare restructuring report, analyzed by Becker's ASC in July 2026, found that physician practices accounted for nearly 30% of healthcare bankruptcy filings in the first half of 2026, on pace for their highest annual filing total since 2019. The mechanism connecting denials to insolvency is arithmetic. Hospital claim denials rose 12% for inpatient care and 14% for outpatient care between 2024 and 2025, while a concurrent survey found that 41% of providers now see denial rates above 10%. On the cost side, median healthcare staff pay rose 4.3% in 2025, up from 2.7% in 2024. Revenue per unit of work is falling. Costs per unit of work are rising. Denials consume the margin. Matthew Bates, a managing director at Kaufman Hall who leads the firm's work with physician enterprises, stated the dynamic plainly on a Medical Economics podcast: "Docs are working harder, but what they're making per unit of work is actually going down."

The patient side of the revenue equation is eroding simultaneously. Insured patients were responsible for 7.3% of their bills in 2025, up from 6.8% in 2024, but they paid less of what they owed: insured patient yield dropped from 45.1% to 42.4%. The median bad-debt rate rose from 1.1% to 1.3%. Kodiak's VP of analytics and data strategy, Dan Szaflarski, noted that these trends are landing amid the payer-mix disruptions of Medicaid disenrollment and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which are expected to increase the self-pay population further. HCA Healthcare, the largest for-profit hospital chain, raised its full-year ACA exchange loss estimate to $1 billion to $1.2 billion.
