When both the insurer side (more denials, lower overturn rates) and the patient side (higher cost-sharing, lower collections) compress simultaneously, the provider is squeezed from both directions.

The game theory reveals why this is not merely a financial problem but a structural trap. The provider network is a shared commons in Hardin's (1968) formulation. Every insurer that processes claims through the same hospitals and physician practices draws from the same pool of provider capacity. Each insurer has an individual incentive to increase denials: lower medical cost ratio, higher quarterly earnings, satisfied analysts. But the collective effect of all insurers increasing denials simultaneously degrades the infrastructure that all of them need. When a physician practice files for bankruptcy because denials consumed its operating margin, every insurer that relied on that practice for in-network coverage loses a provider. The remaining providers face less competition, can negotiate higher rates, and are harder to replace. The insurer's short-term savings from denials create long-term costs from network degradation.

Tragedy of the Provider Commons (Hardin 1968 / Ostrom 1990)

Hardin's (1968) original formulation described rational herders overgrazing a shared pasture: each herder captures the full benefit of adding one more animal but bears only a fraction of the cost of degradation, because the cost is distributed across all herders. The equilibrium prediction is overexploitation to the point of commons collapse. The provider network exhibits the identical structure. When UNH denies a claim at a multispecialty practice, UNH captures the full savings (lower MCR) but bears only a fractional cost of the practice's degradation (shared with Aetna, Cigna, Elevance, and every other insurer whose patients use that practice). The rational insurer maximizes denials up to the point where its marginal savings equal its marginal share of provider degradation. Because its share of degradation is small (one of many insurers), the equilibrium denial rate exceeds the collectively optimal level. Multiply this across every insurer and every practice, and the result is systemic overgrazing: a 25% increase in revenue leakage, a 12-14% increase in denial rates, and physician practice bankruptcies at their highest level in seven years. Ostrom's (1990) extension, for which she received the Nobel Prize, demonstrated that commons tragedies can be avoided through institutional governance, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and collective-choice arrangements. The healthcare system has none of these. No institution monitors the aggregate denial load on any individual provider. No mechanism sanctions an insurer for contributing disproportionately to a practice's financial distress. No collective-choice arrangement limits the total denial burden that converges on the shared infrastructure. The CMS-0057-F reporting mandate measures denial rates per insurer, not denial loads per provider. The metric tracks the herder's behavior but not the condition of the pasture.

The spiral has a second stage that the commons framework predicts. As practices close and the network narrows, surviving providers gain bargaining power. The insurer must either accept higher reimbursement rates from the remaining providers (increasing MCR) or allow the network to shrink below regulatory adequacy standards (triggering state intervention). UNH's Q2 2026 MCR of 86.7%, celebrated by analysts as margin recovery, required exiting 109 counties and forcing 2.9 million MA enrollees to find new plans. The exit was itself a form of network contraction: rather than pay the higher rates that surviving providers demanded, UNH withdrew from markets where the provider commons had already degraded. The enrollees displaced into other plans carry their health needs with them, concentrating demand on the remaining providers in the remaining networks, accelerating the degradation that caused the exit in the first place. The spiral is self-reinforcing: denials cause closures, closures narrow networks, narrow networks increase costs, increased costs motivate more denials. The 41% of providers reporting denial rates above 10% are the providers most likely to close next, which will push the remaining providers' denial rates higher still, because the request pool will be concentrated in a shrinking number of practices handling more complex cases with fewer resources. This is not a market correction. It is a commons collapse in slow motion, funded by the $48 billion in revenue that providers earned but never collected, documented in a report that no insurer has publicly acknowledged.

The Phantom Network: When Provider Directories Become Instruments of Fraud

Every subsection above documents what happens after a patient finds a provider and submits a claim. But a growing body of evidence reveals an earlier mechanism: millions of patients never reach the claim stage because the provider network they purchased does not exist. In health insurance industry parlance, these fictitious directories are called "ghost networks." Senate Finance Committee Chair Ron Wyden was blunter: "When insurance companies host ghost networks, they are selling health coverage under false pretenses."

The most consequential legal test of this claim is Havrilla v. Centene Corp. (N.D. Ill., Case No. 22-cv-04126), a civil RICO class action filed in August 2022 against Centene Corporation, the largest provider of ACA exchange plans in the country. Judge Nancy L. Maldonado ruled in May 2024 that plaintiffs could proceed on the majority of their claims, including a civil violation of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act and consumer protection laws across 11 states. The core allegation: Centene's Ambetter-branded plans, sold across 26 states to approximately 2 million enrollees, published provider directories that defendants "knew to be false." When consumers attempted to use the plans, they discovered that "very few, sometimes none" of listed providers actually accepted Ambetter insurance. In some cases, directory listings included nurses and medical students as in-network primary care physicians. Approximately 90% of Ambetter plans are Silver-tier, qualifying for federal premium subsidies, meaning the alleged fraud extracted hundreds of millions of dollars annually from both consumers and the government. The RICO theory, which treats each fraudulent mailing and electronic plan filing as a separate predicate act in a pattern of racketeering, is legally significant precisely because it bypasses ERISA's preemption of state-law remedies that has historically shielded employer-sponsored plans from consequential litigation.

The Centene case is not an outlier. A Senate Finance Committee secret shopper study released in May 2023 tested the reality behind provider directories for mental health services in Medicare Advantage plans. Staff reviewed 12 plans across 6 states, calling 10 systematically selected providers from each. Of 120 provider listings contacted by phone, 33% were inaccurate, non-working numbers, or unreturned calls. Staff could make appointments only 18% of the time. Appointment success ranged from 0% (Oregon) to 50% (Colorado). More than 80% of listed mental health providers were "ghosts": unreachable, not accepting new patients, or not in-network. The bipartisan REAL Health Providers Act, introduced in 2024 (Fitzpatrick, Panetta, Murphy, Kuster, Schneider), would require annual directory updates for MA plans, but has not been enacted.

And in June 2026, HHS-OIG audited Medicaid managed care provider directories for the three largest parent companies, covering 29 million enrollees across 38 of 42 states with managed care plans. The results confirmed the ghost network is industry-wide, not insurer-specific. Centene had the worst performance: 22% of providers listed in its directories were not actually in-network, and 35% of actual in-network providers were missing from the directory entirely. UnitedHealthcare's numbers were 6% ghost and 25% missing. Elevance performed best at 4% ghost and 11% missing, but even its directories failed to list more than one in ten available providers. The combined effect is that consumers make plan-selection decisions based on provider lists that are simultaneously inflated with phantom providers and incomplete with real ones, producing a decision environment that systematically misleads.

Credence Good Fraud and Network Quality as Unverifiable Signal (Nelson 1970 / Darby & Karni 1973)

Nelson (1970) classified goods by the consumer's ability to evaluate quality: search goods can be assessed before purchase (produce), experience goods only after use (restaurants), and credence goods not even after consumption (auto repair). Darby and Karni (1973) extended the framework to services where the consumer cannot determine whether the service received was appropriate. Provider networks are credence goods taken to their logical extreme. A consumer choosing a health plan examines the provider directory, the "search" phase, but cannot verify whether listed providers will accept the plan, schedule appointments, or be available in a medical emergency until the need arises. The Centene RICO ruling establishes for the first time that systematically falsifying this signal constitutes racketeering rather than mere breach of contract. The game-theoretic implication is structural: in a market where the seller controls both the quality signal (directory) and the product quality (network), and where the buyer cannot verify the signal even after purchase (because healthy enrollees may never test the network), the equilibrium prediction is quality degradation bounded only by the probability of detection, not by competitive pressure. The OIG data quantifies the gap: Centene's directories are simultaneously inflated by 22% (ghost listings) and deflated by 35% (missing real providers), producing a composite inaccuracy rate that approaches 50%. In any other regulated market, a product with 50% specification fraud would be recalled. In health insurance, it is sold to 2 million people with federal subsidies.

The phantom network connects to the denial system through a mechanism that the game theory reveals as sequential. The ghost network operates as a pre-denial filter: patients who cannot find in-network providers either delay care (suffering the treatment delay mortality documented in the Cleveland Clinic study), pay out-of-network rates (absorbing costs the plan was designed to cover), or abandon treatment entirely (the 48.4% pharmacy rejection abandonment rate scaled to an entire network). The patient who successfully navigates the phantom directory and finds a real provider then enters the prior authorization system, where a second filter applies. The patient who clears both filters and receives treatment then encounters the retroactive denial and reprocess ratchet. Each stage functions independently but their cumulative attrition is multiplicative, not additive. If 30% of patients are filtered by network phantoms, 15% by PA denial, and 10% by retroactive denial, the combined attrition is not 55% but 46% (1 minus the product of the passage rates). The system does not need any single stage to deny most patients. It needs every stage to deny some.

The Johns Hopkins study by Xu and Polsky (Health Services Research, February 2026) provides the first formal methodology for distinguishing general ghosts (listed as PCPs but unavailable to any Medicare beneficiaries) from network-specific ghosts (available to Medicare beneficiaries generally but inaccessible to enrollees of a particular MA plan). The distinction matters because it separates passive directory decay (a provider retired and the listing was never removed) from active network manipulation (a provider is listed to inflate the apparent network but has been given contract terms that guarantee they will not see patients). The Centene complaint alleges the second mechanism: Ambetter "routinely refuses to pay for medical services and medications" that plans cover, which "further reduces its provider network by leading a large number of providers to reject Ambetter insurance." The insurer constructs the ghost by making the real provider's participation economically irrational, then lists the ghost provider as if the network were intact. The directory is not merely inaccurate. It is the output of a deliberate mechanism.

The Bilateral AI Arms Race: When Both Sides Deploy Algorithms and Neither Side Saves Money

In April 2026, the Peterson Health Technology Institute convened an unusual gathering: senior leaders from health systems, health plans, technology developers, investment firms, and federal agencies, assembled to assess whether AI was actually reducing administrative costs in healthcare. Their conclusion was unequivocal. "When applied on top of flawed administrative workflows, data complexity, and incentive structures, AI exacerbates the underlying issues," the PHTI report stated. "Realizing the potential for AI to reduce administrative waste will require redesigning the processes on which the technology is being deployed." The report found that AI is "unlikely to be reducing costs at the system level at this early stage in adoption." The arms race could be adding to costs, even as it reduces manual effort for individual transactions.

The mechanism is bilateral and self-reinforcing. On the provider side, AI scribes and automated coding tools have increased coding intensity, enabling physicians to "more completely capture patient complexity" while modestly saving documentation time. Two peer-reviewed studies released in March 2026 confirmed that AI is intensifying coding and revenue capture for maternity admissions and hospital outpatient care, with one estimating an additional $2.3 billion in healthcare spending from AI-enabled billing practices alone. On the payer side, insurers noticed the shift and responded with algorithmic countermeasures. In the past year, Cigna, Aetna, Anthem Blue Cross of California, and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts have all launched or expanded automatic downcoding programs that algorithmically adjust higher-complexity Evaluation and Management claims before payment clears. Cigna's policy, effective October 1, 2025, targets codes 99204-99205, 99214-99215, and 99244-99245, reducing reimbursement by $45 to $120 per encounter. Aetna expanded from a 12-state pilot to all commercial states except Louisiana, with Medicare Advantage expansion planned. BCBS of Massachusetts flags providers whose billing patterns "stand out from peers" and reviews their highest-complexity claims for potential reduction.

The provider response has been both legal and political. Jefferson Health sued Aetna in April 2026 in Pennsylvania's Eastern District Court, alleging systematic downcoding of inpatient hospital stays to observation-level rates in violation of the CMS Two-Midnight Rule and negotiated provider contracts. Texas Medical Association President Jay Shah wrote to Cigna that automatic downcoding programs "place onerous administrative burdens on practices forcing them to fight for appropriate payment rates in an increasingly challenging environment for small and independent physician practices." Maryland's Insurance Administration fined Cigna $80,000 in March 2026 and required the insurer to halt automatic downcoding, ruling that under state law Cigna must formally dispute claims and request documentation rather than algorithmically adjusting reimbursement. Several Dallas-area physicians told D CEO Healthcare that Aetna has been automatically downcoding patient interactions without notice or explanation, "potentially costing practices thousands of dollars in revenue per day." Meanwhile, seven states introduced downcoding-specific bills in their 2026 legislative sessions: California, Connecticut, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Missouri, and Oregon. Indiana enacted HB 1271 on March 4, 2026, prohibiting insurers from using AI as the sole basis to downcode any claim without a healthcare professional's review of the patient's medical record. Illinois passed SB 3114, effective January 2028, banning any algorithm that bypasses billing professional submissions to downcode a claim and prohibiting the targeting of clinicians who treat complex or chronic patients.

The PHTI report identified the structural paradox at the center of the arms race. Provider AI allows physicians to "submit more complete requests with less effort." Payer AI allows insurers to "process more submissions at a lower cost per decision." Each side achieves efficiency gains within its own workflow. But the total cost per claim has not decreased. "Optimizing each side of the transaction risks making the overall process more activity-intensive, rather than more efficient," the report stated. Participants recommended alternatives to prior authorization, including prepayment review and discounted payment rates for providers who bypass upfront review, but acknowledged that the bilateral AI escalation had made those alternatives harder to implement because both sides had already invested in the existing adversarial infrastructure.

Game Theory Concept
The Red Queen Arms Race: Richardson (1960) Escalation Applied to Administrative AI

Lewis Fry Richardson's (1960) mathematical model of arms races predicted that when two adversaries invest in competitive weapons, and each side's investment is a function of the other's, the equilibrium is either mutual escalation or mutual exhaustion, never unilateral disarmament. The model's differential equations describe a system where each side's marginal investment is rational given the other's position, but the combined outcome exceeds what either would choose in isolation. Van Valen's (1973) Red Queen hypothesis extended the logic to evolutionary biology: organisms must "run faster just to stay in the same place," because their competitors are simultaneously evolving. The AI billing arms race maps onto both frameworks with unusual precision. Providers deploy AI scribes that capture higher-complexity codes. Payers deploy AI downcoding algorithms that reduce those codes. Providers respond with AI-driven appeal generators and pre-submission optimization engines designed to reduce "AI-trigger exposure." Payers respond with velocity-based claim flagging and peer-comparison algorithms. Each escalation step is individually rational: the provider captures more revenue per encounter, the payer reduces reimbursement per claim. But the combined system has added an estimated $2.3 billion in billing intensity without reducing the average cost per claim, while generating new administrative overhead (appeals of downcoded claims, re-reviews, peer-to-peer consultations) that did not exist before either side deployed AI. The PHTI's finding that AI is "unlikely to be reducing costs at the system level" is Richardson's arms race equilibrium stated in health economics language: both sides are spending more to maintain the same relative position. The patient bears the cost of the arms race twice: once in the administrative overhead embedded in premiums, and again in the clinical consequences when a downcoded claim reduces the physician's incentive to document complexity. The arms race also creates a distributional equity problem. Large health systems can afford AI billing tools and dedicated denial management teams; small and independent practices, the ones TMA President Shah was defending, cannot. Payer downcoding algorithms that uniformly reduce high-complexity codes punish the practice that documented correctly alongside the one that upcoded, because the algorithm cannot distinguish legitimate complexity from AI-inflated billing without the individualized clinical review that automatic downcoding was designed to eliminate. The escalation thus operates as a regressive tax: the providers least able to invest in counter-AI bear the largest share of the reimbursement reduction, accelerating the practice closures and provider exits documented in the Revenue Leakage Spiral section above.

The MA Cascade: When Insurers Exit Their Own Game

The denial reform story has a structural counterpart that no one is narrating as a unified phenomenon. Across the Medicare Advantage market, insurers are not reforming their practices. They are abandoning their markets.

In August 2026, Humana became the first major insurer to announce its 2027 Medicare Advantage plans, and the headline was retreat. The company will exit markets and plans covering 600,000 members, roughly 8% of its 7.2 million MA enrollment. Humana expects to "recapture" about 40% of disrupted seniors through other plans it offers, meaning 360,000 people must find new coverage on their own. Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, called it "another sign that Medicare Advantage insurers are prioritizing profit growth over enrollment growth."

Humana is not alone. Presbyterian Healthcare Services, one of New Mexico's largest health systems, announced in June that it will discontinue most Medicare Advantage plans for 2027, disrupting 30,000 members and eliminating 150 administrative positions. The decision followed an annual operating loss of $568.2 million and a Fitch Ratings downgrade to AA- with a negative outlook. CEO Rishi Sikka told staff that "continuing in this market would limit our ability to invest in the care, workforce and access to serve New Mexicans where they need us most." Presbyterian operates roughly 30% of New Mexico's total hospital bed capacity. When it exits MA, it removes one of the state's largest integrated delivery options for seniors. Clear Spring Health announced it is exiting Medicare Advantage entirely, shuttering operations in Colorado, Georgia, and Illinois. Molina Healthcare will stop offering MA plans with prescription drug coverage in 2027.

Add these to UnitedHealthcare's ongoing contraction. UNH shed 800,000 Medicare Advantage members between mid-2025 and mid-2026 (from 8.4 million to 7.6 million), exiting 109 counties and shuttering over 100 plans. CEO Tim Noel called it "favoring margin recovery." Across just these five insurers, at least 1.4 million Medicare Advantage members face involuntary disruption for the 2027 plan year. The actual total across the industry will be higher once remaining insurers file their Annual Notice of Changes in September.

New Mexico's state legislature hauled Presbyterian executives before the Legislative Health and Human Services Committee in late June. Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero called the exit part of "a pattern that's beginning to build" in the state: "We have a lot of private interests, corporate interests in our state. But when the need is great but the money's not, there's an exodus." Presbyterian's COO John Johnson told lawmakers the decision was "financially unsustainable" given rising medical costs, regulatory changes, and administrative complexity. The testimony revealed the structural bind: Presbyterian is simultaneously a provider system trying to fill 870 open clinical positions and an insurance plan losing money on every MA enrollee. When the insurer and the provider are the same entity, the exit decision exposes what the market otherwise conceals: the current MA reimbursement structure does not cover the cost of delivering the care the plans promise.

The MA cascade connects directly to the convergence trap documented above. When UNH's denial rate dropped from 34.2% to 19.1%, it lost the cost advantage that aggressive denial provided. The same regulatory and public pressure that forced denial-rate convergence also tightened CMS rate updates, empowered state AI-denial bans, and subjected the star ratings system to litigation that has destabilized quality-bonus revenue. Insurers that cannot profitably serve MA enrollees at the new denial-rate equilibrium have three options: find operational efficiencies, accept lower margins, or exit. The market data shows which option is winning.

Game Theory Concept
Hirschman's Exit-Voice-Loyalty (1970) Applied to Insurer Behavior

Albert Hirschman's framework was developed to explain consumer and citizen responses to declining quality: members of an organization can express dissatisfaction through voice (complaining, lobbying) or exit (leaving). This article has applied Hirschman extensively to patients and providers. The MA cascade reveals the framework operating at a third level: insurers themselves are choosing exit over voice. When prior authorization reform makes the denial model less profitable, and when CMS rate updates fail to offset rising medical costs, the insurer faces the same Hirschman calculus any dissatisfied participant faces. Voice means lobbying for higher reimbursement, engaging in star-rating litigation, and signing voluntary pledges. Exit means shedding members, closing plans, and retreating to profitable geographies. The MA cascade reveals that exit is dominant: Humana's 600,000-member exit is cheaper than reforming its cost structure, just as Presbyterian's full withdrawal is cheaper than sustaining a $568 million operating loss. The patients who remain after the cascade face a concentrated market with fewer choices, higher switching costs (Williamson's 1985 asset specificity: patients built their care around MA network providers and must now rebuild), and the knowledge that their insurer survived precisely because it was already profitable at the equilibrium denial rate. The exit cascade is the market's revealed preference: when given the choice between reforming denial practices and abandoning populations, insurers choose abandonment. The populations most likely to be abandoned are the ones Hirschman's framework predicts: rural, elderly, and chronically ill members whose care costs exceed the MA capitation rate. These are the same populations whose denial rates were highest before the reform.

The Retail Disruption: When Costco Enters the Market Incumbents Are Fleeing

On August 18, 2026, while UnitedHealthcare was still processing the 800,000 MA members it shed over the past year, while Humana was notifying 600,000 members their plans would disappear, while Presbyterian was shuttering its New Mexico operations after a $568 million loss, Costco Wholesale announced an "enhanced strategic partnership" with SCAN Health Plan to offer Costco-branded Medicare Advantage plans. The warehouse retailer's first comprehensive entry into a market worth more than $600 billion annually to insurers. The announcement was first reported by the Wall Street Journal on August 19.

The partnership's structure reveals what Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework looks like from the other direction: when incumbents exit a market, the entry barriers they maintained through scale, regulatory relationships, and brand recognition dissolve, and players from adjacent markets can enter at a cost that would have been prohibitive in the old equilibrium. Costco brings 82 million paying members, a pharmacy network already filling prescriptions for MA enrollees, optical centers, hearing aid centers, and a consumer-trust brand that consistently ranks among the highest in American retail. SCAN brings 460,000 Medicare enrollees across six states, decades of Medicare expertise, and the nonprofit structure that insulates it from the quarterly earnings pressure that drove UNH to exit 109 counties.

The initial rollout is deliberately limited: Medicare Advantage products in two states and a Medicare supplemental plan in a third, covering markets with approximately 5 million Medicare enrollees. SCAN CEO Sachin H. Jain framed the partnership in consumer-trust language that implicitly indicts the incumbents: "As a longtime Costco customer, I know that if I walk into a Costco store, I'm just going to buy the item because they've done the work for me to make sure that it's a high-quality, high-value product. I would say that that's what seniors are increasingly looking for in their Medicare experience." The word "increasingly" is doing strategic work. Seniors are "increasingly" looking for trustworthy Medicare products because their previous products disappeared when their insurers chose exit over reform.

The game theory is Tirole's (1988) theory of entry and market structure, operating in reverse. In Tirole's standard model, an incumbent deters entry through credible commitments: sunk capacity investments, predatory pricing threats, and regulatory relationships that raise the entrant's cost. The MA exit cascade has dismantled each of these deterrents. When UNH exits 109 counties, it withdraws the sunk capacity. When Presbyterian shuts down its plans, it eliminates the local incumbent. When Humana sheds 600,000 members, it creates an unserved demand pool. The entry barrier does not merely lower. It inverts: the market that was too expensive to enter when incumbents operated at scale becomes attractive precisely because the incumbents have left, taking their cost structures with them but leaving the demand behind.

The SCAN angle adds a layer that connects to the Star Ratings litigation documented above. SCAN Health Plan is one of the four insurers suing CMS for star rating adjustments, seeking $125 million over the methodology changes that the Clover Health v. HHS ruling destabilized. SCAN simultaneously sues the regulator for higher quality bonuses and partners with Costco to build a consumer-trust brand that does not depend on the regulatory quality-scoring system it is litigating to preserve. The dual strategy is rational: if the star ratings litigation succeeds, the bonus revenue funds expansion; if it fails, the Costco brand provides an alternative market-access channel that bypasses the CMS quality-bonus mechanism entirely. The partnership hedges against both outcomes of the litigation, which is exactly the kind of strategic flexibility that vertically integrated insurer-providers like Presbyterian could not achieve because their exit was forced by operating losses rather than chosen as a competitive repositioning.

The Costco entry also reveals a structural feature of the post-Thompson MA market that the exit cascade narrative obscures: the market is not shrinking. Medicare Advantage enrollment has surpassed 64.2 million beneficiaries, with slightly more than half in private MA plans. The $600+ billion in annual insurer revenue is not declining. What is happening is a recomposition of the supply side: incumbents whose cost structures were built on aggressive denial rates and star-rating bonus arbitrage are exiting, and entrants whose cost structures are built on adjacent retail infrastructure and consumer trust are entering. The seniors who lose their Presbyterian plan in New Mexico are the same seniors who walk into Costco in Albuquerque. The demand does not disappear when the insurer exits. It migrates to the next available option, and Costco is positioning itself to be that option.

Game Theory Concept
Schumpeterian Creative Destruction and Tirole's (1988) Entry Theory Applied to Post-Crisis Market Recomposition

Joseph Schumpeter's (1942) theory of creative destruction predicted that the most significant market restructurings occur not through incremental reform within existing firms but through the entry of fundamentally different organizations that redefine the competitive basis. The incumbent's investment in the old technology (or in this case, the old business model of denial-based cost management) becomes a liability rather than an asset when the competitive environment shifts. Tirole's (1988) formalization of entry barriers demonstrated that deterrence requires credible commitment: the incumbent must be willing to absorb the cost of fighting the entrant for deterrence to work. When incumbents are instead exiting, they signal the opposite: they are unwilling to bear even the cost of operating the existing business, much less the cost of fighting a new competitor. Costco's entry into Medicare Advantage through SCAN exhibits the classic Schumpeterian pattern: a firm from an adjacent industry (retail) enters with a fundamentally different cost structure (integrated pharmacy, optical, and hearing infrastructure, plus a membership-based trust relationship with 82 million consumers) that the incumbent cannot replicate without dismantling its own organizational architecture. UnitedHealth cannot become Costco. Presbyterian cannot become Costco. The competitive advantage Costco brings is not medical expertise but consumer trust, and that advantage is precisely the asset the incumbent insurers destroyed through the denial practices documented throughout this analysis. The Costco-SCAN partnership is not entering a distressed market. It is entering a market that the incumbents distressed through their own strategic choices, and it is entering with the one competitive asset the incumbents cannot rebuild: the trust of the people they denied.

The Intermediary Chain: $950 Million and the Supply Side of Risk Adjustment Fraud

The Revenue Multiplier section above documented how Kaiser Permanente's $556 million False Claims Act settlement revealed bidirectional extraction: inflating revenue through fabricated diagnoses while simultaneously reducing payouts through claim denials. But Kaiser was not an outlier. By August 2026, federal enforcement had produced seven major MA risk adjustment fraud settlements totaling roughly $950 million, and the pattern they reveal is not a series of independent bad actors. It is a supply chain.

On August 3, 2026, the Department of Justice announced that Complete Health Partners Holdings, a Jacksonville-based management services organization operating affiliated provider groups in Florida, Alabama, and Colorado, agreed to pay $14.1 million to resolve allegations that it caused the submission of false diagnosis codes between 2020 and 2023. The codes fell under Hierarchical Condition Categories 55 (drug and alcohol dependence) and 59 (major depressive, bipolar, and paranoid disorders). The DOJ alleged that Complete Health disseminated incorrect coding guidance to its coders and physicians and prompted doctors to add unsubstantiated diagnoses that were not clinically valid, not supported by patient records, and not considered in the care, management, or treatment of the beneficiary. Because Complete Health received a percentage of the payments its affiliated Medicare Advantage plans received from CMS under risk-sharing contracts, it had a direct financial incentive to inflate beneficiaries' risk scores. A whistleblower, a former associate director of risk adjustment at VIVA Health, initiated the case and will receive approximately $2.47 million from the settlement.

Complete Health is an MSO, not an insurer. It does not bear insurance risk directly. It manages and operates provider groups that serve MA enrollees, and its revenue is a contractual share of the capitation payments CMS sends to the Medicare Advantage organizations. This structural detail transforms the risk adjustment fraud analysis from one about insurer incentives to one about supply chain incentives. The seven recent settlements map onto distinct links in the chain:

Kaiser Permanente ($556 million, January 2026): the insurer itself, pressuring employed physicians to add post-visit diagnoses through internal coding tools and bonus structures tied to diagnosis targets. Aetna ($117.7 million, March 2026): the insurer using chart review programs and failing to withdraw inaccurate codes, with the largest portion stemming from a 2015 retrospective review initiative and $11.5 million from morbid obesity codes submitted between 2018 and 2023. Matrix Medical Network and HealthFair ($56.5 million, June 2026): home health assessment vendors conducting in-home evaluations of MA enrollees and submitting unsupported diagnoses including atrial fibrillation, rheumatoid arthritis, COPD, HIV/AIDS, metastatic cancer, and congestive heart failure. Seoul Medical Group and Renaissance Imaging ($62.85 million, March 2025): a provider group and its affiliated radiology practice fabricating spinal diagnosis codes for enthesopathy and sacroiliitis that patients did not have, with Renaissance creating false radiology reports to support the fabricated diagnoses. Independent Health and DxID ($100 million, December 2024): a vendor that retroactively mined medical records to add diagnoses that inflated risk scores, closing a twelve-year whistleblower lawsuit. Oak Street Health ($60 million, September 2024): a primary care network, subsequently acquired by CVS Health, paying kickbacks of roughly $200 per beneficiary to third-party insurance agents to recruit seniors through its Client Awareness Program.

Each entity occupies a different position in the MA supply chain. Kaiser is the integrated insurer-provider. Aetna is the payer. Matrix/HealthFair is the assessment vendor. DxID is the retrospective data-mining vendor. Seoul Medical is the provider group. Renaissance Imaging is the documentation fabricator. Oak Street is the patient acquisition platform. Complete Health is the management services organization. Every link in the chain had an independent, contractually encoded incentive to inflate risk scores, and every link was caught doing exactly that.

The DOJ's statement on the Complete Health settlement contained a number that reframes the scale of the system under scrutiny: "the government pays private insurers over $530 billion each year" through Medicare Advantage. The $950 million in combined settlements represents 0.18% of one year's MA payments. Even assuming the settlements capture only a fraction of the fraudulent overpayment (Kaiser alone allegedly generated $1 billion in improper payments against a $556 million settlement), the enforcement arithmetic favors fraud at every link. The expected cost of fraud is the probability of detection multiplied by the penalty if caught. When the government pays half a trillion dollars annually through a system whose fraud settlements amount to less than two-tenths of one percent of one year's payments, the probability-weighted penalty is a rounding error on the revenue it generates.

The whistleblower pattern reinforces the analysis. In four of the seven settlements, the case originated from an insider complaint: a physician at Kaiser, a risk-adjustment coding auditor at Aetna, an associate director of risk adjustment at VIVA Health (Complete Health), and the DxID whistleblower. Each whistleblower occupied a position where they could observe the gap between clinical reality and coded diagnoses. Their decision to report, rather than participate, was itself a game-theoretic choice: the False Claims Act's qui tam provisions award 15-30% of the settlement to the relator, creating a financial incentive that partially offsets the career cost of reporting. The $95 million awarded to Kaiser's whistleblowers and the $2.47 million to Complete Health's relator demonstrate that the incentive mechanism works. But it works after the fact: the fraud ran for three to nine years in each case before enforcement caught up. The supply chain's structural advantage is temporal. Each link can extract value for years before the monitoring system detects it, and the settlement, when it comes, costs less than the cumulative extraction.

Game Theory Concept
Akerlof's (1970) Market for Lemons Applied to the MA Coding Vendor Market

Akerlof's Nobel Prize-winning model demonstrated that when buyers cannot observe product quality directly, the market selects for low-quality sellers. In the used car market, sellers know the car's true condition but buyers do not, so buyers offer a price reflecting average quality, which drives high-quality sellers out of the market, leaving only "lemons." The MA risk adjustment supply chain exhibits the same adverse selection dynamic, operating in reverse: instead of buyers being unable to detect low quality, the principal (CMS) cannot distinguish legitimate high-acuity coding from fabricated diagnoses, and the intermediary market selects for the most aggressive coders. Medicare Advantage organizations contract with MSOs, coding vendors, home health assessment companies, and retrospective chart-mining firms. Vendors that code aggressively generate higher risk scores, which produce higher CMS payments, which produce higher revenue for the MAO, which produces higher contract renewal rates and risk-sharing payments for the vendor. Vendors that code conservatively generate lower risk scores and lower revenue. In a competitive vendor market, the conservative coder loses business to the aggressive one, exactly as Akerlof predicted: the good sellers exit, the lemons remain. The $950 million in settlements documents the equilibrium that this selection process produces. Matrix/HealthFair submitted diagnoses for conditions patients did not have. DxID retroactively mined records to add diagnoses. Seoul Medical fabricated radiology reports. Complete Health prompted physicians to add clinically unsupported codes. Each vendor was, in market terms, "succeeding" by generating higher risk scores than its competitors. The adverse selection is compounded by the hierarchical structure that Tirole (1986) analyzed in his theory of collusion in organizations: when monitoring capacity is finite and the principal can observe aggregate output (total CMS payments) but not input quality (individual diagnosis accuracy), each intermediary layer creates an additional opportunity for collusion. The MAO has limited incentive to audit its vendors' coding quality because higher risk scores benefit both parties. The vendor has limited incentive to audit its coders because higher volumes benefit both parties. The coder has limited incentive to question the physician because the guidance came from above. Each layer of the hierarchy delegates monitoring downward while extracting revenue upward, and the system stabilizes at an equilibrium where aggressive coding is the market norm and conservative coding is a competitive disadvantage. CMS's enforcement tool, the False Claims Act settlement, operates on a temporal lag of three to twelve years and at a magnitude that leaves the expected value of fraud positive. The market-for-lemons prediction is not merely theoretical. It is the structural description of why $950 million in settlements across seven entities spanning every link in the supply chain represents a system functioning exactly as its incentives predict, not a system experiencing anomalous failure.

The Information Blackout: When Regulators Dismantle Their Own Instruments

The previous sections have documented how insurers manipulate information: strategic aggregation in transparency reports, phantom provider directories, algorithmic denial without human review, voluntary pledges without enforcement. But the most consequential information manipulation of 2025-2026 did not come from insurers. It came from their regulator.

On June 16, 2025, CMS announced it would not enforce two previously finalized rules from the Contract Year 2025 Medicare Advantage final rule. The first required every MA plan's Utilization Management Committee to include at least one member with expertise in health equity, defined as a physician with experience identifying disparities among different population groups or enacting systemic changes to achieve equitable care delivery. The second required those UM Committees to publish plan-level reports showing rates of PA denials and approvals broken down by population: dually eligible enrollees, low-income enrollees (identified through Part D Low Income Subsidy enrollment), and enrollees with disabilities. This was not a minor paperwork adjustment. It was the first mechanism CMS had built to detect whether prior authorization practices produced disparate outcomes for the most vulnerable MA enrollees.

Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms documented the stakes: dually eligible Medicare-Medicaid beneficiaries face up to twice the denial rate of non-dual enrollees despite having fewer prior authorization requests on average. Dual eligibles are more likely to live in poverty and have higher rates of disability. The suspended rules were designed to make these disparities visible. Without them, each MA plan decides on its own whether to examine population-level denial patterns, and none of what it finds is required to be public. As Georgetown's Ciannah Correa concluded: the suspension "eliminates the first opportunity for CMS, the public and providers to evaluate how prior authorization practices may be different based on enrollee income, Medicaid eligibility and disability." Medicare beneficiaries choosing plans during open enrollment will continue to select based on premiums and supplemental benefits, unable to see the denial rates they are actually buying.

This was the Trump administration's second action to roll back PA oversight. Earlier, it had declined to finalize requirements for AI oversight in PA decisions, MA plan transparency on approval criteria, and service-level PA reporting. The pattern is cumulative: each individual suspension sounds technical; together, they dismantle the information infrastructure that would have made the prior authorization system legible to the people it processes. What remains is the contract-level aggregate reporting required starting in 2026, which CMS-0057-F already showed can be gamed through strategic aggregation across hundreds of plans. The plan-level data that would have revealed where and for whom denials concentrate was the one instrument the aggregate could not absorb. It was removed.

At the same time the federal government was dismantling oversight of MA prior authorization, the HHS Office of Inspector General published the results of its first-ever audit focused specifically on behavioral health PA denials in Medicaid. The OIG selected Community Behavioral Health (CBH), a Pennsylvania behavioral health managed care organization that had the highest number of denied service requests of any behavioral health MCO in the state. The auditors sampled 100 denied prior authorization requests. None met all federal requirements for denying behavioral health services. Zero out of one hundred. CBH sent denial notices to incorrect addresses. CBH issued denial notices with unclear language that failed to distinguish between services denied outright and services denied as requested but available through an alternate pathway. CBH failed to inform Medicaid enrollees of their right to receive, at no charge, all documents and records relevant to the denial. And CBH's processes did not comply with Pennsylvania's own HealthChoices Agreement requirements for enrollees under 21, including mandatory efforts to contact the enrollee's representative before issuing a denial.

The 0% compliance rate is not a statistical artifact of a small sample. The OIG's methodology was designed to detect systemic rather than incidental failures. Every denial in the sample failed on process grounds, meaning the rights violations were structural: embedded in CBH's policies, templates, and procedures rather than individual reviewer errors. And CBH was not a marginal actor. It was the highest-volume behavioral health denier in a major state's Medicaid system. All five of the OIG's recommendations to CBH remain "open unimplemented" as of August 2026, with updates not expected until December.

The juxtaposition is the point. At the federal level, the administration suspended the reporting requirements that would have revealed whether PA denials disproportionately affect disabled, low-income, and dually eligible populations. At the state level, the first audit to actually examine behavioral health denials found that 100% of sampled denials violated enrollee rights. The two findings do not merely coexist. They describe a system in which the mechanism designed to detect harm was dismantled at exactly the moment the first evidence of systemic harm was being documented.

Game Theory Concept
Myerson's (1981) Revelation Principle Applied to Regulatory Information Design

Roger Myerson's (1981, 1983) work on optimal mechanism design demonstrated a foundational result: the information structure of a game determines its outcomes as much as the payoff structure. In any mechanism, the designer can influence equilibrium behavior by choosing which information is revealed, to whom, and when. The Revelation Principle states that for any equilibrium outcome achievable in a game with private information, there exists a direct mechanism that achieves the same outcome by asking agents to truthfully report their private information. The converse is equally powerful: if the mechanism designer suppresses a reporting channel, the set of achievable equilibria shifts in favor of the party whose private information remains private. The Trump administration's suspension of plan-level PA reporting is not deregulation in the conventional sense. It is mechanism redesign. The CY 2025 final rule had created a reporting channel that would have forced MA plans to reveal population-specific denial rates. This channel would have transformed private information (which populations each plan denies at higher rates) into public information (accessible to enrollees, researchers, CMS, and Congress). The suspension did not change the underlying denial practices. It changed the information environment in which those practices operate. Under the suspended rules, an MA plan that denies dual-eligible enrollees at twice the rate of non-dual enrollees would have to disclose that disparity. Under the current rules, the same plan can maintain the same disparity indefinitely because the reporting mechanism that would have revealed it does not exist. The OIG's CBH audit demonstrates the consequence: when the monitoring instrument is absent, systemic rights violations can persist at scale (100% non-compliance in the highest-volume denier) for years without detection. Myerson's framework predicts this precisely. In a mechanism without mandatory disclosure, the informed party (the insurer) retains its informational advantage, and the uninformed parties (enrollees, regulators, providers) cannot observe the disparity that would trigger corrective action. The regulator's choice to suppress the reporting channel is equivalent, in mechanism-design terms, to choosing the equilibrium that maximizes the informed party's payoff. Whether that choice reflects regulatory capture, ideological preference for deregulation, or simple administrative convenience is irrelevant to the game-theoretic outcome: the information structure has been redesigned, and the beneficiary of the redesign is the party whose private information remains private.

The Hysteresis Trap: Why the Old Equilibrium Cannot Be Restored

Twenty months after the shooting, a pattern has emerged that no section of this analysis has yet named directly: the reforms are becoming structurally irreversible, not because they are popular (though 71% voter support helps), but because each reform dismantles a pillar of the old equilibrium that cannot be quietly reconstructed.

In physics and economics, hysteresis describes a system whose current state depends on its history. Push a magnet past its coercive threshold and it retains its new orientation even after the forcing field is removed. Avinash Dixit's (1989, 1992) application to entry and exit decisions in markets under uncertainty showed that sunk costs create "bands of inaction": once a firm has invested in entering a market or exiting one, the reversal cost ensures it stays even when the original conditions that prompted the move have changed. The post-Thompson insurance landscape exhibits precisely this dynamic across five domains.

Transparency data, once published, cannot be unpublished. CMS-0057-F went live on March 31, 2026, forcing insurers to report prior authorization denial rates, decision times, and appeal outcomes for the first time. KFF's August 13 cross-market analysis immediately exposed UnitedHealth's 17% MA denial rate as 3.4 times Elevance's 5%. That comparison now exists in the public record. Even if a future administration revoked the reporting rule, the baseline data has been captured, archived by researchers, cited in congressional testimony, and embedded in the evidentiary record of pending litigation (the Senate Permanent Subcommittee's bipartisan document demands, the Lokken discovery order). Revoking transparency does not restore opacity when the data has already been extracted.

Administrative infrastructure, once dismantled, is expensive to rebuild. UnitedHealthcare eliminated prior authorization for 1,500 rural hospitals, two-thirds of pediatric PA requirements, and committed to a 30% overall reduction in 2026. Aetna automated 88% of submissions and processes 83% in real time. These are not policy announcements. They are systems changes: modified decision logic, retrained staff workflows, updated provider portals, rebuilt claims-processing pipelines. Reinstating the eliminated PAs would require rebuilding the administrative infrastructure that processed them, re-hiring or re-training the staff who executed them, and re-establishing the provider communication channels that transmitted them. Dixit's framework predicts that the sunk cost of dismantling creates a hysteresis band: even if the political pressure that motivated the reform subsides, the cost of reversal exceeds the benefit of reimposition for any individual insurer acting alone. The first insurer to reinstate PAs while competitors maintain the reformed posture would face adverse selection in plan enrollment without recouping the administrative rebuilding cost.

State legislation, once enacted, requires repeal. Eight states have enacted binding restrictions on AI in coverage decisions. Washington SB 5395 prohibits AI-only PA denials. California SB 363 threatens escalating fines up to $1 million per case. Indiana HB 1271 bans algorithmic downcoding. Each statute required a legislative coalition to pass. Repealing each requires a new legislative coalition, organized opposition, floor time, and a governor's signature. The asymmetry between enactment and repeal is a structural feature of the legislative process: statutes have inertia. And insurers have already invested in compliance systems for each state's requirements. Those compliance costs are sunk. The regulated-state footprint functions as a ratchet: each new state law raises the floor, and the floor does not lower itself.

Litigation discovery, once compelled, enters the permanent record. The Lokken discovery order forced UnitedHealth to produce documents across six categories covering nH Predict's development, financial benefits, and employee incentive structures. The Senate Permanent Subcommittee's bipartisan demand for internal records from UNH, Humana, and CVS has subpoena authority. The Kaiser whistleblower case produced evidence of retroactive diagnosis inflation tied to physician bonuses. Each disclosure creates what Shin (2003) formalized as a "disclosure cascade": information forced into the open on one front becomes available to every other enforcement body simultaneously. A document produced in the Lokken class action can be cited in the Senate investigation, referenced by state insurance commissioners, and introduced as evidence in future class actions. The information entropy of the system has increased permanently. The pre-shooting equilibrium required that the inner workings of the denial machine remain proprietary. That condition no longer holds.

The narrative, once established, persists independently of the narrator. Mangione's allocution entered the federal court record on August 14, 2026. His observation that UnitedHealthcare's annual gathering was attended by "company executives, the board of directors, and hundreds of investors, not doctors, nurses, and patients" does not require his freedom, his trial, or his continued public presence to circulate. The 71% bipartisan voter support for a PA ban, the 70% NORC finding that Americans blame insurance industry practices, the AMA's finding that 26% of physicians report PA-related serious adverse events: these data points exist independently of the shooting that made them politically salient. The Schelling focal point coordinated attention. But the underlying grievances, documented in peer-reviewed studies, government audits, and now the insurers' own mandatory reporting, would persist even if the focal point dissolved. The shooting did not create the dysfunction. It made the dysfunction legible.

Game Theory Concept
Dixit (1989) Hysteresis in Markets Under Uncertainty and Arthur's (1989) Path Dependence

Avinash Dixit's (1989) model of entry and exit under uncertainty demonstrated that sunk costs create asymmetric thresholds: the price at which a firm enters a market exceeds the price at which it exits, producing a "band of inaction" where neither entry nor exit occurs. Within this band, history determines state. Brian Arthur's (1989) work on path dependence and increasing returns showed that small early events can lock complex systems into one of multiple possible equilibria, and the lock-in persists even when the initial conditions that produced it have vanished. Applied to the post-Thompson insurance reform: the shooting was the small event that pushed the system past its coercive threshold. The sunk costs of reform (dismantled PA infrastructure, enacted state laws, published transparency data, compelled discovery, embedded compliance systems) now define the lower boundary of the hysteresis band. For the industry to return to the pre-shooting equilibrium, it would need to: rebuild administrative infrastructure that was deliberately dismantled, repeal statutes across eight states with more pending, suppress transparency data that has already been archived and cited, re-seal litigation discovery that has entered the public record, and reverse the narrative shift in an electorate where 71% support a PA ban. Each of these reversal costs exceeds the benefit of reimposition for any individual firm, and collective reversal faces the same coordination problem that prevented collective reform before the shooting: Olson's (1965) free-rider barrier applies symmetrically to both directions. The pre-shooting equilibrium was stable because no individual insurer had incentive to reform unilaterally. The post-shooting equilibrium is stable because no individual insurer has incentive to regress unilaterally. The system has crossed the hysteresis threshold. The old equilibrium is not merely unlikely. It is structurally inaccessible.

The First Terminations: When the Denominator Shrinks in Real Time

On August 14, 2026, two things happened. Luigi Mangione stood in a federal courtroom and said, "I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan." And in Nebraska, roughly 200 Medicaid enrollees received notice that their coverage had been terminated under the new federal work requirements. The system's two responses to the same event, criminal punishment of the actor and administrative removal of the population he claimed to represent, converged on the same calendar date.

Nebraska's terminations are the first concrete data point in what CMS's own interim final rule (published June 3, 2026, effective July 31) projects will become a mass-coverage event. The agency's internal model estimates 2.3 million people will lose Medicaid coverage in fiscal year 2027, rising to between 3.1 million and 3.3 million annually thereafter. CMS projects a 15% disenrollment rate among affected adults: 9% for failing to satisfy the 80-hour monthly requirement, and 6% for paperwork and administrative barriers alone. That second figure is the admission that matters. The government's own model predicts that 40% of its projected coverage losses will result not from people declining to work, but from people unable to navigate the documentation process. This is the prior authorization mechanism applied to eligibility itself: the barrier is bureaucratic, not behavioral.

A peer-reviewed microsimulation published in JAMA Health Forum on July 16, 2026, by Sanjay Basu and colleagues at Waymark and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, quantified what those CBO numbers mean in bodies. The study modeled the broader consequences of the 2025 Budget Reconciliation Bill (H.R. 1) on health outcomes, health systems, and local economies, incorporating empirically derived parameters from quasi-experimental studies of Medicaid expansions (a 6.1% relative reduction in all-cause mortality, baseline 0.32%) and federal data showing uninsured individuals have 33% higher rates of preventable hospitalizations. The results are precise: for every 100,000 people who lose Medicaid coverage, there will be 13 to 14 excess deaths, 810 to 924 preventable hospitalizations, and up to $1.2 billion in lost economic output annually. Under the CBO's base-case projection of 7.6 million newly uninsured by 2034, that scales to approximately 1,064 excess deaths and 68,000 preventable hospitalizations per year. Under the higher-impact scenario of 14.4 million uninsured, the model projects up to 2,284 excess deaths and more than 145,000 preventable hospitalizations annually. Basu stated: "The data shows that rural and underserved communities would bear a disproportionate burden of these policy changes." The study quantified rural hospital vulnerability using empirical relationships between Medicaid coverage and institutional viability, projecting that the coverage contraction will push already fragile rural facilities past their financial breaking point.

The Waymark/UNC estimate is methodologically distinct from, and more granular than, the Lancet's estimate of 14,660 excess deaths from Medicaid expansion rollback. The Lancet figure captures the mortality impact of reversing expansion itself. The JAMA Health Forum model captures the incremental impact of the OBBBA's specific mechanisms: work requirements, enhanced eligibility verification every six months, and reduced federal matching rates. The two estimates are additive, not substitutive. A separate PNAS study (Basu et al. 2024) projected 7,900 additional deaths (95% UI: 1,613-16,339) from the unwinding of Medicaid's continuous enrollment provision alone, with 456,966 people with diabetes losing access to vital primary care. And a Penn LDI analysis using the RESPOND model projected that 156,000 people will lose access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD), causing over 1,000 excess fatal overdoses per year, because the overdose rate among those losing treatment doubles in the first year following coverage loss. A Bloomberg Government analysis of an NEJM study (Roberts et al.) projected 18,000 preventable deaths annually among dual Medicare-Medicaid eligibles who lose their Medicaid and, with it, their automatic enrollment in Medicare's Low Income Subsidy program, based on a 4% higher mortality rate observed over 11-month periods in the study population.

The most comprehensive single estimate came from a study published on June 16, 2025, in the Annals of Internal Medicine by Adam Gaffney and colleagues at Harvard Medical School and the City University of New York's Hunter College. The researchers examined the combined effects of all Medicaid provisions in the House reconciliation bill using CBO enrollment estimates and peer-reviewed analyses of mortality effects from prior Medicaid expansions and contractions. Their mid-range projection: enactment of the bill as passed would increase the number of uninsured by 7.6 million and result in 16,642 medically preventable deaths annually. That figure breaks down into staggering component harms: 1.9 million people losing access to a physician, 1.3 million forgoing needed medications, 1.2 million incurring medical debt, 380,270 women missing a mammogram, and 246,000 people turned away from medical care because of existing debts. Gaffney, an ICU physician, wrote: "In the ICU, I see what happens when patients do not get the regular care they need: They get sicker, sometimes gravely or even mortally ill." The authors characterized their estimates as conservative, excluding harms from provider payment reductions, benefit shrinkage, and cascading effects from states increasing taxes or shifting expenditures to compensate for federal shortfalls. The study also evaluated the six individual Medicaid cut options on the Budget Committee's menu, projecting that each would independently produce between 651 and 12,626 medically preventable deaths per year. The Senate's proposed cuts are deeper than the House version, meaning the enacted legislation may produce mortality somewhere above the 16,642 annual floor.

Each study uses different methodology, different populations, and different coverage-loss mechanisms. Together, they converge on the same structural finding: the denominator contraction documented in this section is not merely an administrative reshuffling. It is a mortality event operating through bureaucratic channels that no insurer denial statistic will ever capture.

The administrative architecture compounds the problem. States must begin notifying members by August 31, 2026, with compliance required by January 1, 2027. CMS has distributed $200 million in grants and committed over $600 million for technology upgrades, at an estimated cost of $15 million per state. But the systems being built must accommodate a requirement that the CMS Administrator, Dr. Mehmet Oz, has framed as a guardrail: "If you can work, you should get up and work." The framing obscures what CMS's own data reveals. More than nine in ten Medicaid expansion enrollees are already working, looking for work, in school, caregiving, or in fair or poor health. The projected losses are driven by documentation failures among people who already satisfy the requirement but cannot prove it in the format the system demands. Gig workers without HR departments. Caregivers whose exemptions require physician documentation they cannot obtain within the 30-day response window. People who never received or never opened the notice because their address on file was wrong.

The legal challenge has not kept pace with the administrative calendar. Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia sued CMS in late June. A federal judge in Boston heard arguments on a preliminary injunction motion on July 28. No ruling had been issued by the time the rule took legal effect on July 31. The specific legal dispute is narrow: whether CMS exceeded its authority by adding a condition Congress did not write to the "medically frail" exemption, requiring enrollees to demonstrate that their condition "significantly impairs" their ability to complete 80 hours. The plaintiff states argue this forces medically frail people "to jump through unnecessary administrative hoops" for coverage they are entitled to by statute. But even if the injunction is granted, it would address only the exemption definition, not the work requirement itself, which is statutory. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's text is clear, and the CBO's 5.2 million disenrollment projection accounts for administrative churn, not just noncompliance.

Meanwhile, the ACA Marketplace is contracting from the other direction. On July 22, 2026, HHS appealed the Columbus II ruling to the Fourth Circuit, seeking to restore the vacated provisions of the Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Rule. The government requested a decision by December 31, arguing "potential mootness" because several provisions were designed to sunset at end of 2026. The appeal seeks to reinstate the $5 auto-enrollment surcharge, past-due premium barriers, shortened open enrollment, and documentation verification requirements that the district court found "arbitrary and capricious." Even if the appeal fails, the underlying premium spiral continues: insurers have proposed a median 14% increase for 2027, the second consecutive year of double-digit hikes. The covered population is being squeezed from both ends.

Game Theory Concept
Dual-Track Population Contraction as Equilibrium Maintenance (Selten 1978 / Edgeworth 1881)

Selten's (1978) chain-store paradox demonstrated that a monopolist's threat to punish entrants is incredible in a finite game because backward induction unravels the commitment. But when the game has two tracks, punishment of the actor (criminal prosecution) and reduction of the constituency (administrative disenrollment), the dominant player can maintain the equilibrium through population contraction rather than deterrence. The system does not need to deter future actors if it can reduce the population that would support them. CMS's own projection that 40% of coverage losses will be administrative rather than behavioral is the mechanism design equivalent of Edgeworth's (1881) recontracting problem: the system iterates toward an equilibrium that excludes the participants who generate the most costly claims, not through explicit denial (which is now monitored and reported) but through eligibility attrition that requires no coverage decision at all. A person who loses Medicaid for failing to submit paperwork does not appear in any insurer's denial statistics. They do not file an appeal. They do not contribute to the 80.7% MA overturn rate. They exit the denominator entirely, and every PA reform metric improves because the population generating the worst outcomes is no longer being measured. Nebraska's 200 terminations on August 14 are the first empirical observation of this mechanism in operation. The 2.3 million projected for fiscal 2027 will be the confirmation. The denominator shrinks, the scorecard improves, and the people who needed coverage most are the ones who cannot prove they deserve it.

The convergence of dates is not a coincidence of scheduling. It is a structural feature of a system that processes violence and policy through parallel channels with different speeds. The criminal justice system required 20 months to reach a guilty plea. The administrative system required 14 months from the One Big Beautiful Bill's signing to the first terminations. Both timelines were set in motion by the same event: a shooting that made health insurance denial a subject of national political salience. The shooting triggered reform (6.5 million fewer PA requirements) and contraction (2.3 million projected coverage losses) simultaneously. The net effect on the insured population is not reform. It is restructuring: better rules for a smaller group, with the excluded population bearing the cost of the inclusion they can no longer access. The prior authorization reforms documented throughout this analysis save statistical lives among the covered. The Medicaid and ACA contractions create statistical deaths among the excluded. Whether the first number exceeds the second is the moral arithmetic the system is not designed to perform, because the two populations are measured by different agencies, reported in different datasets, and governed by different statutes. The denominator's shrinkage is invisible to the numerator's reform.

The Definitional Weapon: When Exemption Narrowing Creates a Second Coverage Wave

The first coverage wave documented above operates through work requirements: fail to document 80 hours, lose Medicaid. But a second mechanism, subtler and potentially more consequential, emerged in June 2026 when CMS published an interim final rule that redefined who qualifies for medical exemption from those requirements. The 26 states that sued in Boston federal court identified the mechanism precisely: CMS "dramatically narrowed the Congressionally established categorical exclusions" for medically frail individuals. Before the rule, states could identify medically frail enrollees through health record review, checking claims history, diagnostic codes, and utilization patterns to flag people whose conditions should exempt them from work requirements. The interim final rule shifted the burden: patients must now self-document their frailty with physician notes. The definition did not change on paper. The proof requirement changed in practice.

This is not an administrative adjustment. It is what William Riker (1986) called heresthetics: the art of political manipulation through restructuring the dimensions of choice. Riker distinguished heresthetics from rhetoric (persuading people to change their preferences) and from agenda control (determining which options are voted on). Heresthetics restructures the choice situation itself so that the existing preferences of the players produce a different outcome without anyone changing their mind. CMS did not change the statutory definition of "medically frail." It did not argue that fewer people should qualify. It restructured the proof mechanism so that the same definition, applied to the same population, produces fewer exemptions, because the barrier is no longer clinical identification but patient-initiated documentation.

The parallel to prior authorization is structural, not metaphorical. Prior authorization denies treatment through administrative friction: the physician must submit paperwork, wait for review, appeal if denied, and resubmit. The patient absorbs the delay. Exemption narrowing denies coverage through definitional friction: the patient must obtain a physician note, submit it through a process designed for administrative compliance rather than clinical assessment, and resubmit if the documentation is deemed insufficient. In both cases, the barrier is bureaucratic rather than medical. In both cases, the people least equipped to navigate the process are the ones most likely to need what it gatekeeps. The difference is the layer: prior authorization operates within coverage, filtering which treatments reach patients who have insurance. Exemption narrowing operates beneath coverage, filtering which patients retain insurance at all. It is the same mechanism applied one level deeper in the stack.

Judge Stearns denied the 26 states' preliminary injunction request on July 30, 2026. The hearing on the medically frail definition challenge is scheduled for October 20. Meanwhile, the first empirical consequences have arrived. Nebraska terminated roughly 200 Medicaid enrollees on August 1 under the work requirements that the narrowed exemptions failed to shield them from. Drew Gonshorowski, Nebraska's Medicaid director, confirmed the figure: approximately 200 terminations from a population of 72,000 enrollees subject to the requirements, out of 346,000 total Medicaid recipients in the state. These are the first Americans to lose Medicaid coverage under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's work requirements. CMS's own model projects 2.3 million losing coverage in fiscal year 2027, with 40% of those losses attributable to paperwork failures rather than actual noncompliance. The narrowed exemption definition compounds this: people who would have been automatically flagged as medically frail through state record review must now produce documentation that many lack the resources, health literacy, or physician access to obtain.

The game-theoretic structure is Myerson's (1981) mechanism design applied in reverse. Mechanism design asks: given the outcome you want, what rules produce it? The standard application is constructive: design an auction that maximizes revenue, a matching algorithm that produces stable pairings, a voting rule that aggregates preferences. The CMS exemption narrowing is deconstructive mechanism design: given the population you want to exclude, what proof requirement produces the exclusion without explicitly denying anyone? The answer is a documentation standard calibrated to the capacity gap between the exempt population and the general population. Medically frail Medicaid enrollees, by definition, have conditions that impair their ability to work. Many of those same conditions impair their ability to navigate administrative systems: cognitive impairment, severe mental illness, substance use disorder, chronic pain requiring opioid management. Requiring self-documentation from a population defined by its functional limitations is not a neutral administrative choice. It is a screening mechanism that selects for exclusion precisely the people the exemption was designed to protect.

The redetermination frequency change compounds the definitional narrowing. Starting December 31, 2026, Medicaid eligibility reviews will occur every six months instead of annually. CMS projects this change alone will produce approximately 700,000 additional coverage losses. The interaction between the two mechanisms is multiplicative, not additive: a medically frail person who fails to self-document exemption status must do so twice as often, and each failure triggers a new termination-and-reapplication cycle that resets the administrative burden. The Arkansas precedent is instructive. Between 2018 and 2019, approximately 18,000 Arkansans lost Medicaid under that state's work requirement waiver. Diaz and Shubeck's modeling of the national rollout, published in JAMA Oncology (January 2026), projects the screening cascade: 7.5 million adults losing coverage translates to 405,706 missed mammograms, 679,745 missed colorectal screenings, 67,213 missed lung cancer screenings, 2,341 undetected cancers, and 155 excess cancer deaths within two years. The medically frail exemption was the firewall that was supposed to prevent the sickest patients from falling through. The definitional narrowing weakened the firewall without removing it, producing the appearance of protection while reducing its effectiveness.

Stigler's (1971) theory of regulatory capture predicts that regulated industries will eventually co-opt the agencies that oversee them, bending regulation to serve industry interests rather than public ones. The CMS exemption narrowing inverts the standard capture model. In classic Stigler, the regulator is captured by the industry it regulates and weakens oversight to benefit incumbents. Here, the regulator is not captured by insurers. It is weaponizing its own definitional authority against the population it administers, reducing the enrolled population to achieve budget targets ($326 billion in savings over ten years, the largest single savings source in the OBBBA according to CBO). The beneficiary of the definitional narrowing is not the insurance industry, which will lose Medicaid managed care revenue as enrollment shrinks. The beneficiary is the federal budget, and the cost is borne by the people whose conditions made them eligible for exemption under the definition Congress wrote but no longer qualify under the proof standard CMS imposed.

The American Indian and Alaska Native population illustrates the boundary condition. Their work requirement exemption is written directly into statute, not delegated to CMS rulemaking. The National Council of Urban Indian Health published compliance guidance on August 14, 2026, noting that AI/AN enrollees are categorically exempt regardless of the CMS interim final rule's documentation requirements. This is the control case: when Congress specifies the exemption in statutory text rather than delegating definitional authority to the administering agency, the exemption survives administrative reinterpretation. The medically frail exemption was not written with that specificity, which is why CMS could narrow it through rulemaking rather than legislation.
