The lesson is architectural: a statutory right that delegates its own boundary conditions to the agency that benefits from narrowing them is not a right. It is a parameter in someone else's optimization function.

Game Theory Concept
Definitional Heresthetics: Restructuring Eligibility Through Exemption Narrowing (Riker 1986 / Myerson 1981 / Stigler 1971)

Riker's (1986) heresthetics describes the manipulation of political outcomes by restructuring the dimensions of choice rather than persuading voters or controlling the agenda. Applied to the CMS interim final rule: the agency did not change who is medically frail. It changed what counts as proof of medical frailty, shifting the burden from institutional identification (state record review) to patient self-documentation (physician notes). Myerson's (1981) mechanism design framework reveals this as a screening mechanism: the documentation requirement is calibrated to the capacity gap between the target population and the general population, ensuring that the people most likely to qualify for exemption are also the people least likely to complete the proof process. Stigler's (1971) regulatory capture theory, applied in reverse, explains the regulator's incentive: CMS is not captured by the insurance industry (which loses managed care revenue when enrollment shrinks) but by the federal budget constraint (which gains $326 billion over ten years from coverage contraction). The definitional narrowing achieves population reduction without explicit denial, producing budget savings that appear in CBO scores while the resulting mortality appears only in epidemiological models that no federal agency is required to run. Prior authorization is the denial mechanism within coverage. Exemption narrowing is the denial mechanism beneath coverage. Together they constitute a two-layer administrative attrition system: the first layer determines which treatments reach patients, the second determines which patients reach treatment at all, and both layers use the same instrument (bureaucratic friction calibrated to population vulnerability) to produce the same outcome (cost reduction through access reduction) at different points in the coverage stack.

The NHeLP/Benefits Tech Hub guide released in August 2026 documents state-level strategies for reducing procedural terminations: automatic exemption identification through claims data, extended notice periods, multiple contact modalities, and real-time eligibility verification. These are mechanism design countermeasures: redesigning the proof process to reduce the capacity gap that the CMS rule exploits. But they are voluntary state choices, not federal requirements. A state that implements them incurs administrative costs to preserve enrollment that the federal government is financially incentivized to reduce. The game-theoretic prediction is straightforward: states that invest in exemption preservation will bear costs that states which allow administrative churn to proceed will avoid, creating a race-to-the-bottom dynamic where the states most willing to let the definitional narrowing take effect receive the largest per-capita budget relief. The 26 states that sued are, by definition, the ones most likely to implement countermeasures. The states that did not sue are the ones where the definitional weapon will cut deepest.

The Invented Evidence: When Regulatory Analysis Becomes Strategic Fiction

The Brookings Institution's Center on Health Policy published the most damaging critique of the CMS work requirement on August 5, 2026. Sherry Glied and Richard G. Frank, two of the nation's leading health economists, submitted a formal comment letter to CMS (addressed to Administrator Oz, dated July 31, 2026) finding that the interim final rule's Regulatory Impact Analysis is "fundamentally defective in both its substance and its analysis." The RIA's central behavioral assumption, that 29% of beneficiaries subject to the work requirement will begin working or otherwise become "community-engaged," has, in their assessment, "no empirical justification." Three separate research strands contradict it. Studies of welfare-to-work programs, which conditioned receipt of cash benefits on employment and included childcare, transportation, and case management support that the Medicaid rule lacks, found employment effects "under 5%." Studies of the ACA Medicaid expansion found that gaining Medicaid had "little or no effect on employment," implying that withdrawing coverage would produce little employment increase. And direct studies of SNAP and Medicaid work requirements, including Arkansas's Medicaid waiver, found "substantial coverage losses but no measurable increase in employment." CMS's 29% assumption is, Glied and Frank write, "over six times greater than the largest estimate in any of these literatures."

The mathematical inconsistency that follows from the invented behavioral response is the critique's most consequential finding. CMS projects that only 3.1 to 3.3 million people will lose Medicaid annually, roughly 40% fewer than the CBO's estimate of 5.7 million. Yet CMS simultaneously projects $350 billion in federal savings over ten years, 10% more than CBO's $317 billion estimate. Fewer people losing coverage but more money saved. Glied and Frank show that reconciling these figures requires CMS to assume that each disenrolled person costs the federal government approximately $11,000 per year, roughly double CBO's implied $5,600. But Medicaid spending is heavily concentrated: the most expensive beneficiaries have serious health conditions that should qualify them for the medically frail exemption. CMS does not explain how a smaller pool of disenrollees generates larger savings unless it is implicitly assuming that the exemption system will fail to protect the very people it was designed for. The analysis reveals its own assumption about the definitional narrowing's effectiveness: the budget math works only if the medically frail exemption does not.

Glied and Frank also dismantle the RIA's claimed health benefits. CMS asserts that those induced into employment by the work requirement will become healthier, citing correlational studies showing that employed people have better health outcomes than unemployed people. But correlation is not causation. Healthier people are more likely to work. Education, family resources, and housing stability affect both employment and health. The causal evidence, from studies exploiting changes in retirement rules and other sources of exogenous variation, is mixed: some find modest benefits from continued work, while others find that working harms health through injury risk. Meanwhile, CMS "largely omits" the strongest causal evidence in the field: randomized and quasi-experimental studies showing that Medicaid coverage improves access to care, financial security, and, in several credible studies, mortality. Randomized trials of depression care have found increases in job retention and hours worked. The causal arrow points from health coverage to employment, not the reverse. The RIA inverts it.

The substance of the rule compounds the analytical deficiency. Glied and Frank note that the exemption for substance use treatment participation is restricted to care provided by nonprofit organizations. But nearly half of people receiving substance use treatment are served by for-profit providers, and the share is "particularly high among opioid treatment programs providing methadone." A patient receiving methadone-assisted treatment through a for-profit clinic, the only provider available in many rural communities, would lose both the treatment exemption and potentially the coverage financing the treatment. The exemption is calibrated not to clinical need but to provider organizational form, a distinction that has no bearing on whether a patient's condition impairs their capacity to work 80 hours per month.

Game Theory Concept
Strategic Regulatory Analysis as Bayesian Persuasion (Crawford & Sobel 1982 / Kamenica & Gentzkow 2011)

Crawford and Sobel's (1982) strategic information transmission model analyzes communication when the sender has a systematic bias toward a particular outcome. When the sender's bias is small, equilibrium messages are informative: the receiver can extract useful information despite knowing the sender's preferences. As bias increases, message precision degrades until, at maximum bias, the signal becomes uninformative. Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) extended this to Bayesian persuasion, showing that a sender can design the information structure itself to maximally shift the receiver's posterior toward the sender's preferred action. Applied to the CMS Regulatory Impact Analysis: CMS is not a neutral analyst. It is a player with an objective function aligned to federal budget savings ($350 billion over ten years). The RIA is the persuasion mechanism through which CMS must convince two audiences: the courts (under APA arbitrary-and-capricious review) and the public (under Executive Order 12866 transparency requirements). The 29% employment assumption was not derived from evidence because no evidence supports it. It was selected because it is the behavioral parameter needed to reconcile two simultaneous objectives: projecting enough disenrollment to generate the budgetary savings Congress mandated, while projecting enough "community engagement" to claim the rule produces health benefits that offset its coverage losses. Glied and Frank's critique exposes the sender's bias: CMS's estimate is six times the highest figure in the empirical literature, making the RIA uninformative under Crawford-Sobel and strategically designed under Kamenica-Gentzkow. The RIA does not analyze the mechanism. It is the mechanism: a persuasion device calibrated to the judicial review standard that requires "reasonable" assumptions rather than the best available evidence. The definitional narrowing documented in the previous section operates on patients. The invented evidence operates on the analysis itself. Both use the same instrument: administrative documents designed to produce predetermined outcomes while maintaining procedural compliance.

The External Review Paradox: When Neutral Arbiters Prove the Denial System Wrong

A research letter published in JAMA Internal Medicine in April 2026 by Joseph Dov Bruch and colleagues at the University of Chicago quantified something the industry had long resisted measuring: what happens when denied claims reach reviewers who have no financial stake in the outcome. The researchers analyzed 51,394 closed external appeal cases in New York state from May 31, 2019, to December 10, 2025, the largest published dataset of independent review organization (IRO) decisions. The results were devastating. Overall, 46.7% of external appeals were overturned. When independent physicians and clinical specialists not affiliated with the insurer examined the denial rationale, they reversed it nearly half the time.

The category-level breakdowns were worse. Of 6,469 denied home health care services claims that reached external review, 78.4% were overturned. More than half of surgical services, dental or orthodontic procedures, and pharmacy or prescription drug denials were reversed. These are not marginal cases that reasonable clinicians might evaluate differently. A 78.4% overturn rate means the insurer's clinical rationale for denying home health services was wrong four out of five times when subjected to neutral scrutiny. The denominator matters: these 51,394 cases represent only the fraction of patients who navigated two prior levels of internal appeal before reaching external review. The patients who abandoned their claims at the first denial, the second denial, or somewhere in the months-long appeal process are not in this dataset. The 46.7% overturn rate measures the insurer's accuracy only against the most persistent patients with the strongest cases and the greatest capacity to endure administrative friction.

The Bruch study confirms and extends a pattern visible in multiple independent datasets. The Staffingly 2026 PA Burden Report found that 80.7% of challenged Medicare Advantage denials are overturned, but only 11.5% are ever challenged. The CMS plan year 2024 data showed a 95% overturn rate for skilled nursing facility denials appealed from naviHealth. The KFF cross-market analysis documented overturn rates ranging from 38% to 81% depending on market segment and insurer. Each dataset, using different methodologies, populations, and time periods, converges on the same structural finding: the denial system does not work by being right. It works by being uncontested.

Penn Medicine's Perelman Center for Advanced Medicine published the institutional response in the May 2026 issue of Gastroenterology & Endoscopy News. Beginning in spring 2021, Penn Medicine's outpatient gastroenterology clinic built a dedicated prior authorization denial team, reassigning appeal responsibilities from physicians to advanced practice providers and pharmacists, standardizing the documentation process, and building a library of more than 15 appeal letter templates covering the most common denial scenarios. The team cut the time to write an appeal letter roughly in half, from 45-60 minutes to 20-30 minutes. Pharmacy technicians spent 20 to 90 minutes per denial on follow-up calls alone. The model worked: providers rated it 9.79 out of 10 at the first site and a perfect 10 at the second. But the volume of denials did not decrease. It continued to rise, from approximately 29 per month in early 2021 to between 35 and 50 per month by late 2022. Penn Medicine built a machine for fighting denials. The machine works. The denials kept coming.

The AGA survey data that motivated Penn Medicine's intervention frames the broader burden. A 2021 survey of American Gastroenterological Association members found that 89% reported an increase in prior authorizations over the prior five years, 96% called them burdensome, and 99% said they hindered appropriate care. A 2022 study found that 90% of insurance policies were inconsistent with AGA clinical guidelines, and that prior authorizations created an average treatment delay of 10.2 days, with complex cases averaging 24.6 days. Those delays corresponded with a 13% increase in IBD-related healthcare utilization, including emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and surgery. The insurer saves money by denying the initial treatment. The patient and the healthcare system pay more when the delay produces a complication that requires emergency care. The cost is not eliminated. It is transferred.

Penn Medicine's model exposes the deepest structural problem with the appeal system as a reform mechanism. The model requires dedicated staff, standardized workflows, template libraries, and institutional investment to contest denials that the insurer generates algorithmically at near-zero marginal cost. A gastroenterologist at a community practice with three physicians does not have a PharmD and an APP dedicated to writing appeal letters. A patient at a rural clinic does not have access to a template library or a peer-to-peer call coordinator. The model that works at Penn Medicine cannot scale to the practices that need it most, because the resource asymmetry between generating a denial and contesting a denial is structural, not operational. The insurer can deny 1,000 claims with a single algorithmic rule update. Contesting those 1,000 denials requires 1,000 individual appeal letters, each referencing the patient's specific clinical history, each citing the relevant evidence base, each navigating the insurer's specific appeal procedures. This is the mechanism through which the 4% challenge rate is sustained: not because patients accept the denial as medically justified, but because the cost of challenging it exceeds the cost of absorbing it for 96% of denied claims.

Game Theory Concept
War of Attrition with Asymmetric Costs (Maynard Smith, 1974; Riley, 1980)

Maynard Smith's (1974) war of attrition models contests where the winner is not the stronger player but the player willing to bear costs longer. When the costs of persisting are symmetric, the equilibrium involves mixed strategies and escalation is bounded. Riley (1980) extended the model to asymmetric costs, showing that when one player's per-period cost of continuing the contest is substantially lower than the other's, the low-cost player wins with near certainty regardless of the value at stake. The insurance denial system is a war of attrition with maximally asymmetric costs. The insurer's cost of maintaining a denial through three levels of appeal is trivial: automated letter generation, a clerk's time to process the internal appeal, and a modest fee to the IRO if the case reaches external review. The patient's cost includes lost work hours, navigating bureaucratic procedures designed by the opposing party, finding and citing clinical evidence, coordinating with physicians whose time is already constrained, and bearing the medical risk of delayed treatment. The 46.7% overturn rate at external review means the insurer's position is wrong nearly half the time when tested. But the 4% challenge rate means the insurer never faces the test in 96% of cases. The war of attrition does not select for the medically correct outcome. It selects for the party with lower per-period costs. Penn Medicine's dedicated denial team is an institutional attempt to reduce the provider's per-period cost, and it works at a top-5 academic medical center with pharmacists, APPs, and template libraries. But the structural asymmetry remains: the insurer sets the rules of the attrition game (appeal procedures, documentation requirements, timeline constraints), and the patient must play on the insurer's terrain. Riley's model predicts that reducing the patient's cost (through AI appeal tools, dedicated teams, or state-mandated response timelines) will increase the challenge rate, which will increase the overturn rate, which will force the insurer to either improve denial accuracy or reduce denial volume. Milgrom's unraveling result (1981) makes the same prediction from a different direction: as appeal costs approach zero, the denial rate must converge to the clinically defensible floor. The Bruch data and the Penn Medicine experience together quantify the gap between the current equilibrium (46.7% wrong, 96% unchallenged) and the defensible floor, a gap sustained entirely by the cost asymmetry that the war of attrition framework was designed to analyze.

The Attention Economy: When Reform Must Outlive Its Catalyst

Every reform documented in this analysis depends on a variable that game theory rarely models: public attention. Anthony Downs described the pattern in 1972. A dramatic event reveals a problem. The public reacts with alarm. Policymakers scramble. Then the cost of meaningful change becomes apparent, competing issues intrude, and attention migrates. The problem persists, but the electorate has moved on. Downs called it the "issue-attention cycle," and his original case study was environmentalism. The cycle applies to every policy domain where the costs of reform are concentrated on organized interests (insurers, their lobbyists, congressional allies) while the benefits are dispersed across millions of unorganized patients who will never form an effective political constituency.

The health insurance denial crisis follows Downs' five-stage model with uncomfortable precision. Stage one (the pre-problem stage) lasted decades: denial rates climbed, appeal rates remained below 1%, and the industry's quarterly earnings calls never mentioned the word "denial" except in investor-friendly formulations like "medical cost management." Stage two (alarmed discovery) arrived on December 4, 2024, when shell casings etched with "delay, deny, depose" compressed decades of diffuse institutional violence into a single, legible act. Stage three (recognizing the cost of significant progress) began within months: the Consolidated Appropriations Act's PBM reforms carry a January 2028 implementation date, state AI-denial bans cover only 14 of 50 states, CMS-0057-F's electronic PA mandates do not take full effect until 2027, and the Improving Seniors Timely Access to Care Act, despite 298 House cosponsors and a 42-0 committee vote, has not yet reached a floor vote. The cost of change is not abstract. It is the $35 billion annual PA administrative economy (AMA), the $16 billion Star Ratings bonus pool that insurers are suing to protect, and the lobbying infrastructure that makes health insurance the fifth-largest industry for federal campaign contributions.

The standard prediction from Downs' model is that American health insurance denial will enter stage four (gradual decline of public interest) sometime in 2027 or 2028. The federal sentencing is scheduled for December 18, 2026. The state double jeopardy motion will be resolved by then. The news cycle will find its next crisis. Polling data already shows the trajectory: the Emerson survey's 41% "acceptable" finding among 18-29 year-olds was measured in the immediate aftermath. No longitudinal re-survey has been published. NORC's 70% figure on blaming denial practices has not been re-measured either. The AELP's 71% support for a PA ban (August 2026) was gathered at peak salience. Whether that number holds when the next election cycle's issues compete for the same cognitive bandwidth is an empirical question without current data.

But the Downs model contains an escape clause that the existing literature has underexplored. Stage five (the post-problem stage) is not a return to stage one. Downs noted that each cycle through the five stages leaves behind "recurrent spasms of interest and then renewed neglect" but also institutional residue: agencies created, laws enacted, monitoring systems built. The question for insurance denial reform is whether the institutional residue from stages two and three is structurally sufficient to survive stage four's attention withdrawal.

The evidence is mixed, and the honest answer requires separating three categories of reform by their dependence on sustained attention.

Category one: attention-independent reforms. These are structural changes that persist regardless of public engagement. CMS-0057-F's electronic PA mandate and public reporting requirement is codified regulation that requires an affirmative regulatory action to reverse. The 14 state AI-denial laws are enacted statutes. The CMS January 2027 electronic PA deadline and 72-hour/7-day decision timeframes are binding on plans as a condition of participation. The Consolidated Appropriations Act PBM provisions are statutory. The Lokken discovery order's algorithmic disclosure is a court order. These reforms do not need the public's attention to survive. They need only the absence of active repeal, and repeal is politically more expensive than enactment because the beneficiaries (patients who no longer face specific denials) become the constituency for preservation.

Category two: attention-dependent reforms. These require sustained political will to complete. The seven federal bills in the pipeline (Improving Seniors Act, Stop Deadly Denials Act, Prior Authorization Accountability Act, Patient Refunds Act, Joyce compliance-scoring bill, DeSaulnier ERISA package, H.R. 9734 Automated Denials Act) are all in committee or waiting for floor votes. Congressional bills that do not pass before a session ends die. The voluntary industry pledge (6.5 million PA reductions) has no enforcement mechanism and is already fracturing (8 signatories backed out of technology commitments, KFF July 2026). The Senate PSI investigation has subpoena authority but its scope depends on whether committee leadership sustains interest through the next Congress. These reforms are vulnerable to Downs' stage-four decline because they require repeated affirmative political action that becomes harder to justify as media coverage wanes.

Category three: paradoxically attention-resistant reforms. This is the analytically novel category. Some of the most significant changes triggered by the shooting are not policy reforms but market restructurings that create self-reinforcing equilibria independent of public attention. Buffett's $1.6 billion UNH buy and subsequent exit repriced the stock; the repricing is permanent regardless of whether anyone remembers the trade. The provider lawsuit wave (Jefferson Health v. Aetna, CHA v. Anthem, BCBS $2.67B settlement) created legal precedents that constrain insurer behavior through stare decisis, not public opinion. The CMS-0057-F disclosure data, once published, cannot be unpublished; the KFF's cross-market analysis created a baseline against which future denial rates will be permanently measured. The ProPublica/Optum ABA playbook leak documented internal strategy that is now available to plaintiff attorneys in perpetuity. Each of these is a one-way information ratchet: the disclosure itself is the reform, and no amount of public attention withdrawal can reverse disclosed information.

Game Theory Concept
The Attention Cycle as Asymmetric Contest: Downs (1972) Meets Tullock (1980)

Anthony Downs' (1972) issue-attention cycle is descriptive, not strategic. It describes what happens but not why the outcome favors organized incumbents. Tullock's (1980) theory of rent-seeking contests supplies the strategic mechanism: when the costs of lobbying for and against reform are asymmetric, the organized minority (insurers) can outspend the diffuse majority (patients) during stage four's attention decline, because the concentrated benefits of maintaining the denial system justify concentrated expenditure on its preservation, while the dispersed benefits of reform justify no comparable expenditure by any individual patient. The standard Tullock prediction is that the insurer wins the contest of attrition by simply outlasting public attention. But the post-Thompson reforms have created a structural modification to the Tullock contest that the standard model does not anticipate: the institutional residue from stages two and three has converted some of the contest's stakes from contestable (requiring ongoing political defense) to non-contestable (codified in statute, court order, or irreversible disclosure). The fraction of reform that is non-contestable determines whether the Downs cycle resets to the pre-problem equilibrium (stage one) or to a higher baseline (a new stage five where the worst practices are permanently constrained even as political attention decays). The empirical question for the insurance denial system is what fraction of the 6.5 million eliminated PA requirements, 14 state AI laws, 7+ federal bills, CMS electronic PA mandate, 400+ sources of litigation discovery, and permanently disclosed algorithmic practices falls into each category. The hysteresis analysis above suggests the non-contestable fraction is large enough that the old equilibrium is structurally inaccessible. But Downs' model warns that the contestable fraction, the pending bills, the voluntary pledges, the unenforced mandates, remains vulnerable to exactly the attention withdrawal that his theory predicts. The reform survives if and only if the non-contestable residue is sufficient to sustain the new equilibrium without the political energy that created it.

The empirical test is already running. The AAFP's July 2026 CME article, "Prior Authorization Reforms: The New Reality," is written in the imperative voice of practitioners who expect the reforms to stick. It instructs physicians on how to exercise gold-card rights, navigate the electronic PA APIs, and invoke the new PBM transparency mandates. The AMA's 2024 model legislation has been adopted by 17+ states. The Health Affairs Forefront analysis (2026) documents an "unprecedented" volume of state-level activity: 18 states passed PA legislation in 2025 alone, with 90+ bills across 30 states. This is not the behavior of an issue entering stage four. It is the behavior of a policy domain where the institutional residue has reached critical mass: enough state laws, federal rules, court orders, and published data to sustain a self-reinforcing reform ecosystem even when the cable news cameras point elsewhere.

The counterargument is the VA scandal of 2014. Forty veterans died waiting for care at the Phoenix VA Medical Center. The public reacted with alarm. Congress passed the Veterans Access to Care Act within weeks. By 2016, wait times had returned to pre-scandal levels, and the Phoenix VA's problems had metastasized to other facilities. The institutional residue (the CHOICE Act, later the MISSION Act) created new bureaucratic pathways without fundamentally altering the incentive structure that produced the waits. The attention cycled through all five of Downs' stages in under two years. The insurance denial system could follow the same path if the voluntary pledges substitute for binding reform and the pending legislation dies in committee. The difference, and this is not a certainty but a structural argument, is that the post-Thompson reforms have produced more non-contestable institutional residue in 20 months than the VA scandal produced in a decade: 14 state laws versus zero, mandatory CMS reporting versus voluntary compliance, algorithmic discovery orders versus sealed internal reviews, and a $2.67 billion antitrust settlement with binding injunctive relief versus no comparable structural remedy.

Whether the non-contestable fraction is large enough to sustain the new equilibrium without sustained public attention is the most consequential empirical question this analysis raises. The answer will not be known for years. But the structure of the question is knowable now: the reform survives if the institutional residue outweighs the attention deficit. If the hysteresis analysis holds, the old equilibrium is already inaccessible. If Downs' pessimism holds, the industry needs only to wait.

The Multi-Principal Trap: When Regulators Contradict Each Other on the Same Patient

In July 2026, three institutions issued simultaneous and contradictory directives about the same treatment for the same patient population. On July 29, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz hosted a ceremony in Washington where insurers signed a voluntary behavioral health pledge. Optum CEO Patrick Conway told Becker's his company would be "the first in the private sector to sign on." The pledge addressed "timely access to treatment, evidence-based practice, measures, individualized treatment and whole-person care." It explicitly stated that it was "not a minimum standard of care, federal mandate or replacement for clinical judgment." The same month, CMS issued a Medicaid ABA oversight toolkit in response to a 421% increase in Medicaid spending on Applied Behavior Analysis therapy for autistic children, calling for tightened state-level documentation, billing integrity reviews, and provider auditing. And in the federal courts, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers of the Northern District of California ruled that a UnitedHealthcare plan term explicitly excluding "Intensive Behavioral Therapies such as Applied Behavior Analysis" for autism spectrum disorders violated the "plain terms" of the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, ordering coverage.

The three directives cannot be simultaneously followed. The court says: you must cover ABA, excluding it violates federal parity law. CMS says: ABA spending is growing too fast, states should tighten oversight. The pledge says: we voluntarily commit to improving behavioral health access, but this is "not a minimum standard of care" and does not replace "clinical judgment." An insurer processing an ABA authorization request on August 1, 2026, faces a legal mandate to cover, a regulatory signal to scrutinize, and a voluntary pledge to improve access that explicitly disclaims binding force. The insurer's revealed behavior resolves the contradiction: ProPublica's internal Optum documents, published months before the pledge ceremony, showed the company deploying 90+ "care advocates" to question ABA medical necessity, pursuing "market-specific action plans" to limit provider networks, and targeting utilization reduction in the states with the highest Medicaid ABA costs. The same company that signed the pledge is the one the court ordered to cover the therapy it was internally restricting.

The contradiction is not accidental. It is the structural output of a multi-principal regulatory system. CMS regulates Medicare Advantage and sets Medicaid guidelines. DOL/EBSA enforces MHPAEA for employer-sponsored plans. State insurance commissioners regulate fully insured plans. The federal courts adjudicate individual claims. Each principal has a different objective function: CMS wants to control federal spending, DOL/EBSA wants parity compliance (but has formally suspended enforcement), state regulators want solvent insurers, and courts want individual relief. No single principal has authority over the full behavioral health denial system. An insurer operating across all four domains can satisfy each principal's most visible criterion, signing the voluntary pledge for HHS, tightening ABA documentation for CMS, reporting lower medical/surgical PA rates for state regulators, and settling individual court orders, while maintaining the aggregate restriction that each principal's narrow mandate fails to detect.

Game Theory Concept
Multi-Principal Agency Problem (Bernheim & Whinston 1986; Dixit 1996)

In the standard principal-agent model, one principal designs a contract to align the agent's incentives. When multiple principals simultaneously regulate the same agent, Bernheim and Whinston (1986) showed that the resulting equilibrium is generically inefficient: each principal designs incentives that account for its own objective but ignores the externalities its contract imposes through the agent on other principals. Dixit (1996) extended this to public bureaucracies, demonstrating that agents facing multiple principals with conflicting objectives receive weak incentives from each and strong incentives from none. The ABA denial system instantiates both results. CMS's spending-control objective creates an incentive to restrict ABA access. The court's parity mandate creates an incentive to expand it. HHS's pledge creates an incentive to signal improvement without operational commitment. The insurer, as the common agent, faces three weak and contradictory incentive structures. The optimal response is to comply with the cheapest signal (the pledge, which costs nothing to sign), resist the most expensive mandate (the court order, which applies only to the individual plaintiff), and align operational behavior with the principal whose objective matches the insurer's own profit function (CMS's spending-control posture). The result is a system where parity law exists on paper, spending scrutiny operates in practice, voluntary pledges provide political cover, and autistic children in Louisiana continue to receive fewer hours of therapy than their clinicians recommend. The multi-principal framework predicts that reform will remain structurally incoherent until either one principal acquires authority over the full system or the principals coordinate their objectives, a coordination problem that is itself a game with its own equilibrium failures.

The CMS toolkit's framing reveals the deeper tension. The Medical Daily reported that the toolkit "does not establish new federal requirements, does not reduce Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic and Treatment obligations, does not endorse any single treatment approach, and does not direct states to limit access to medically necessary care." Like the pledge, it is carefully worded to avoid binding force. But its publication alongside a 421% spending-growth headline creates a framing effect that gives state Medicaid directors political cover to impose exactly the restrictions it disclaims. And the entity best positioned to exploit that cover is the managed care organization that administers Medicaid in those states. In over two dozen states, that entity is Optum. The multi-principal trap closes: the court orders ABA coverage for the individual plaintiff while the regulatory apparatus signals spending concern to the insurer managing millions of Medicaid children. The individual plaintiff wins. The population loses. The insurer satisfies every principal it faces, because no single principal can see the full pattern.

The Shadow Queue: Prior Authorization as Covert Rationing

Every healthcare system rations. The question is not whether but how, and whether the rationing mechanism is visible to the people it affects. The United Kingdom uses NICE, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which evaluates treatments against a publicly stated threshold of approximately 20,000 to 30,000 pounds per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Treatments that fall below the threshold are approved. Those above it are denied, and the denial is published, debated in Parliament, and subject to democratic accountability. Canada rations through wait times: provincial health authorities establish queue priorities based on clinical urgency, publish median wait durations by procedure, and face political consequences when the queues grow too long. Both systems ration care explicitly. Both are imperfect. And both are structurally transparent: the citizen who is denied a treatment knows the criteria, can access the decision-making process, and can petition elected officials to change the threshold or the queue rules.

The American prior authorization system rations care covertly. The Commonwealth Fund's 2025 Affordability Survey (published June 2026, 4,589 privately insured adults aged 19-64) quantified the mechanism: 21% of privately insured adults reported that they or a family member were denied coverage for doctor-recommended care in the past year. Thirteen percent experienced a prior authorization denial. Eight percent experienced a post-care claim denial. One percent experienced both. Among those denied, 41% said the PA denial delayed their medical care. Twenty-eight percent said their health worsened as a result. More than 60% said the denial caused significant worry or anxiety. And more than half reported that the denied bill exceeded $1,000, converting a coverage denial into medical debt. Collins, the Commonwealth Fund senior scholar, stated plainly: "Clearly, prior authorization is hitting both high-value and low-value care. If patients are telling us that their health problems are worsening, it's an indication that the care they're waiting for approval on was actually important to their health."

The covert nature of this rationing is not incidental. It is the mechanism's core design advantage. When the UK's NICE rejects a cancer drug, the rejection generates headlines, parliamentary questions, and organized patient advocacy. The political cost of the denial falls directly on the entity that made it. When an American insurer denies a prior authorization request, the denial is experienced atomistically: one patient, one letter, one phone tree. There is no aggregate disclosure, no parliamentary debate, no published threshold. Until CMS-0057-F's first reporting cycle in March 2026, there was not even a publicly available denial rate by insurer. The system rationed care at industrial scale while maintaining the appearance that each denial was an individualized clinical judgment rather than a systematic allocation decision. KFF's August 2026 cross-market analysis revealed what the opacity concealed: denial rates ranging from 5% (Elevance, MA) to 25% (Centene, ACA Marketplace), with UnitedHealth at 17% in Medicare Advantage, the highest among major insurers. The variation across insurers treating overlapping patient populations demonstrates that the PA system is not making consistent clinical judgments. It is making business decisions dressed in clinical language.

The Commonwealth Fund data also revealed the behavioral consequence that distinguishes covert rationing from explicit rationing: treatment abandonment. Nearly half of patients who experienced a denial did not appeal. Focus group participants explained why: they did not know they had appeal rights, they could not navigate the process, they feared bills would be sent to collections during the appeal, or they simply gave up. This is the mechanism by which covert rationing achieves its allocative function. NICE achieves rationing through a published "no": a treatment is evaluated, found cost-ineffective, and excluded from the formulary. The decision is final and visible. The PA system achieves rationing through a published "maybe": a treatment is submitted for approval, subjected to delays, denied, made available for appeal, and then subjected to further delays if appealed. The friction is the rationing. The 78% of patients who abandon treatment after a PA denial (AMA physician survey) are not being denied care. They are being denied the administrative endurance to access care they are contractually entitled to receive.

The distributional consequences are precisely what mechanism design theory predicts when a rationing system uses administrative friction instead of explicit criteria. NICE's QALY threshold rations care roughly by clinical value: treatments that produce more health per pound are approved regardless of the patient's income, education, or bureaucratic stamina. The PA system rations care by the patient's capacity to navigate administrative processes: patients with education, time, employer-provided advocates, and English fluency complete the prior authorization process. Patients without those resources abandon it. The JACC: Advances heart failure data (Mukhopadhyay, NYU) showed that PA produced 3-6x fill delays for SGLT2 inhibitors, with 2.23x higher odds of never filling the prescription for Black, Hispanic, and lower-SES patients. The JAMA Network Open caregiver study (Thom, UNC) found that patients with direct PA involvement, those without someone else to manage the paperwork, faced 2.12x increased denial risk. The PA system does not ration by clinical need. It rations by administrative capacity, which correlates with income, education, race, and the availability of an unpaid family member willing to spend hours on hold.

Game Theory Concept
Tragic Choices and the Political Economy of Covert Rationing (Calabresi & Bobbitt 1978)

Guido Calabresi and Philip Bobbitt's "Tragic Choices" (1978) analyzed how societies allocate scarce goods when the allocation involves life and death and when the society cannot politically bear to acknowledge that it is making such allocations. Their framework identified a cycle: societies adopt a rationing mechanism (market pricing, lottery, merit criteria), use it until its distributional consequences become politically visible, then switch to a different mechanism that obscures the same distributional pattern behind new institutional language. The prior authorization system is the American healthcare system's current position in Calabresi and Bobbitt's cycle. Explicit rationing by price (pre-ACA coverage exclusions for preexisting conditions) became politically visible and was abolished in 2010. Explicit rationing by coverage (plan exclusions, benefit caps) was constrained by Essential Health Benefits and out-of-pocket maximums. The PA system emerged as the next mechanism in the cycle: it rations care through administrative process rather than price or coverage, producing the same distributional outcome (sicker and poorer patients receive less care) while maintaining the political fiction that every patient has "access" to every covered service. The genius of the mechanism, from the insurer's perspective, is that it places the blame for non-receipt of care on the patient ("you didn't complete the appeal") rather than on the system ("we denied your claim"). Calabresi and Bobbitt predicted that every covert rationing mechanism eventually becomes visible, triggering the next cycle. The post-Thompson disclosure cascade, CMS-0057-F reporting, KFF cross-market analysis, OIG audit data, and 422 sources documenting the system's operation, may represent exactly the visibility threshold that forces the next mechanism switch. The question is whether the successor mechanism will be more transparent (explicit clinical criteria, published thresholds, democratic accountability) or simply more opaque (algorithmic denial with proprietary models, vertical integration that eliminates the claim-denial interface entirely, or population contraction that removes patients from the system before they can generate claims).

The comparison to explicit rationing systems is not an argument for adopting the UK or Canadian model. It is an argument for recognizing what the American system already does and refusing to let the opacity of the mechanism excuse the distributional consequences of the allocation. When NICE denies a cancer drug, the denial is a policy choice made by an accountable institution. When UnitedHealth denies a prior authorization at a 17% rate while Elevance denies at 5% for overlapping patient populations, the denial is a business choice disguised as a clinical judgment. The Commonwealth Fund data makes the disguise empirically untenable: 28% of denied patients report worsened health, 41% report delayed care, and more than half incur medical debt they would not have incurred if the treatment had been approved. These are not the outcomes of a clinical gatekeeping system working as designed. They are the outcomes of a covert rationing system achieving its allocative function through administrative friction while the political system pretends the friction is not there. The 6.5 million PA eliminations celebrated in 2026 removed some of the friction. But the mechanism remains intact for the hundreds of millions of remaining prior authorization requests, each one a miniature tragic choice made in private, experienced alone, and invisible to the political process until CMS-0057-F made the aggregate pattern undeniable.

The Formulary Fortress: When Exclusion Replaces Denial

Prior authorization reform targets the denial decision. It mandates faster timelines, electronic submission, transparency reporting, gold card exemptions. Every reform assumes the patient reaches the decision point: a claim is filed, a PA request is submitted, and the insurer must approve or deny within a regulated timeframe. The formulary fortress bypasses the decision point entirely. By removing a drug from the formulary before the plan year begins, the insurer eliminates the PA request, the denial, the appeal, the transparency report, and the regulatory surface area where every post-Thompson reform operates. There is no denial to report under CMS-0057-F because there was never a covered benefit to deny.

GLP-1 receptor agonists are the clearest case study because the coverage contraction is occurring at industrial scale during the same period that PA reform is accelerating. GoodRx Research tracking of commercial insurance formularies through MMIT data found that in 2026, the number of commercially insured Americans with no coverage for Zepbound (tirzepatide, prescribed for weight loss) rose to 109 million, representing 56% of the commercially insured population, up from 51% in 2025. The number with no coverage for Wegovy (semaglutide, prescribed for weight loss) rose by 42% year-over-year, leaving over 41 million with no coverage. CVS Caremark, the largest pharmacy benefit manager, removed Zepbound from its standard formulary in July 2025, directly driving the coverage decline. The share of commercially insured Americans with unrestricted access to Zepbound fell from 5% to 4%; restricted access fell from 45% to 40%. Altogether, 8.5% of commercially insured Americans, over 16 million people, lack coverage for any GLP-1 agonist prescribed for weight loss. And of those who retain some form of coverage, over 88% face prior authorization or step therapy requirements. The layered system operates in sequence: the formulary removes the drug for the majority; PA blocks most of the remainder.

The mechanism is not limited to PBM decisions. Point32Health (Harvard Pilgrim/Tufts Health) terminated all existing prior authorization approvals for weight-loss medications effective January 1, 2026, with no grandfathering: patients who had been approved and were actively taking the medication had their authorizations revoked. KFF Health News reported that 12 million people were on plans that dropped Zepbound coverage and 12 million were on plans that dropped Wegovy coverage between 2025 and 2026. Howard County, Maryland schools dropped GLP-1 coverage entirely after calculating that $10 million in annual drug costs would require a 20% premium increase for the county school system. The decision was not made by the insurer's utilization management committee. It was made by the employer choosing between medication access and premium affordability, a choice the insurer's pricing made inevitable. At the federal level, CMS declined to finalize the Biden-era proposal to cover anti-obesity medications under Medicare and Medicaid, citing pushback from payers and a projected $35 billion increase in federal spending over ten years. The April 2025 MA/Part D final rule explicitly deferred both GLP-1 coverage and AI-in-PA regulation to future rulemaking. The coverage gap is thus reinforced from three directions simultaneously: PBMs removing drugs from commercial formularies, employers dropping coverage to avoid premium increases, and the federal government declining to extend public coverage.

The Aetna lumbar artificial disc replacement settlement, which received final court approval on June 5, 2026, illustrates the lifecycle of the formulary fortress from construction to judicial demolition. Aetna classified single-level L-ADR surgery as "experimental or investigational" for at least seven years, denying coverage to a class of 381 ERISA-governed plan members despite FDA approval of the procedure since 2006. The $2.56 million settlement provided up to $55,000 per patient for those who paid out of pocket, and required Aetna to authorize future L-ADR surgeries for current plan members without utilization review if a surgeon deems the procedure medically necessary. The "experimental" classification was not a formulary exclusion in the strict pharmaceutical sense, but it operated identically: by categorizing a proven procedure as investigational, the insurer removed it from the effective benefit set before any individual claim could reach the PA decision point. Six spine surgeons interviewed by Becker's Spine Review after the settlement noted that Aetna's policy change "took way, way, way too long" and that "it's a shame that it took a class-action lawsuit to finally get this addressed." The clinical evidence had not changed between 2006 (FDA approval) and 2023 (when Aetna reversed its position under litigation pressure). What changed was the expected cost of maintaining the fortress.

Game Theory Concept
Constrained Regulatory Instruments and the Displacement Equilibrium (Laffont & Tirole 1993)

Jean-Jacques Laffont and Jean Tirole's A Theory of Incentives in Procurement and Regulation (1993) formalized the fundamental problem of regulating a firm when the regulator can observe and constrain only a subset of the firm's decision variables. When the regulator imposes a binding constraint on one instrument (say, a price cap or a quality floor), the firm's optimal response is to intensify extraction on the dimensions the regulator cannot observe or does not constrain. The result is a displacement equilibrium: regulation improves the measured outcome while degrading the unmeasured one, and the net welfare effect can be negative if the unmeasured dimension is more consequential than the measured one. Applied to the PA reform landscape: CMS-0057-F mandates electronic PA and creates per-insurer denial rate reporting. State laws impose response time limits, gold card exemptions, and AI-denial bans. Every reform constrains the denial instrument. But formulary design, the upstream decision about which drugs and procedures are covered in the first place, is subject to far weaker regulatory constraint. Essential Health Benefits under the ACA require coverage of drug categories but not specific drugs. State formulary adequacy reviews are infrequent and retrospective. There is no federal requirement to disclose formulary exclusion rates by drug class or therapeutic area. The rational insurer response, predicted by Laffont and Tirole's framework, is to shift restriction from the constrained instrument (PA denial, which is now measured, reported, and politically costly) to the unconstrained instrument (formulary exclusion, which is made annually, in aggregate, and generates no patient-facing denial letter, no appeal right, and no CMS-0057-F reporting obligation). The GLP-1 data quantifies the displacement: PA reform is reducing denial rates, but 109 million Americans lost Zepbound coverage and 41 million lost Wegovy coverage through formulary decisions that occur entirely outside the PA reform framework. The displacement is self-concealing because the metric that regulators, journalists, and patient advocates monitor (PA denial rate) improves even as the population-level access outcome worsens. A plan that removes a drug from its formulary and thereby eliminates 100,000 PA requests has simultaneously reduced its PA volume, improved its approval rate on remaining requests, and blocked 100,000 patients from treatment. All three effects are produced by the same action. Only the first two are visible to the regulatory apparatus.

Maryland offers the first glimpse of a regulatory response to the formulary fortress. In 2026, the Maryland Prescription Drug Affordability Board, the first such body in the nation, set upper payment limits on Ozempic (semaglutide) and Jardiance (empagliflozin) for state and local government insurance plans, effective 2027, with commercial plans to follow a year later. The mechanism attacks the fortress from the cost side: if the drug's price drops below the threshold at which formulary exclusion is the insurer's dominant strategy, the exclusion incentive weakens. Whether drug manufacturers will accept the price, and whether other states will follow Maryland's model, remains to be seen. But the structural insight is that PA reform and formulary regulation are complements, not substitutes. Constraining the denial instrument without constraining the exclusion instrument is Laffont and Tirole's displacement equilibrium in operation. The patient who was denied a PA request in 2024 and the patient whose drug was removed from the formulary in 2026 experience the same outcome: no medication. The difference is that the first patient's experience generates a data point, an appeal right, and a political narrative. The second patient's experience generates nothing. The formulary fortress is the next mechanism in Calabresi and Bobbitt's cycle: a new form of covert rationing, deployed precisely as the old form becomes visible.

The Enrollment Trap: When Patient Choice Becomes Insurer Selection

Every game theory model in this analysis assumes that the patient enters the insurer's system and then encounters denial. But a Department of Justice lawsuit, filed in 2025 and surviving a motion to dismiss in March 2026, reveals that the game begins earlier than that: at the enrollment decision itself. The DOJ alleges that CVS Health's Aetna, Elevance Health, and Humana paid "hundreds of millions of dollars" in illegal kickbacks to three of the largest Medicare Advantage brokers, eHealth, GoHealth, and SelectQuote, to steer Medicare beneficiaries into their plans regardless of suitability. The three insurers cover a combined 12.3 million MA enrollees (CVS 5.8 million, Humana 4.2 million, Elevance 2.3 million). Roughly one-third of all MA beneficiaries use brokers to select their coverage, according to the Commonwealth Fund, meaning the corrupted enrollment channel touched a significant fraction of the 33+ million Americans in MA during the alleged period (2016-2021).

The complaint's language is precise about the mechanism. In public, the brokers claimed to be "unbiased," "carrier-agnostic," and to "have your best interests in mind." In private, the DOJ alleges, they "repeatedly directed Medicare beneficiaries to the plans offered by insurers that paid them the most money, regardless of the quality or suitability of the insurers' plans." The brokers set up dedicated teams that could sell only the paying insurers' plans and at times "shut off" or refused to sell plans from competitors that did not pay kickbacks. The payments were disguised as "marketing," "co-op," or "sponsorship" arrangements.

The disability discrimination allegation adds a selection dimension that connects the enrollment stage directly to the denial pipeline. The DOJ alleges that Aetna and Humana threatened to withhold extra payments to pressure brokers into enrolling fewer disabled seniors. Federal law bars insurers from discriminating based on health status. But the alleged mechanism operates upstream of the regulatory surface: by paying brokers to avoid enrolling high-cost patients, the insurer never has to deny a claim because the patient never enters the system. The discriminatory selection occurs at the broker level, invisible to CMS audit frameworks that monitor coverage decisions within plans but not enrollment steering across plans. The patient who was steered away from the optimal plan never generates a denial, an appeal, or a CMS-0057-F reporting entry. She simply has worse coverage, higher out-of-pocket costs, and a narrower provider network, all attributable to a "personal choice" she made with "expert guidance." In March 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts denied all defendants' motions to dismiss, allowing the kickback and discrimination claims to proceed under the False Claims Act. The court dismissed only the unjust enrichment claim, finding that the FCA provided an adequate legal remedy.

This reframes the entire denial game. The models in this analysis treat the insured population as exogenous: patients arrive with coverage, and the insurer decides whether to approve or deny. But if the enrollment channel is corrupted, the composition of the insured population is itself a strategic variable. Insurers that successfully steer healthy seniors into their plans and disabled seniors away from them face lower expected claims per enrollee before a single PA request is filed. The denial system then operates on a pre-selected population with lower baseline acuity. The observed denial rate understates the total access barrier because the highest-cost patients were filtered out at enrollment. The 6.5 million eliminated PA requirements and the falling denial rates celebrated in industry press releases exist within a population that was already adversely selected by the enrollment channel. Every metric of PA reform improvement is measured against a denominator that was corrupted at the point of entry.

Game Theory Concept
Corrupted Search Intermediaries and the Diamond Paradox (Diamond 1971 / Dulleck & Kerschbamer 2006)

Peter Diamond's (1971) search paradox demonstrated that even small search costs can sustain monopoly pricing in a competitive market: when consumers cannot costlessly compare all options, firms extract rents from the information gap. Insurance brokers exist to solve this problem. A Medicare beneficiary facing dozens of MA plans with different networks, formularies, cost-sharing structures, and PA requirements faces prohibitive comparison costs. The broker is a search-cost intermediary, reducing the informational burden so the beneficiary can make an informed choice. But Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2006), formalizing the credence goods literature (Darby & Karni 1973), showed that when the intermediary's recommendation quality is unverifiable by the consumer, and the intermediary is paid by the seller rather than the buyer, the intermediary becomes an instrument of extraction rather than a solution to it. The beneficiary cannot evaluate whether she was steered to the best plan or the highest-paying one, because doing so would require exactly the comparison effort the broker was hired to eliminate. The DOJ's allegations describe the textbook case: consumers paid nothing for broker services (the insurer paid), the intermediary's advice was unverifiable (the beneficiary lacked the expertise to audit plan suitability), and the intermediary's compensation was linked to the seller's identity rather than the buyer's outcome. In this configuration, the search intermediary does not reduce the consumer's search costs; it eliminates her search entirely and replaces it with the intermediary's commercially motivated selection. The net effect is worse than no intermediary at all, because the beneficiary who searches independently at least faces an unbiased distribution of options, while the beneficiary who relies on a corrupted broker faces a distribution systematically skewed toward plans with higher kickback budgets, which are plans that can afford those budgets precisely because they extract more value from enrollees through narrower networks, higher denial rates, or more aggressive utilization management. The enrollment trap and the denial system are not sequential failures. They are complementary mechanisms of a single extraction architecture.

The timing compounds the structural concern. The DOJ lawsuit covers 2016 to 2021. The court denied the motion to dismiss in March 2026. The Biden administration's 2024 rule capping broker compensation was challenged in court and its key provisions delayed. The Trump administration has not signaled urgency to reinstate those caps. The enrollment channel remains structurally corrupted during the same period that PA reform is being measured and celebrated. Every post-Thompson reform, from the June 2025 voluntary pledge to the 6.5 million eliminated PA requirements, operates downstream of an enrollment process that the government itself alleges steered patients into plans based on kickback payments rather than clinical suitability. The patient who was placed into an Aetna plan by eHealth in 2019 because Aetna paid the highest kickback is the same patient whose PA denial appears in CMS-0057-F reporting in 2027. The denial was not random. It was the downstream consequence of an enrollment decision made six years earlier by a broker who never met the patient.

The Influence Machine: When the Regulated Write the Regulations

Every game theory model in this analysis assumes a regulator with independent preferences. But a KFF Health News investigation published in September 2024 documented a different structure: the Medicare Advantage industry has constructed a $462 billion feedback loop in which the regulated entities systematically shape the regulatory environment through political contributions, revolving-door hiring, dark-money astroturfing, and beneficiary mobilization. The result is not a game between insurer and regulator. It is a game in which the insurer plays both roles.

The revolving door is the most visible mechanism. Senior CMS personnel have cycled out of government to take jobs tied to the Medicare Advantage industry and then returned to the agency. The pattern creates what economists call a "deferred compensation" incentive: a career regulator who anticipates a post-government position at an MA insurer or its trade association faces a payoff matrix in which aggressive enforcement reduces expected future income. The KFF investigation documented that federal officials resolved more than a decade ago to crack down on overpayments to MA plans, which were siphoning off billions of tax dollars annually. CMS has yet to demand any refunds. The industry, meanwhile, morphed into what KFF called "a politically potent juggernaut" that "has managed to deflate or deflect financial penalties and steadily gain clout in Washington."

The astroturfing operation quantifies the capture. A secretive advocacy group called Medicare Advantage Majority, which does not reveal its funders, spent more than $3.1 million on hundreds of Facebook ads and organized a comment campaign on CMS's January 2026 proposal to keep MA reimbursement rates essentially flat. Of 16,400 comments posted on the federal government website, 82% were identical to a template letter that appeared on the group's website. Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said Medicare Advantage fraud "is wasting taxpayer dollars to the tune of billions." "The question is, what's CMS doing about it? The agency must tighten up its controls and work with the Justice Department to prosecute and recover improper payments. Clearly that's not happening, at least to the extent it should be." David Lipschutz, attorney at the Center for Medicare Advocacy, offered the structural diagnosis: "The health plans throw a temper tantrum and then CMS will back off."

The game theory maps precisely. In a standard regulatory game, the regulator sets rules and the firm decides whether to comply or evade, with penalties for evasion. In a captured regulatory game, the firm invests in shaping the rules themselves, so that the payoff from "compliance" includes the profit-maximizing denial rate. The industry's lobbying spending is not a cost of doing business alongside the insurance business. It is the insurance business. Every dollar spent on the Medicare Advantage Majority campaign, every revolving-door hire, every mobilized beneficiary letter is an investment in maintaining the gap between what CMS could enforce and what CMS does enforce. The $1.54 million in fines CMS levied against 14 insurers (documented in the Enforcement Gap section) is not evidence of regulatory failure. It is the equilibrium output of a captured regulatory process: fines calibrated to demonstrate activity without creating deterrence. The ratio of industry lobbying investment to regulatory penalty is the revealed price of the equilibrium. When the investment exceeds the penalty by orders of magnitude, the investment is paying for itself. And the 82% template-comment rate on the 2026 rate proposal demonstrates that the industry has solved the public-comment mechanism: a process designed to aggregate citizen preferences has been converted into a channel for manufacturing the appearance of democratic support for higher insurer payments.

Game Theory Concept
Regulatory Capture as Endogenous Rule Formation (Stigler 1971 / Peltzman 1976)

George Stigler's (1971) foundational paper "The Theory of Economic Regulation" overturned the public-interest theory of regulation by demonstrating that regulated industries actively seek regulation as a tool for capturing rents, not merely as a constraint to be evaded. The regulated firm's optimization problem includes a lobbying investment variable: spend resources to shape rules such that the regulatory equilibrium maximizes industry profits rather than consumer welfare. Sam Peltzman (1976) formalized this as a model in which the regulator maximizes a political support function that weights both consumer welfare and industry contributions, producing equilibria where regulations are neither maximally strict nor maximally permissive but calibrated to the industry's lobbying investment. Applied to Medicare Advantage, the model predicts exactly what KFF documented: CMS identified billions in overpayments over a decade ago, resolved to recoup them, and never did. The Stigler-Peltzman framework explains this not as bureaucratic incompetence but as an equilibrium outcome. The industry's investment in the regulatory relationship (revolving-door hiring, campaign contributions, dark-money comment campaigns, beneficiary mobilization) shifted the regulator's political support function until the equilibrium enforcement level fell below the deterrence threshold. The 82% template-comment rate on the 2026 rate proposal is a measurable output of Stigler's model: the public-comment process, designed as a democratic input mechanism, has been converted into a lobbying instrument where the industry manufactures the appearance of broad-based support to shift the regulator's perceived political cost of enforcement. Peltzman's extension predicts the observed pattern of "selective reform": the regulator implements visible but non-threatening changes (PA electronic submission timelines, transparency reporting frameworks) while preserving the structural features that generate industry rents (star ratings bonuses, risk-adjustment overpayments, ERISA preemption). The post-Thompson reforms are themselves interpretable through this lens: reform enough to satisfy the political demand created by the shooting, but not so much as to threaten the $462 billion annual flow that sustains the political support function. The capture model also predicts the industry's response to Mangione: not substantive structural reform, but a June 2025 voluntary pledge that KFF later found 8 of 60 signatories backed out of, with no federal dashboards, no enforcement mechanism, and no penalties for non-compliance. In Stigler's framework, a voluntary pledge is the optimal industry response to a political crisis: it satisfies the regulator's need to demonstrate responsiveness without creating binding constraints on industry behavior.

The capture extends to the information environment. The industry funds academic research through grants and consulting arrangements, sponsors medical society conferences, and maintains relationships with the physician organizations that supply the clinical guidelines insurers cite when denying claims. The American Hospital Association, the American Medical Association, and specialty societies that loudly oppose PA requirements simultaneously depend on insurer reimbursements for their members' revenue. This creates a structural tension where the institutional voice for reform is funded by the entity being reformed. The net effect is what Lipschutz described: a system in which the industry's preferences are expressed through every channel that the regulator monitors, while patient preferences are expressed primarily through the one channel the system was not designed to process: a shooting on a Manhattan sidewalk.

The 2026 lobbying data quantifies the paradox of simultaneous reform and capture. A Washington Post analysis of federal lobbying disclosures (July 21, 2026) found that the 100 biggest healthcare spenders reported close to $285 million combined in H1 2026. AHIP, the insurance industry's trade group, spent $8.33 million in the first half of 2026, including a record $5.3 million in Q1 alone, its highest quarterly lobbying expenditure in organizational history (HealthLeaders Media, OpenSecrets). CVS Health increased its lobbying spending 31% year-over-year to $6.89 million. Cigna rose 4% to $5.61 million. These are the same companies that signed the June 2025 voluntary pledge to reduce prior authorization. The temporal alignment is important: the quarter in which AHIP set its all-time lobbying record was also the quarter in which the industry reported its 6.5 million PA reduction figure. The companies were spending record sums to influence the regulatory environment while simultaneously claiming credit for voluntary reform within that environment. The dual investment is not contradictory. In Stigler's framework, it is optimal: the voluntary pledge reduces political pressure (stage two of the Downs cycle) while the record lobbying spending ensures the regulatory response remains calibrated to industry preferences (the Peltzman equilibrium). The pledge is the visible reform. The lobbying is the invisible constraint on how far the reform goes.

An American Economic Association conference paper (2026) provides the formal mechanism. Using firm-level panel data across the U.S. health insurance industry, the study demonstrates that insurers' political donations to state officials are positively associated with higher Medicare and Medicaid premiums and negatively associated with regulatory guidance from financial exams, controlling for firm characteristics and state corruption indices. The effect is stronger for donations to federal elections than local elections, and stronger in states with higher measured corruption. The paper's key finding is that donations weighted by state corruption indices predict regulatory slack at the 1% significance level: insurers that donate more in more corrupt jurisdictions are less likely to receive the corrective orders (increased capital reserves, improved internal controls) that regulators use to discipline risk-taking. This converts the lobbying investment from a cost of doing business into a measurable return on regulatory capital. Applied to the MA system, the framework predicts that the industry's $8.33 million H1 2026 AHIP spend is not an expense deducted from insurance margins. It is an investment that generates returns through preserved rate structures, deferred enforcement, and regulatory formulas that favor industry positions. The formation of the Great American Health Alliance (GAHA) as a 501(c)(4), a dark-money entity with unlimited lobbying capacity and no donor disclosure requirements, run by the same political operatives who managed Trump's 2017 transition and RFK Jr.'s Senate confirmation, demonstrates that the capture apparatus is expanding, not contracting, during the reform window.

The Danger Premium: When Risk Pricing Reveals the True Incentive

The 2025 proxy season produced one data point that crystallizes everything documented in this analysis into a single number: 748. That is the ratio of UnitedHealth Group CEO Stephen Hemsley's 2025 compensation ($60,950,571) to the company's median employee salary ($81,474). His predecessor, Andrew Witty, whose resignation was precipitated by the triple crisis of Thompson's murder, soaring Medicare costs, and UNH's first earnings miss in years, had a 2024 pay ratio of 348:1. The man who replaced the CEO who resigned after a CEO was murdered for running the company's denial apparatus now earns 2.15 times more than the man who left.

The structure of Hemsley's package makes the board's calculation legible. On May 14, 2025, two days after Witty's departure, UNH's Compensation and Human Resources Committee approved a $1 million annual base salary, no annual cash incentive, and a one-time $60 million equity award in nonqualified stock options with cliff vesting after three years, with no additional annual equity awards during that period. The SEC filing specifies that the Committee considered "market data, advice from the Committee's independent compensation consultant, and other factors." The "other factors" are doing significant work in that sentence. The $60 million grant is not a salary. It is a price. It is what the board determined it would cost to recruit a 72-year-old former CEO back into the role that just became the most dangerous executive position in American corporate life.

The industry comparison makes the premium visible. Among the seven largest health insurers, Hemsley's 748:1 ratio stands apart. CVS Health CEO David Joyner: $21.2 million, 336:1. Cigna CEO David Cordani: $22.9 million, 310:1. Elevance CEO Gail Boudreaux: $22.6 million, 286:1. Molina CEO Joseph Zubretsky: $18.3 million, 228:1. Humana CEO Jim Rechtin: $18.8 million, 226:1. Centene CEO Sarah London: $19.5 million, 206:1. The Equilar 500 median pay ratio for 2025 was 219:1, up from 210:1 the prior year. The S&P 500 median CEO compensation was $17.7 million. Hemsley's total is 3.4 times the national median. His pay ratio is 3.4 times the Equilar 500 median. Every peer insurer CEO earns a ratio between 206:1 and 336:1. Hemsley earns 748:1. The gap is the danger premium.

The labor economics is precise. Sherwin Rosen's (1986) theory of equalizing differences formalizes what Adam Smith observed in 1776: workers demand higher compensation for bearing undesirable job attributes, including physical risk, unpleasant conditions, or reputational cost. The compensating differential is the wage premium that makes a rational worker indifferent between a risky job and a safe one. In industrial labor markets, this theory explains why coal miners earn more than office clerks, why combat soldiers earn hazard pay, why deep-sea welders command premiums over their onshore counterparts. The risk is exogenous: the coal seam will collapse regardless of the miner's decisions. The compensating differential compensates for bearing a risk the worker did not create.

Hemsley's $60 million grant inverts this logic. The risk is endogenous. The danger of leading UnitedHealth Group in 2025 exists because of the company's own denial practices, the practices that provoked the shooting, the congressional investigations, the shareholder derivative suit, the DOJ probes. The board is not compensating Hemsley for bearing an external hazard. It is compensating him for willingness to lead the company whose institutional behavior created the hazard. The premium is not for risk tolerance. It is for operational continuity: the implicit guarantee that the executive accepting this package will maintain, or at least manage, the business model that generated both the $60 billion in annual revenue and the assassination that made the job dangerous.

W. Kip Viscusi's (1993) extension of compensating differentials theory predicted exactly this sorting mechanism. Viscusi demonstrated that in labor markets with heterogeneous risk preferences, workers with lower risk aversion self-select into riskier occupations. The compensating differential does not just price risk. It sorts the applicant pool. The candidate who accepts the UNH CEO role at $60.95 million is, by revealed preference, the candidate whose personal risk-tolerance threshold (or whose assessment of the probability of recurrence) falls below the threshold that screened out alternatives. The board's pricing decision is simultaneously a selection mechanism: the premium selects for the executive most willing to continue the practices that created the need for the premium. If the new CEO's first act were to dismantle the denial architecture that makes the job dangerous, the danger premium would become retroactively unjustified. The compensation structure contains its own preservation logic.

The shareholders confirmed this. Bloomberg Law reported that UNH shareholders approved Hemsley's pay package in an advisory vote at the June 2026 annual meeting. The same proxy in which they approved $60.95 million for the CEO is the same proxy under which the Interfaith Center's 300+ member coalition was blocked from voting on a patient-impact analysis under the SEC's "ordinary business" exclusion. The shareholders who approved paying the CEO 748 times the median worker were denied the opportunity to assess whether the business model generating those returns was killing their fellow citizens. The approval is not hypocrisy. It is rational portfolio optimization. A shareholder who objects to the pay ratio can sell UNH stock. But if that shareholder holds an S&P 500 index fund, she cannot: UNH is a mandatory constituent.
