The universal owner problem, documented in the Index Fund Paradox section, extends to compensation: the retirement saver who votes to approve the CEO's $60 million package through her index fund's proxy is the same person whose insurer denied her MRI last month. The vote and the denial are processed by different systems, each individually rational, each mutually reinforcing.

The comparison to the murdered executive's compensation sharpens the paradox. Brian Thompson, the UnitedHealthcare CEO killed on December 4, 2024, earned approximately $10.2 million in 2023 total compensation. Hemsley's $60.95 million is nearly six times Thompson's final-year pay. Thompson ran the division. Hemsley runs the parent company. But the multiplier exceeds organizational hierarchy. The CEO of the company whose subsidiary executive was assassinated for overseeing claim denials now earns more, adjusted for the danger that the assassination created, than any health insurer CEO in the country. The market has priced the post-Thompson risk and found it worth approximately $40 million per year above the peer-group median. That figure, the gap between Hemsley's $60.95 million and the next-highest insurer CEO's $22.9 million, is the market's revealed valuation of assassination risk in the health insurance industry. It is a number that did not exist before December 4, 2024.

Game Theory Concept
Compensating Differentials with Endogenous Risk (Rosen 1986 / Viscusi 1993)

Sherwin Rosen's (1986) "The Theory of Equalizing Differences" formalized the hedonic wage model: in competitive labor markets, workers receive compensating differentials for bearing undesirable job attributes (risk, difficulty, unpleasant conditions), and the equilibrium wage schedule traces the locus of tangencies between heterogeneous workers' indifference curves and firms' isoprofit curves. The model assumes risk is exogenous: the coal mine's geology does not change with the miner's decisions. W. Kip Viscusi (1993), in "The Value of Risks to Life and Health," extended this framework to show that workers with lower risk aversion self-select into riskier occupations, creating a sorting equilibrium where the compensating differential simultaneously prices risk and selects the risk-tolerant. Applied to UnitedHealth Group's post-Thompson CEO compensation, the framework exposes a structural inversion. Standard compensating differentials compensate for bearing externally imposed risk. Hemsley's $60 million one-time equity grant compensates for bearing risk created by the firm's own operational decisions: the denial practices, the algorithmic claims processing, the MCR optimization that provoked the shooting. When risk is endogenous rather than exogenous, the compensating differential creates a moral hazard loop. The premium rewards the executive for tolerating the consequences of the firm's business model, and the executive who accepts that premium has revealed, per Viscusi's sorting mechanism, a preference function compatible with maintaining the model. The board's pricing decision ($60.95M for Hemsley vs. the ~$22M peer median) implicitly values the post-Thompson assassination risk at ~$38 million. This figure represents the market-clearing price of operational continuity: the amount required to recruit an executive willing to lead the company whose practices generated the risk being priced. If the new CEO reformed the denial system sufficiently to eliminate the danger, the premium would become retroactively unjustified, and the cliff-vesting structure (three-year lockup) would represent a sunk cost. The compensation structure thus contains an embedded incentive to maintain the risk-generating practices during the vesting period. Rosen's original model predicts that firms offering riskier jobs earn lower profits (the differential is a cost). The UNH case inverts this: the firm's stock recovered 51% under Hemsley precisely because he maintained the MCR-reducing practices that made the job dangerous. The danger premium is not a cost of doing business. It is the price of the business itself.

The temporal structure of the grant reinforces the analysis. The $60 million vests as a single cliff after three years: all or nothing in May 2028. During those three years, Hemsley has a $60 million incentive to keep the stock price at or above the grant-date level (approximately $260, UNH's price on May 14, 2025, near its 52-week low). At the current price of approximately $390, the options are already deeply in the money. Each dollar of stock appreciation above $260 generates option value that makes the compensation package more lucrative. And the mechanism that has driven UNH's stock recovery from $260 to $390 is MCR improvement: spending less on patient care per premium dollar. The compensation structure aligns the CEO's personal wealth with the same metric, the medical cost ratio, that the entire post-Thompson reform movement is trying to constrain. The board designed a package that pays the CEO more when patients receive less. This is not an unintended consequence. It is what the board's independent compensation consultant recommended, what the Compensation Committee approved, and what shareholders ratified. The danger premium and the denial incentive are the same dollar.

The Enforcement Awakening: When the Government Discovers Its Own Leverage

Every game theory analysis in this article has documented a system where the expected penalty for fraud falls below the expected profit. The Enforcement Gap section quantified it: CMS fined 14 Medicare sponsors a combined $1.54 million for 18 violations that harmed enrollees in 89% of cases. The Intermediary Chain section showed $950 million in FCA settlements across seven entities amounting to 0.18% of one year's $530 billion in MA payments. The probability-weighted cost of fraud was a rounding error on the revenue it generated. In fiscal year 2025, the arithmetic began to shift.

The Department of Justice reported on January 16, 2026, that False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $6.8 billion in FY2025, the highest annual recovery in the statute's 162-year history and more than double the $3.1 billion recovered in FY2024. Healthcare fraud accounted for $5.7 billion of the total, roughly 83%. Three healthcare verdicts alone generated $2.8 billion, led by the $1.6 billion judgment against Janssen Products, the largest FCA verdict ever. Whistleblowers filed 1,297 qui tam lawsuits, shattering the previous record of 980 set just one year earlier, a 32% increase that signals a structural shift in insider willingness to report. The government opened 401 new investigations of its own, 183 of them in healthcare, the highest number on record and more than double the 87 healthcare investigations launched in FY2024. Since Congress strengthened the FCA in 1986, cumulative recoveries now exceed $85 billion.

The qui tam surge is the number that matters most for the game theory. Whistleblowers are insiders who observe the gap between what is coded and what is real. Their decision to report is a defection from the cooperative fraud equilibrium: they sacrifice their position within the organization in exchange for a 15-30% share of the recovery. The 32% increase in filings means the expected payoff of defection is rising relative to the expected payoff of cooperation. Two consecutive record-breaking years indicate that the information asymmetry protecting fraudulent billing is eroding from within. The supply chain documented in the Intermediary Chain section, where every link from MSO to coding vendor to assessment company had independent incentives to inflate risk scores, is now a supply chain where every link also contains a potential whistleblower whose expected return on reporting has never been higher.

Simultaneously, CMS announced the most aggressive expansion of Medicare Advantage oversight in the program's history. The agency plans to audit all eligible MA contracts annually, roughly 550 plans, up from approximately 60 audits per year under the previous regime. To execute this nine-fold expansion, CMS is scaling its medical coder workforce from 40 to approximately 2,000 by deploying AI-assisted systems to flag unsupported diagnoses for manual verification, then increasing the number of records reviewed per plan from 35 to as many as 200. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) provided the fiscal rationale: Medicare payments to private MA plans were 20% higher per person than spending for similar beneficiaries in traditional Medicare in 2025, translating to $84 billion in excess federal spending in a single year. HHS-OIG audits of four Medicare Advantage organizations found that roughly 83% of high-risk diagnosis codes reviewed lacked sufficient documentation, resulting in $15.5 million in identified overpayments across just four plans. Extrapolate that documentation failure rate across 550 plans and a $530 billion program, and the fiscal exposure dwarfs the $6.8 billion in annual FCA recoveries.

Congress added a legislative layer. On April 27, 2026, Senators Roger Marshall (R-KS) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) introduced the Medicare Advantage Improvement Act of 2026, a bipartisan bill that would expedite PA approval turnaround times, limit retroactive denials after authorization has been granted, require MAOs to publicly report PA data, prevent MAOs from applying stricter medical necessity standards than traditional fee-for-service Medicare, and strengthen network adequacy requirements for post-acute care. The bill is notable less for its individual provisions than for its bipartisan sponsorship in a Congress where healthcare legislation typically dies on partisan lines. Senator Marshall, an obstetrician, and Senator Whitehouse, a longtime healthcare oversight advocate, represent opposite ends of the political spectrum. Their co-sponsorship signals that MA reform has crossed the partisan threshold that the Influence Machine section documented the industry spending $3.1 million in astroturfing to prevent.

Game Theory Concept
Becker's (1968) Optimal Deterrence and the Credibility Revolution

Gary Becker's foundational model of crime and punishment established that rational actors commit fraud when the expected benefit exceeds the expected cost, where expected cost equals the probability of detection multiplied by the penalty if caught. The pre-2025 enforcement equilibrium was an under-deterrence trap: CMS audited 60 of 550 eligible plans per year (10.9% annual detection probability), fines averaged $110,000 per violation ($1.54M across 14 sponsors), and FCA settlements across the entire supply chain amounted to 0.18% of annual MA payments. A rational insurer or vendor could calculate that the expected cost of aggressive coding was a fraction of the expected revenue. The FY2025 enforcement data represents what Becker's model predicts when the probability term shifts. Scaling audits from 60 to 550 plans raises annual detection probability from 10.9% to functionally 100%. Scaling coders from 40 to 2,000 increases the granularity of what each audit can find. The 1,297 qui tam filings add an endogenous detection channel that operates independently of government audit capacity: every employee in the supply chain is a potential monitor whose expected reward for reporting has doubled in two years. The $6.8 billion in FY2025 recoveries is not the deterrent. The deterrent is the structural shift in detection probability that makes the next $6.8 billion more likely than the last. Polinsky and Shavell's (2000) extension of Becker's model showed that optimal enforcement requires not just high penalties but credible penalties, meaning the target must believe the penalty will actually be imposed. The 50-fold expansion of audit workforce is a credibility signal that no press release or voluntary pledge can replicate. When CMS can audit every plan every year with 200 records per plan, the "probability of detection" variable in Becker's equation approaches 1, and the only rational response is compliance.

The enforcement awakening intersects with the post-Thompson reform in a way that neither the industry's voluntary pledges nor the state legislative wave can replicate. Voluntary pledges are cheap talk. State laws are jurisdictionally fragmented. But a $6.8 billion FCA recovery year backed by 2,000 medical coders auditing every MA contract annually changes the payoff matrix at the federal level. The insurers documented in the Intermediary Chain section, those who inflated risk scores through MSOs, coding vendors, and assessment companies, now face an environment where the expected cost of aggressive coding exceeds the expected revenue for the first time. The question is whether this enforcement regime survives the political pressures that the Influence Machine section documented. Senator Grassley's observation that MA fraud "is wasting taxpayer dollars to the tune of billions" and that CMS enforcement is inadequate now has a quantitative counterpoint: $6.8 billion recovered, 1,297 whistleblowers filing, 2,000 coders deploying. The credibility revolution is underway. Whether it is sustained or captured is the next equilibrium the game must find.

The Data Gatekeeper: When Infrastructure Monopoly Structures Every Game

Every game analyzed in this article assumes that the payer and provider operate on a shared informational playing field, disputing coverage decisions through claims, appeals, and litigation. But on August 14, 2026, the same day Luigi Mangione entered his guilty plea, the Federal Trade Commission revealed it was investigating a player that sits beneath the entire game: Epic Systems, the electronic health records company whose software holds the medical data of more than 280 million Americans. The FTC sent investigative demands to health technology companies seeking information about how Epic grants or withholds access to patient data, probing whether the company's dominant market position constitutes an antitrust violation. The investigation opened two distinct lines of inquiry: one focused on Epic's non-compete agreements that bar employees from working for competitors across large swaths of the health technology industry, and another examining whether Epic leverages its 42% market share to prevent rival companies from accessing patient data needed to build competing platforms.

The probe did not emerge in isolation. In December 2025, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Epic, accusing the company of "shutting out would-be rivals by holding data hostage" through restrictions and fees imposed on health systems attempting to use competitors' products. Particle Health, a rival payer data platform, had previously filed an antitrust lawsuit alleging that Epic set up barriers preventing Particle's clients from accessing clinical records that federal law requires to be interoperable. A federal judge denied Epic's motion to dismiss Particle's case, and discovery continued through 2026. Epic disputed all allegations, pointing to its 1,000+ published APIs, 3,000+ connected applications, and its status as the first EHR to connect to TEFCA, the federally sponsored interoperability network. An Epic spokesperson told Healthcare IT News that healthcare organizations using Epic "exchange over 28 million patient records daily, many between Epic and non-Epic systems." But a TechTarget investigation (April 2026) documented a different reality: the interoperability landscape had split into "two worlds," those inside Epic's ecosystem and those outside it. Dan D'Orazio, CEO of healthcare consultancy Sage Growth Partners, noted that "companies developing these technologies could be left out if they cannot forge a partnership with Epic. Ultimately, Epic can choose which companies can access its troves of data and its health system clients."

The connection to prior authorization is structural, not incidental. Epic's Payer Platform is the mechanism through which insurers and providers exchange PA requests electronically. When CMS administrator Mehmet Oz convened 29 "early adopter" organizations in May 2026 to pledge support for electronic PA, Epic was among the signatories, alongside nine major insurers and twenty health systems. Oz's diagnosis was blunt: "Fifty percent of prior auth questions are sent back by fax. It's just dumb. We should just ax the fax." But the solution to the fax problem runs through Epic's infrastructure. Cohere Health, a prior authorization automation company processing 5.5 million PA requests annually, launched its integration specifically through Epic's Payer Platform. Anthem, Humana, and other major insurers built their electronic PA workflows on the same infrastructure. The company that controls the platform through which PA requests flow is not a neutral intermediary. It is a player whose market position determines the speed, cost, and accessibility of the information exchange that every denial, appeal, and reform depends on.

The CMS January 1, 2027 electronic PA deadline, mandating standardized FHIR APIs, 72-hour urgent and 7-day standard decision timeframes, and public denial-rate reporting, was designed in part to break infrastructure lock-in by requiring open standards that any vendor could implement. But Epic's dominance creates an implementation paradox: the largest health systems that handle the most PA volume are the ones most deeply embedded in Epic's ecosystem, and their compliance timelines depend on Epic's engineering priorities. An EHR vendor that controls 42% of the market and whose hospital customers collectively treat 280 million patients does not merely participate in the PA infrastructure. It is the PA infrastructure for the majority of American healthcare. The switching costs for a large health system to leave Epic have been estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars, creating an asset specificity that makes exit from the ecosystem practically impossible on any reform-relevant timeline.

Game Theory Concept
Residual Control Rights and Infrastructure as Meta-Game (Grossman & Hart 1986 / Hart & Moore 1990)

Oliver Hart and Sanford Grossman's property rights theory of the firm establishes that when contracts are incomplete, the party that controls the asset controls the residual decisions: everything not explicitly specified in the agreement. Applied to health data infrastructure, Epic's market position creates residual control rights over how patient information flows between providers and insurers. The company does not need to participate in denial decisions directly. By controlling the platform through which PA requests are submitted, processed, and returned, it determines the information environment in which the payer-provider game is played. When 50% of PA requests arrive by fax despite two decades of EHR adoption, the infrastructure has not been neutral: its development has tracked the vendor's commercial incentives (selling Payer Platform licenses to insurers) rather than the system's efficiency needs (standardized open-source PA exchange). Williamson's (1975) asset specificity framework explains why the gatekeeper position is self-reinforcing: once a health system's clinical workflows, training, data formats, and regulatory compliance are built around a single EHR, the switching costs create a bilateral monopoly where the vendor can extract surplus by selectively developing interoperability features. The FTC probe and Texas AG lawsuit represent the first regulatory recognition that the games documented throughout this article, denial optimization, appeal attrition, transparency evasion, and complexity engineering, are not played on neutral ground. They are played on infrastructure owned by a private company whose commercial interests may diverge from the open information exchange that reforms like CMS-0057-F and the January 2027 electronic PA mandate require. The meta-game is the game about which games are possible.

The timing of the FTC probe is itself a data point. The federal government is simultaneously investigating the company that processes insurance claims (UNH, DOJ criminal and antitrust probes), the companies that broker insurance enrollment (CVS/Aetna, Elevance, and Humana, DOJ kickback lawsuit), and now the company that controls the data infrastructure connecting providers and insurers. Each investigation targets a different node in the same system: the claims processor, the enrollment channel, and the information substrate. Taken together, they suggest that federal enforcers have arrived at the structural diagnosis that game theory predicted: the problem is not any single player's behavior but the architecture of the game itself. Whether the probes produce structural remedies or settle into the attrition pattern documented in this article's Attrition Shield section remains the open question. Epic's response, emphasizing its 1,000+ APIs and 28 million daily record exchanges, is the same kind of voluntary-compliance signaling that the Credibility Gap section documented from insurers: technically true, strategically selective, and insufficient to address the residual control rights that make the gatekeeper indispensable.

The Managed Care Carve-Out: When States Remove the Intermediary Instead of Regulating It

Every reform documented in this analysis assumes the managed care intermediary remains in the game. States regulate denial timelines. Federal rules mandate transparency. Courts compel discovery. Gold card programs exempt high-performing providers. But the intermediary itself, the managed care organization that sits between the patient and the care, survives each reform as the indispensable node through which payment flows. Indiana has begun asking a different question: what if the efficient response to an intermediary that adds negative value is not regulation but removal?

In March 2026, Indiana Governor Michael Braun (R) signed into law a change that will move nursing home patients out of the state's Medicaid managed care program after 100 days. The policy is narrow in scope but radical in structure. Rather than imposing denial-rate limits, appeal-turnaround requirements, or AI transparency mandates on managed care organizations, Indiana chose to extract the patient population most harmed by managed care denials from the managed care system entirely. Nursing home patients who remain past 100 days will be covered under traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, where the state pays providers directly and no intermediary can deny or delay authorized care. Nebraska had already implemented a smaller version of the same approach. By August 2026, the Health Care Association of Michigan was pushing for its own carve-out, with President and CEO Melissa Samuel citing "frequent denials, major payment delays and clawed-back payments" as the operational reality of Medicaid managed care for long-term care facilities.

The KFF analysis published August 13, 2026, provided the quantitative backdrop. Medicaid managed care organizations denied 14% of standard prior authorization requests in 2025, higher than Medicare Advantage's 12% and second only to the ACA Marketplace's 18%. But managed Medicaid has been, as McKnight's Long-Term Care News reported on August 21, "largely absent from national conversations about insurance practices that often prevent seniors and those with disabilities from accessing post-acute care." The asymmetry is structural: Medicare Advantage denial reform has bipartisan congressional attention, a Senate subcommittee with subpoena authority, and an OIG that audits 19 organizations per report. Medicaid managed care has none of these federal oversight mechanisms applied with comparable intensity. The 42 states that have adopted some form of Medicaid managed care, accounting for 29% of all nursing home Medicaid spending nationally, have outsourced both the payment function and the denial function to private intermediaries, and the resulting denials affect a population with even less capacity to appeal than MA enrollees.

The Indiana carve-out inverts the logic of every other reform in this analysis. Gold card programs exempt providers from PA requirements. State AI bans restrict the tools insurers use to deny. Federal transparency mandates force disclosure of denial rates. Each presupposes the managed care model and constrains its behavior. The carve-out presupposes nothing: it removes the managed care model from the equation for a specific population and a specific care setting. The managed care organization cannot deny what it does not administer.

The exit cascade on the insurer side is accelerating the same structural question from the opposite direction. On August 21, 2026, Becker's Hospital Review reported that Providence Health Plan was winding down its MA business after failing to reach a deal with a national carrier to maintain coverage. Providence joins Humana (600,000 members), Presbyterian Healthcare Services ($568M operating loss), Clear Spring Health (full exit), and Molina (prescription drug plan cuts) in the 2027 exit wave. A JAMA study found that 10% of MA enrollees had to disenroll from their plan heading into 2026 as a result of insurer exits. Providence's failure to find an absorption partner is the more telling data point: it means the exit cascade is not merely reshuffling enrollees across existing carriers but producing genuine coverage gaps that no incumbent wants to fill. The markets Providence is leaving are markets where the equilibrium denial rate does not generate sufficient margin to sustain operations.

Game Theory Concept
Vertical Separation as Disintermediation (Tirole 1988 / Williamson 1985)

Jean Tirole's analysis of vertical integration and separation establishes that the efficient organizational boundary depends on whether the intermediary's coordination benefits exceed its transaction costs. When prior authorization denials, payment delays, and clawed-back payments impose costs that exceed the managed care organization's contribution to care coordination, the intermediary destroys rather than creates value. Indiana's nursing home carve-out is the first state-level application of vertical separation to health insurance: the state determined that for long-term care patients past 100 days, the managed care intermediary's transaction costs (denial, delay, clawback) exceed its coordination benefits (network management, quality oversight), and the efficient response is to return to the direct payer-provider relationship that managed care was originally designed to improve. Williamson's (1985) asset-specificity framework predicts which populations will be carved out first: those with the highest per-patient costs, the least capacity to navigate administrative barriers, and the longest care episodes, because these are the populations where the intermediary's denial-based cost reduction is most valuable to the insurer and most harmful to the patient. Nursing home residents fit all three criteria. If the Indiana model produces measurable improvements in access, cost predictability, or patient outcomes, the carve-out logic extends to other populations where the managed care model's administrative overhead exceeds its coordination value: behavioral health (where the GAO found 0 of 100 denials met federal requirements), pediatric developmental services (where Optum's internal playbooks target 10,000 Medicaid children), and post-acute rehabilitation (where the OIG found 95% of appealed denials overturned). The game theory implication is that managed care organizations face a new competitive threat: not rival insurers but the absence of insurers, as states discover that for some populations, the cheapest and most effective reform is to stop playing the game altogether.

The Compensation Referendum: When Direct Democracy Becomes a Bargaining Chip

The Danger Premium section documented the number: 748:1. Stephen Hemsley's $60.95 million in total compensation, divided by the median UnitedHealth employee's $81,474. The industry comparison made it visible: every peer insurer CEO earns between 206:1 and 336:1. The shareholders approved the package. The proxy blocked a patient-impact vote. Representative institutions, the SEC's ordinary-business exclusion, the index fund's mandatory constituent problem, the proxy advisory firms' fiduciary framing, absorbed the compensation structure without disrupting it. California's healthcare workers attempted the one mechanism those institutions cannot absorb: the ballot initiative.

On August 1, 2025, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West filed the Healthcare Executive Compensation Act, a statewide ballot initiative that would cap total annual compensation for hospital and medical group executives, administrators, and managers at $450,000 per year, indexed at 3.5% annually. The proposal applied to both nonprofit and for-profit entities. By April 2, 2026, the campaign had submitted more than one million signatures to county registrars. The Attorney General issued the title and summary. Signature verification proceeded. The measure was on track for the November 2026 ballot. This was not SEIU-UHW's first attempt. It was their sixth.

The California Hospital Association responded not by opposing the measure on the ballot but by filing its own: a counter-initiative that would restrict healthcare unions from spending on state or local ballot measures without following member consent requirements, including annual notice of prior-year political spending. Both sides raised tens of millions of dollars. The CHA's counter-measure did not address executive compensation. It targeted the organizational capacity of the entity proposing the cap. The strategic logic was transparent: make the cost of pursuing the executive pay cap include the risk of losing the union's own political spending power.

On June 25, 2026, hours before the state qualifying deadline, both sides withdrew. The CHA pulled the union-spending measure. SEIU-UHW pulled the executive pay cap. CalMatters reported the deal as a mutual stand-down. CHA president Carmela Coyle praised it as "an important step in strengthening the health care system." SEIU-UHW president Lorena Gonzalez cited "the continued operation of hospitals in all areas of the state." Neither statement mentioned executive compensation. A separate SEIU-backed measure imposing a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to offset Medi-Cal funding cuts remained on the November ballot, unaffected by the withdrawal agreement.

The withdrawal illuminates a structural feature of healthcare reform that the rest of this analysis assumes but does not isolate: the difference between a credible threat and an enacted policy. The ballot initiative was never primarily a policy instrument. A $450,000 cap on hospital executive compensation would have affected not just insurer executives but system administrators, department heads, and physician-executives at academic medical centers. The operational complexity of implementation, the inevitable legal challenges under contract and takings clauses, the competitive disruption to physician recruitment in a state that already faces specialty shortages, would have consumed years in litigation before producing any redirection of dollars to patient care. SEIU-UHW's own six-attempt history suggests the organization understood this. The initiative's function was not to pass. Its function was to exist on the ballot, where it could impose costs on the hospital industry through campaign spending, reputational defense, and the possibility, however remote, of voter approval. The CHA's counter-measure confirmed the threat's credibility by responding with a symmetric threat rather than a substantive defense.

The $450,000 figure itself reveals the strategic framing. Hemsley's 2025 compensation was $60.95 million. The proposed cap would have represented a 99.3% reduction. CVS Health CEO David Joyner's $21.2 million would have been cut by 97.9%. Even Centene CEO Sarah London's $19.5 million, the lowest among the seven largest payer CEOs, would have required a 97.7% cut. The number was not designed to survive cost-benefit analysis. It was designed to be legible on a ballot, to compress the 748:1 ratio into a single figure that voters could compare to their own salaries, and to force the industry to spend resources defending compensation levels that cannot be defended in populist terms. The median California household income in 2025 was approximately $95,000. The proposed cap was 4.7 times that. The current median payer CEO compensation was 223 times that. The ballot initiative made the ratio the campaign.

Game Theory Concept
Credible Threats and Nash Bargaining with Outside Options (Nash 1950 / Schelling 1960 / Romer-Rosenthal 1979)

The California ballot initiative withdrawal is a textbook application of Nash bargaining with outside options, where the outcome depends not on either side's ideal policy but on each side's threat point: the payoff it receives if negotiations fail and the ballot measures proceed. SEIU-UHW's threat point was a ballot fight it had initiated six times, each time imposing reputational and financial costs on the industry. The CHA's counter-measure converted the game from a one-sided threat into a bilateral Nash bargaining problem where both sides faced losses if the measures reached voters. Schelling's (1960) analysis of credible threats explains why the withdrawal occurred on the deadline day: only a commitment device with a time-bound, irreversible consequence (ballot qualification) makes the threat credible enough to induce concessions. But the six-attempt history introduces a deeper dynamic: Romer and Rosenthal's (1979) setter model, developed to analyze school budget referenda, shows that the agenda setter's power comes not from the proposal itself but from the reversion point, what happens if the proposal fails. SEIU-UHW's reversion point was not $450,000 executive pay caps. It was the status quo with a demonstrated capacity to impose campaign costs every two years. The industry's rational response was not to defeat the measure (which would cost tens of millions and might fail) but to bargain it away by sacrificing a counter-measure the industry itself valued. The withdrawal was not a failure of direct democracy. It was direct democracy functioning as designed by the game theory: a mechanism for extracting concessions from concentrated interests that representative institutions cannot deliver, precisely because the concentrated interests have captured the representative institutions. The fact that six attempts produced zero enacted policy and zero change in executive compensation is itself the equilibrium prediction: the ballot initiative's value to the union is not passage but perpetual credible threat, and the industry's optimal response is perpetual negotiated withdrawal, not reform. The compensation structure documented in the Danger Premium section survives both mechanisms, representative governance (proxy votes, SEC exclusions) and direct democracy (ballot initiatives as bargaining chips), because the surplus it distributes to executives is smaller than the surplus the broader system distributes to shareholders, and shareholders control both channels.

The Rate-Filing Shield: When Regulatory Approval Becomes Judicial Immunity

Every mechanism documented in this analysis, the denial lottery, the enforcement gap, the phantom network, the complexity trap, assumes that some institutional backstop exists to challenge insurer behavior when regulatory oversight fails. The courts are that backstop. In August 2026, a federal judge in Virginia demonstrated what happens when even the courts refuse to look.

In 2017, Anthem and Aetna abandoned Virginia's ACA marketplace, leaving a large swath of Central Virginia with a single option: Optima Health, a subsidiary of Norfolk-based Sentara Health. A family of four paying $940 per month for Anthem's least-expensive plan in 2017 found themselves facing a $2,920 monthly premium for Optima's cheapest offering the following year, along with a $14,400 deductible. Charlottesville's ACA premiums became the highest in the nation. Three whistleblowers, Ian Dixon, Karl Quist, and Sara Stovall, filed a False Claims Act lawsuit alleging that Sentara, aided by actuarial consulting firm Milliman Inc., used its monopoly power to dramatically inflate premiums while absorbing federal premium tax credits to cushion consumers from some of the increase. The inflated premiums cost federal taxpayers an estimated $665 million in elevated subsidies. Under ACA medical loss ratio requirements, Sentara returned $99 million to policyholders, but $92 million of that was funded by CMS risk adjustment payments Sentara was legally required to accept, meaning the company recycled federal money through the regulatory system and back to consumers while retaining the premium structure.

The whistleblowers assembled an all-star legal team led by Rick Mountcastle, the former federal prosecutor whose pursuit of Purdue Pharma over OxyContin was dramatized in Hulu's Dopesick, along with two national law firms fresh off a $1.6 billion FCA victory against a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary. The Biden DOJ signaled intervention in December 2024, but the Trump administration withdrew in 2025, citing discretionary factors. When DOJ investigators met with Sentara, they discovered nearly 7,000 pages that the company had not previously disclosed, some of which turned up in a PowerPoint presentation. The court ordered the whistleblowers to proceed independently.

Chief U.S. District Judge Elizabeth Dillon never tested the truth of the fraud allegations. She dismissed the case with prejudice on grounds of the filed-rate doctrine, a long-standing legal principle holding that courts may not second-guess rates approved by regulatory agencies. "To find that fraud was committed," Dillon wrote, "the court must find that the premium rates approved by BOI were unreasonable. The filed-rate doctrine prohibits it from doing so." The Virginia Bureau of Insurance had reviewed the rates, even revisited them after the whistleblowers filed formal complaints, and again found them actuarially reasonable. That approval, Dillon concluded, placed the dispute beyond the authority of the courts. She rejected arguments that the False Claims Act should override the filed-rate doctrine or that whistleblower lawsuits deserve a special exception. "The Affordable Care Act does not explicitly override application of the filed-rate doctrine," she wrote. The whistleblowers confirmed they will appeal to the 4th Circuit.

The ruling exposes a structural vulnerability in every reform mechanism this analysis has documented. The entire enforcement architecture, from CMS fines to DOJ investigations to qui tam whistleblower suits, assumes that courts can evaluate whether insurer conduct was fraudulent. The filed-rate doctrine eliminates that assumption in the one context where it matters most: monopoly markets. When multiple insurers compete, the filed-rate doctrine is a reasonable restraint on judicial micromanagement, courts should not second-guess market-tested rates. But when a market collapses to a single insurer, the regulatory approval process loses its competitive benchmark. The state regulator approves the rate because the ACA requires rate review and actuarial certification, not because competitive dynamics constrain the rate to a reasonable level. The regulator's stamp becomes a legal shield, not a market validation. The DOJ can investigate, the whistleblowers can document, the consumers can file complaints, but if the court cannot examine whether the approved rate was inflated, none of those mechanisms produce a remedy.

The Virginia case is not an anomaly. Across the ACA marketplace, the number of counties with a single insurer peaked at 52% in 2018 and has remained above 20% in most years since. In every one of those counties, the filed-rate doctrine operates as a moat: rates are approved by regulators who lack competitive signals, and courts decline to look behind the approval. The Sentara case demonstrates the endgame: a 210% premium increase, $665 million in excess federal subsidies, a legal team that has defeated billion-dollar pharmaceutical companies, and a judicial system that says it cannot evaluate whether the rates were reasonable because a state bureau said they were.

Game Theory Concept
Time Inconsistency of Optimal Policy and the Commitment Trap (Kydland & Prescott, 1977)

The filed-rate doctrine is a commitment device that was optimal under one market structure and harmful under another. Kydland and Prescott's Nobel Prize-winning analysis demonstrated that a policy which is optimal when announced can become suboptimal when conditions change, but the commitment prevents adaptation. The filed-rate doctrine was designed for regulated monopolies (utilities, telecommunications) where a single provider operates under continuous regulatory supervision and the rate-approval process substitutes for market discipline. Transplanted into the ACA marketplace, where market structure can shift from competition to monopoly in a single year (as when Anthem and Aetna exited Virginia), the doctrine immunizes the exact behavior it was never designed to protect: monopoly pricing in a nominally competitive market. The game-theoretic mechanism is precise. In competitive markets, the regulator's approval adds a redundant check on market-tested rates. The filed-rate doctrine's judicial deference is costless because the market itself constrains pricing. In monopoly markets, the regulator's approval is the only check, and it operates without the competitive benchmark that makes rate review meaningful. The doctrine's judicial deference is now maximally costly because it eliminates the last institutional actor capable of evaluating whether the rate is reasonable. The policy cannot adapt because it is structural: the filed-rate doctrine does not ask whether the market is competitive. It asks only whether a regulator approved the rate. The commitment that was efficient when it was made, defer to regulatory expertise in rate-setting, becomes a trap when the market structure changes underneath it. The 4th Circuit appeal will determine whether the federal False Claims Act can pierce the filed-rate shield in ACA monopoly markets, but the broader pattern is already visible: every regulatory safe harbor documented in this analysis, from ERISA preemption to the ordinary business exclusion in shareholder proxies, shares the same time-inconsistency structure. The rules were designed for a market that no longer exists.

The Diagnostic Inversion: When Insurers Profit from False Positives

Every subsection in this analysis has documented the denial side of the extraction: insurers refusing to pay for care that patients need. The QuantaFlo case exposes the revenue side, and in doing so reveals a structural inversion of the incentives that Arrow (1963) assumed would govern health insurance markets.

In 2017, UnitedHealth launched a nationwide screening program using QuantaFlo, a device manufactured by Semler Scientific that clips a light sensor to a patient's fingers and toes to detect changes in blood volume. The device was marketed as a diagnostic tool for peripheral artery disease (PAD), a serious condition involving narrowed blood vessels that increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and limb amputation. PAD diagnoses trigger significant pharmacological and surgical interventions, and they add a diagnosis code to the patient's medical record that, in Medicare Advantage, increases the patient's risk adjustment score. Higher risk scores mean higher monthly payments from CMS to the insurer. The financial incentive is straightforward: each PAD diagnosis on an MA patient's record increases the per-member-per-month payment CMS sends to UnitedHealth, regardless of whether the patient actually has the disease.

The problem was that QuantaFlo could not reliably diagnose PAD. The device uses photoplethysmography, a technology that Medicare has explicitly refused to reimburse for vascular diagnostics since 1980. Medicare National Coverage Determination 20.14 states that photoplethysmography "is considered useful only in determining whether or not a pulse is present, and does not provide reproducible measurements of blood flow." When the FDA cleared QuantaFlo, the agency told Semler that the device did not perform an ankle brachial index (ABI) test and could not be called a "digital ABI." The CPT billing codes Semler marketed the device under (93922, 93923, and 93924) all require ABI testing. A clinical evaluation of QuantaFlo's diagnostic accuracy found that the device falsely diagnosed over 66% of the patients in the study: two-thirds of patients who did not have PAD were told they did.

In September 2025, Semler settled with the DOJ for $29.75 million and its former distributor, Bard Peripheral Vascular, paid $7.2 million, a combined $36.95 million resolution of False Claims Act allegations. Semler entered a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG. The whistleblowers, Robert Kane and Franklin West, who had filed the qui tam lawsuit nine years earlier in 2016, received approximately $6.5 million as their share of the recovery. The settlements resolved allegations of fraudulent Medicare Part B billing, the traditional fee-for-service Medicare program.

The Part C case, Medicare Advantage, remains open. The whistleblowers allege that UnitedHealth added false positive PAD diagnoses generated by QuantaFlo to patients' risk scores and collected inflated monthly payments from CMS. The DOJ declined to intervene against UnitedHealth, leaving the whistleblowers and their counsel at Walden Macht Haran & Williams to litigate what their lead attorney, Dan Miller, described as "potential billion-dollar fraud allegations against a behemoth like United" in "a David vs. Goliath situation." The case (United States ex rel. Kane and West v. Semler Scientific Inc. et al., C.A. No. 3:16-cv-1516J-20MCR, M.D. Fla.) is proceeding into litigation with hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars at stake.

The mechanism documented here is not an aberration. It is the logical consequence of paying insurers more when patients are sicker. In a traditional insurance market, the insurer loses money on false positive diagnoses: each unnecessary diagnosis leads to unnecessary treatment the insurer must pay for. Arrow's (1963) foundational theory of optimal insurance assumed this alignment, that the insurer's financial interest in minimizing unnecessary claims would produce an incentive to invest in diagnostic accuracy. Medicare Advantage's risk adjustment system inverts this incentive completely. A false positive PAD diagnosis on an MA patient's record does not cost the insurer anything in treatment, because the insurer controls the treatment authorization pipeline. The false diagnosis generates revenue from CMS, which pays a higher per-member-per-month rate based on the inflated risk score. The treatment that the false diagnosis would normally trigger can be managed, delayed, or denied through the very PA system this analysis has documented. The insurer captures the revenue benefit of the diagnosis while controlling the cost exposure through utilization management. The diagnostic tool becomes a revenue extraction mechanism: the less accurate it is, the more diagnoses it produces, and the more revenue the insurer collects.

Game Theory Concept
Adverse Diagnostic Selection (Akerlof 1970, inverted)

Akerlof's market-for-lemons model predicts that when quality is unobservable, markets drive out high-quality sellers. The QuantaFlo case demonstrates the inverse: when the buyer profits from low quality, markets drive out accurate diagnostics. In a competitive market for PAD diagnostic devices, an insurer operating under traditional fee-for-service reimbursement would select the most accurate test, because false positives generate claims the insurer must pay. In the MA risk-adjustment market, the insurer benefits from false positives (higher risk scores, higher CMS payments) and controls the cost of false diagnoses (through PA). The rational insurer selects the least accurate test that regulators will tolerate, because inaccuracy maximizes revenue per screening encounter. QuantaFlo's 66% false positive rate is not a defect from UNH's perspective; it is a feature. And the market structure ensures convergence: a device manufacturer offering a more accurate PAD screening tool would generate fewer diagnoses per encounter, lower risk-score yields per patient screened, and less revenue for the MA insurer. The accurate device would lose the contract to the inaccurate one. The market for diagnostic lemons runs in reverse: instead of low-quality goods driving out high-quality goods through consumer ignorance, low-quality diagnostics drive out high-quality diagnostics through purchaser preference. The $36.95 million settlement addresses the Part B billing fraud; the Part C risk-score inflation, where the financial incentives are orders of magnitude larger, is still being litigated against the nation's largest MA insurer. CMS pays roughly $500 billion annually to MA plans based substantially on the risk scores that devices like QuantaFlo inflate.

The Moral Injury Machine: When the Denial System Breaks Its Own Operators

The prior authorization system doesn't just harm patients and providers financially. It produces a specific, diagnosable form of psychological damage in the physicians forced to operate within it, and the resulting workforce attrition may be the system's most consequential long-term externality.

Physicians for a National Health Program released "Moral Injury in Medicine: The Human Costs of Practicing in a Profit-Driven System" in March 2026, a two-year study funded by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation that surveyed and interviewed 1,207 physicians. The findings quantify what clinicians had been describing for years: 47% say they often or always lack enough time for optimal patient care. 44% regularly recommend treatments they know patients cannot access because of insurer practices or systemic barriers. 35% report that administrative and insurer pressures to reduce costs directly affect their ability to provide the best possible care. 25% are considering leaving their jobs entirely because of this distress. The numbers don't describe workload stress. They describe a workforce being systematically forced to violate its own professional obligations.

The distinction matters. Drs. Wendy Dean and Simon Talbot, who first applied the moral injury framework from military psychiatry to medicine in 2018, argue that standard burnout interventions (resilience training, mindfulness, reduced duty hours) have consistently failed to slow physician attrition because they treat a systemic problem as a personal one. Burnout manifests as exhaustion and depersonalization. Moral injury produces guilt, shame, loss of meaning, and erosion of professional identity. One family medicine physician in the PNHP study captured it: "There's no amount of yoga that will make me less distressed about how my patients are harmed. My staff is harmed. I'm harmed by this system." KFF Health News documented the pattern across emergency medicine (Dr. Keith Corl, Brown University: "The real priority is speed and money and not our patients' care"), surgery (nurse practitioners retiring early after corporate buyouts cut annual exam time in half), and social work (Jamie Leavitt: "Often my job was impossible to do" because of insurance restrictions).

The PNHP report finds 41% of physicians report feeling complicit in structural racism perpetuated by the health care system, a number that connects directly to the disparity data in this analysis: if prior authorization denial rates and appeal outcomes track vulnerability rather than clinical need, as the KFF cross-market data shows, then physicians are not imagining their complicity. They are accurately perceiving the mechanism they are being forced to participate in. The system doesn't just harm patients through denials; it harms the people it conscripts to administer those denials, and their exit accelerates the provider deserts that compound the harm.

Meanwhile, a January 2026 JAMA Network Open study (Chopra, Hoffman, and Ryan at the University of Michigan) found that the MA enrollment explosion has created an entirely separate penalty distortion. Across 3,200+ hospitals, the exclusion of MA data from the Hospital Readmission Reduction Program has produced an unwarranted redistribution of nearly $300 million per year in readmission penalties. Because healthier patients migrate to Medicare Advantage (54% of seniors now, up from 29% in 2012), the remaining traditional Medicare cohort at hospitals with high MA penetration appears sicker by comparison, not because of anything the hospital did wrong, but because of selection effects the HRRP cannot capture. Hospitals treating more MA patients are penalized on their sicker traditional Medicare remainders, creating a financial punishment for operating in markets where MA is most popular. The penalty falls disproportionately on larger, nonprofit, teaching-oriented urban hospitals, the exact institutions most likely to serve vulnerable populations. CMS has issued a rule to incorporate MA data, but it won't affect penalties for several years.

These two studies describe the same structural dynamic from opposite ends: the physician surveys show the human cost of operating within a system designed to deny, while the HRRP analysis shows how the system's financial architecture punishes institutions for the enrollment patterns it creates. Both represent externalities that the prior authorization reform conversation has largely ignored. The moral injury data suggests that even if PA is reformed to zero denials, the workforce damage from decades of operating a denial machine may take a generation to repair.

Identity Dissonance as Endogenous Workforce Externality (Akerlof & Kranton 2000)

Akerlof and Kranton's identity economics posits that individuals derive utility not just from consumption and income but from conformity to their identity-prescribed behavior. Physicians enter medicine with a strong professional identity ("I am someone who heals"), and their utility function includes an identity component that rewards behavior consistent with that role. The denial system forces physicians into identity-inconsistent behavior (recommending treatments they know patients can't access, participating in gatekeeping they believe is clinically unjustified), generating identity dissonance that reduces utility independent of workload, compensation, or working conditions. This explains why burnout interventions fail: they address the consumption-side utility (rest, resilience, schedule flexibility) while leaving the identity-side utility loss untouched. The physician doesn't need more time off; they need to stop being forced to harm their patients. Exit is not a workload response; it is an identity-preservation response. The 25% considering departure are not overworked physicians who need a break; they are professionals whose identity utility has been driven below their reservation level. The workforce attrition becomes an endogenous externality of the denial system: the same mechanism that saves insurers money by denying claims destroys the human capital required to deliver the care that the denials are ostensibly gatekeeping. The system consumes the resource it purports to allocate.

The Criminal Pivot: When Denial Becomes Aggravated Assault

On June 8, 2026, Pennsylvania State Representative Emily Kinkead introduced House Bill 2611, which would create a new category of aggravated assault in the state's criminal code: if a health insurer's highest-ranking officer issues an adverse benefit determination of a medically necessary benefit that leads to serious bodily injury or death, that executive is "guilty of aggravated assault." Not the company. The person. In Pennsylvania, aggravated assault is a first-degree felony carrying up to 20 years in prison and a $25,000 fine.

"When insurance executives -- rather than treating medical professionals -- determine patient care, and a decision to deny care leads to serious harm or death, there must be accountability," Kinkead, a Democrat from Allegheny County, said in a news release announcing the bill. She had already established her criminal justice credentials: in April 2024, the House passed her resolution directing the Joint State Government Commission to study the entire Pennsylvania Crimes Code for provisions that are "duplicative, inconsistent, unenforceable, carries improper offense grading, or is outdated for modern society." HB 2611 is not a symbolic gesture from a legislator unfamiliar with criminal law. It is a targeted addition to the code by someone actively restructuring it.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on June 8, where it remains. It would not apply to TRICARE, Medicare supplement, short-term limited-duration, dental-only, vision-only, or other narrow-scope policies. But for comprehensive health insurance -- the kind that covers the 155 million Americans in employer-sponsored plans and the millions more in individual and Medicare Advantage markets -- the mechanism is stark: the CEO personally bears criminal liability for the outcome of the coverage decision.

The game theory matters because HB 2611 directly inverts the payoff structure documented in this analysis's Enforcement Gap section. CMS fined 14 insurers a total of $1.54 million in Contract Year 2025 audits. UNH's share was $48,869, or 0.0006% of its quarterly operating earnings. This analysis applied Becker's (1968) framework to demonstrate that the penalty fell below the indifference threshold: the expected cost of non-compliance was measured in fractions of a cent per incorrectly denied claim. The rational insurer treated the fine as an operating expense. HB 2611 proposes to solve the Becker problem by changing the unit of analysis from the firm to the individual. Prison time cannot be externalized to shareholders. It cannot be amortized across quarterly earnings. It cannot be offset by MCR improvement. It sits in the CEO's personal payoff matrix at negative infinity: no expected profit from a denial can exceed the expected disutility of incarceration. Polinsky and Shavell's (2000) extension of Becker showed that optimal enforcement requires penalties the target believes will actually be imposed. A $48,869 fine lacks credibility. A 20-year prison sentence does not.

The connection to the Thompson shooting is not subtext. HB 2611 was introduced in the same state where Luigi Mangione was arrested. Pennsylvania is also the state where Aetna was fined $550,000 for behavioral health parity violations, where the state legislature had already been studying criminal code reform under Kinkead's direction, and where the public mood around insurer accountability had been shaped by months of national attention to denial practices. The bill is the legislative formalization of the same impulse that produced the shooting: the belief that the people making denial decisions should personally bear the consequences. Thompson's death and HB 2611 represent opposite poles of the same feedback mechanism -- one extralegal, one institutional -- both targeting the individual decision-maker rather than the corporate entity.

The bill's structural logic also maps onto the danger premium analysis documented in the executive compensation section. This analysis showed that Hemsley's $60.95 million package included a compensating differential for endogenous assassination risk. HB 2611 adds a second source of personal risk: criminal prosecution. If both channels are active simultaneously, the CEO position prices in physical danger from the public and legal danger from the state, creating a compound risk premium that further inflates the cost of the denial model. The question is whether the compensation required to attract executives willing to bear both risks eventually exceeds the profit generated by the denial system itself. Lazear and Rosen's (1981) tournament theory predicts that the prize at the top of the corporate hierarchy must compensate for all risks of holding the position. If criminal liability is added to assassination risk, the tournament prize escalates -- or the applicant pool contracts to individuals whose discount rate on both risks is unusually high, selecting for exactly the type of decision-maker least likely to reform the system.

HB 2611 has not advanced beyond committee referral, and its prospects in a divided Pennsylvania legislature are uncertain. But legislative proposals do not need to pass to alter behavior. Shavell's (1986) analysis of individual versus enterprise liability showed that the mere credibility of personal liability changes the target's calculations even before enforcement begins. Oscar Health's proxy already cited "the current climate and security risk profile for executives in the health insurance industry" to justify $361,000 in security spending for its CEO. If state legislatures begin attaching criminal penalties to the same decisions, the D&O insurance market, the executive recruiting market, and the board governance market will price in the risk regardless of whether any prosecution occurs. The threat is the deterrent. The bill does not need to become law to become a variable in the game.

Personal Liability as Deterrence Escalation (Shavell 1986 / Polinsky & Shavell 2000)

The enforcement literature distinguishes between enterprise liability (fines imposed on the firm) and individual liability (penalties imposed on the person who made the decision). Enterprise liability works when the firm can monitor and discipline its own agents, because the penalty is transmitted through internal incentive structures. But this analysis has documented the opposite: UNH's board designed a compensation package that aligns the CEO's personal wealth with MCR reduction, the $60 million cliff-vesting option grant rewards denial-driven stock appreciation, and the governance apparatus that should constrain self-dealing was controlled by the actors it was meant to constrain ($237 million in insider stock sales, an internal audit shut down after discovering $200 million in unsupported Medicare billing). When the firm's internal incentive structure rewards the harmful conduct, enterprise liability cannot deter because the penalty is absorbed as a cost of doing business while the reward structure for the decision-maker remains intact. Shavell (1986) demonstrated that individual liability becomes the superior enforcement instrument precisely in this condition: when the agent's interests diverge from the social optimum and the firm cannot or will not correct the divergence internally. HB 2611 proposes to bridge the gap by making the CEO's personal liberty contingent on the clinical appropriateness of coverage decisions -- the one penalty that the corporate structure cannot absorb, redistribute, or insure away. Whether it passes or not, the proposal marks a phase transition in the deterrence escalation ladder: from voluntary pledges (2025) to transparency mandates (CMS-0057-F, 2026) to monetary fines (CMS audits, state parity penalties) to criminal prosecution of the individual. Each rung was reached only after the prior instrument failed to produce compliance. Becker's 1968 model predicted this sequence: when the price of non-compliance is below the indifference threshold, the only options are to raise the price or to change who pays it.

The Boarding Cascade: When One Denial Fills an Emergency Room

Every subsection in this analysis has documented harm inflicted on the patient whose claim was denied. But the denial system's most destructive externality may be the harm inflicted on patients who never filed a claim at all. A study published in JAMA on August 17, 2026, by the RESQUE-NET consortium (56 hospitals across 17 health systems) quantified a phenomenon emergency physicians have been describing for years: 23% of patients who have already been accepted for hospital admission wait more than four hours in the emergency department before an inpatient team assumes their care. Many wait 12 or even 24 hours. Patients over 65, those on Medicare, and those at hospitals serving large Medicaid populations are disproportionately affected. The Joint Commission has identified four-hour ED boarding as a critical patient safety threshold. Nearly one in four admitted patients exceeds it.

The chain connecting insurance denial to this crisis runs through a single bottleneck: post-acute discharge. The OIG's June 2026 review of the 19 largest Medicare Advantage organizations found that MA plans denied 65% of prior authorization requests for long-term acute care hospitals, 54% for inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and 12% for skilled nursing facilities. When enrollees appealed SNF denials, the plans overturned 95% in their favor. But most enrollees never appeal. The patient who has been approved for transfer to a skilled nursing facility but whose MA plan denies the PA cannot leave the hospital bed. The hospital bed that patient occupies cannot accept the next admitted patient from the ED. That ED patient boards, taking up a treatment bay that cannot receive the next ambulance. The ambulance that cannot offload goes on diversion, adding minutes to the response time for the next cardiac arrest or stroke in the community. A single post-acute PA denial propagates through the system like a pressure wave.

A study published in BMJ Emergency Medicine Journal in February 2026 quantified these propagation effects with precision that makes the externality calculable. For a typical 25-cubicle emergency department, each additional five medical boarders (20% of capacity) is associated with a 10-minute increase in ambulance handoff delay, a 52-minute increase in Category 3 ambulance response time, and a 12-minute increase in overall ED length of stay. These are not hypothetical projections. They are measured associations from operational data. Category 3 ambulances respond to conditions including chest pain, breathing difficulty, and abdominal pain with abnormal vital signs. A 52-minute delay in response to those conditions has a body count that is epidemiologically quantifiable but institutionally invisible, because the death certificate will list the cardiac arrest, not the PA denial three floors up that blocked the SNF discharge that occupied the hospital bed that filled the ED that diverted the ambulance.

The post-acute groups that bear the downstream costs have been explicit about the mechanism. The National Association of Long Term Hospitals stated in June 2026 that "when access to medically necessary LTCH care is delayed or denied, patients face longer recoveries and increased complications, and potentially worse outcomes." AHCA/NCAL's president called it "unconscionable that insurers are making frail seniors and their families jump through numerous hoops at a critical time for their recovery." Both organizations are backing the Medicare Advantage Improvement Act of 2026 specifically to address the post-acute PA bottleneck. But the hospital system is not waiting for legislation. Trinity Health piloted risk-sharing agreements with SNFs where hospitals guarantee 50% of the per diem for up to two days if the insurer ultimately denies the PA, accepting financial liability to break the discharge logjam. In a pilot of 50 patients, average hospital length of stay dropped 1.7 days per patient, and fewer than 5% of pending authorizations were ultimately denied. The hospital was paying to solve a problem the insurer created.

Starting in January 2027, the federal government will require hospitals to report ED boarding times through electronic health records, with public reporting on CMS's Care Compare site and, by 2030, financial penalties tied to boarding performance. The measurement infrastructure that will make the boarding cascade visible at scale is being built. The question is whether it will be designed to trace the causal chain back to the PA denial that started it, or whether boarding will be treated as a hospital efficiency problem disconnected from the insurer decisions that drive it.

Negative Externality Cascade Under Legal Constraint (Meade 1952 / Coase 1960)

Meade's (1952) analysis of "unpaid factors of production" identified cases where one economic actor's production function uses another actor's resources as a free input. The insurer's denial decision treats hospital inpatient capacity, ED treatment bays, and ambulance availability as costless inputs: the denial saves the insurer the cost of the SNF stay while imposing boarding costs on the hospital, delayed-care costs on other ED patients, and response-time costs on ambulance systems. Under Coase's (1960) theorem, this externality could theoretically be resolved through private bargaining if transaction costs were low enough. But EMTALA legally prohibits the hospital from refusing the externality: it must continue treating all arrivals regardless of capacity consumed by boarding patients whose discharge is blocked by PA denials. The hospital cannot negotiate with the insurer for compensation for the boarding costs because the boarding itself results from the insurer's unilateral denial decision, made without the hospital's participation and often without its knowledge until the patient's discharge pathway is already blocked. The legal structure creates an asymmetry that Coase's framework assumes away: one party (the insurer) can impose costs on another (the hospital and its other patients) without constraint, while the other party (the hospital) is legally obligated to absorb those costs without the ability to refuse. This is not a market failure amenable to Pigouvian taxation or Coasean bargaining. It is a structural transfer of costs from a regulated entity (the insurer, subject to PA reform) to a legally captive absorber (the hospital, subject to EMTALA), mediated by a patient who has no knowledge that their blocked discharge is filling an emergency room with other people's emergencies. The CMS 2027 boarding-time reporting mandate may make the externality measurable, but measurement alone does not create a bargaining channel. Until the insurer bears the downstream cost of its denial decisions, the cascade will continue to propagate through the system's most capacity-constrained nodes.

Section IV

The Moral Calculus: Statistical Lives Saved

How many people are alive today because of what happened on December 4, 2024?

The question sounds provocative, but the methodology is standard. The U.S. federal government routinely prices the reduction of mortality risk when evaluating policy. The Department of Transportation's current Value of a Statistical Life is $14.2 million per person in 2025 dollars. Every highway speed limit, every air quality regulation, every drug approval timeline contains this calculation implicitly. The question here is whether the post-shooting reforms reduced mortality risk enough to be quantified.

Even under conservative assumptions, the answer is yes.

The Verified Inputs

Six bodies of peer-reviewed evidence anchor this estimate:

1. Reform volume. 6.5 million prior authorization requirements eliminated industry-wide between June 2025 and April 2026 (AHIP/BCBSA pledge tracking, verified by AJMC). UnitedHealthcare committed to an additional 30% reduction in 2026 and separately eliminated PA for approximately 1,500 rural hospitals and two-thirds of pediatric PA requirements for members under 18. These UNH-specific cuts are additive to the 6.5 million industry total, but their exact volume has not been disclosed publicly.

2. Denial mortality. At Memorial Sloan Kettering in 2023, researchers analyzed 1,752 prior authorization requests for cancer pain medication. Of the 62 patients whose requests were denied, 3 died within two weeks (4.8%). Another 14 ended up in the emergency department (22.6%) and 4 transitioned to hospice (6.5%). The study's lead author, Dr. Fumiko Chino, called these numbers, derived from one of the best-resourced cancer centers in the world, a "gross underestimate of the human impact." Notably, 89.4% of all requests were ultimately approved, suggesting most denials function as delay mechanisms rather than clinical gatekeeping. The OIG's June 2026 data corroborated this pattern at scale: across 19 Medicare Advantage organizations, 95% of appealed skilled nursing facility denials were overturned. naviHealth's overturn rate was 97%.

3. Treatment delay mortality. A Cleveland Clinic analysis of 3,672,561 cancer patients found that each week of delayed treatment initiation increased absolute mortality risk by 1.2% to 3.2%, depending on cancer type and stage. For stage I non-small cell lung cancer, five-year survival dropped from 56% to 43% when treatment was delayed more than six weeks. A separate BMJ systematic review of 1,272,681 patients across 34 studies found a 6-8% mortality increase per four-week surgical delay for breast and colorectal cancers.

4. Physician-reported harm. The AMA's 2024 survey of 1,000 practicing physicians found: 24% reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event (hospitalization, permanent injury, or death). 78% said patients abandon treatment due to PA barriers. Practices spend an average of 12 hours per week processing 43 prior authorizations, with 65% of physicians waiting at least one business day for a decision. An updated AMA survey cited by the Medical Society of the State of New York in May 2026 found the numbers worsening: 26% of physicians now report PA has resulted in a serious adverse event, 95% say it delays access to necessary care (up from 94%), and 79% report patients abandon treatment because of authorization challenges (up from 78%).

5. Patient-reported harm. The Commonwealth Fund's 2025 Affordability Survey of 4,589 privately insured adults found: 28% of those denied prior authorization reported their health problem worsened. 41% experienced a care delay. 21% of all respondents reported at least one denial in the past year.

6. Denial rates. Prior authorization denial rates range from approximately 4.2% (Anthem) to 13% (CVS/Aetna), with an estimated industry average near 10%.

The Calculation

Start with the reform volume: 6.5 million eliminated PA requirements. At an average 10% denial rate, approximately 650,000 denials did not occur. The question is what fraction of those avoided denials would have resulted in death.

Three estimates, ranging from conservative to aggressive. All are Fermi estimates, transparent in their assumptions and wide in their uncertainty. This is health economics, not epidemiology.

Conservative Estimate
500 to 1,500 Statistical Lives Saved Per Year

Apply only the delay-elimination effect. Even approved PAs cause delay: 65% of physicians report waiting at least one business day, 26% report three or more days. For the estimated 15-20% of eliminated PAs involving cancer or cardiovascular treatment (roughly 975,000 to 1.3 million procedures), eliminating even a one-week delay yields measurable mortality reduction. Using the lower bound of the Cleveland Clinic coefficient (1.2% per week): 975,000 × 1.2% = 11,700 patients whose mortality risk decreased by approximately one percentage point. Scaling for the fraction where delay was genuinely life-threatening: 500 to 1,500 lives.

Central Estimate
2,000 to 5,000 Statistical Lives Saved Per Year

Include denial mortality. 650,000 avoided denials. The MSK data shows 4.8% two-week mortality among denied cancer patients, but most denials involve less immediately lethal conditions. Adjusting to a cross-condition average of 0.3% to 0.8% yields 1,950 to 5,200 lives from denial elimination alone. Add the treatment abandonment pathway: the AMA reports that 78% of physicians say patients abandon treatment due to PA. If 10% of the 6.5 million affected patients would have abandoned treatment, and 2% of those abandonment events involved conditions with meaningful mortality risk, that adds another 1,300 lives (with substantial overlap with the denial count). Net central range: 2,000 to 5,000 lives.

Upper Bound
8,000 to 12,000 Statistical Lives Saved Per Year

Include secondary cascade effects. The Commonwealth Fund's 28% "worsened health" figure encompasses chronic disease progression that manifests as excess mortality over a one-to-five year horizon. Apply a 0.5% mortality multiplier to the 182,000 patients (28% of 650,000 denied) whose conditions worsened: 910 additional deaths over the follow-up period. Add the behavioral chilling effect: patients who avoided seeking care entirely due to prior PA experience (not captured in reform data). Incorporate the full AMA signal (7% of physicians reporting at least one patient death from PA). Upper bound: 8,000 to 12,000 statistical lives per year. This estimate carries the widest uncertainty and should be treated as a ceiling, not a point estimate.

Under the conservative estimate, the implied value of statistical lives saved ($7 to $21 billion) represents a significant fraction of the market capitalization destroyed at a single company. Under the central estimate ($28 to $71 billion), the value approaches or exceeds shareholder losses across the insurance sector. Under the upper bound ($114 to $170 billion), the figure is comparable to UNH's total market cap decline.

For scale: the Lancet estimates that rolling back Medicaid expansion would cause 14,660 excess deaths per year among working-age adults. A July 2026 JAMA Health Forum microsimulation (Basu et al., Waymark/UNC) projects an additional 2,284 deaths and 145,000+ preventable hospitalizations annually from the specific OBBBA mechanisms (work requirements, verification frequency, reduced federal matching). The central estimate for lives saved by post-Thompson PA reform is roughly one-fifth to one-third of the Lancet figure, achieved through voluntary and regulatory reform triggered in under 18 months. But the reforms and the contraction are operating simultaneously: the PA reforms save lives among the covered population while the Medicaid and ACA contractions project mortality among the population being excluded. The two vectors are measured by different studies, governed by different statutes, and reported in different datasets.
